title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: The 2016 FiveThirtyEight presidential model was mostly the same as the 2008 and 2012 models, with no candidate-specific variables for Trump or Clinton, new procedures for third-party candidates such as Gary Johnson, and three published versions: polls-plus (polls plus economic index), polls-only, and a now-cast, which is polls-only told the election is today.
evidence_quote: There’s no special variable for Republican Donald Trump or Democrat Hillary Clinton.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: The 2016 model's probabilities are based on the historical accuracy of election polls since 1972, effectively 11 elections from 1972 to 2012.
quantities: elections in calibration = 11 elections (1972-2012)
evidence_quote: Our probabilities are based on the historical accuracy of election polls since 1972.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: All versions of the model gain more information from state polls than from national polls. National polls mainly help calibrate the trend-line and house-effects adjustments and contribute, with state polls, to the national popular vote estimate.
evidence_quote: All versions of our models gain more information from state polls than from national polls.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: 2016 poll inclusion excluded polls conducted directly for a presidential campaign or affiliated PAC or super PAC, as well as banned pollsters. Polls are listed by polling company, not media sponsor. Version priority was likely voters, then registered voters, then adults; the version including Johnson was preferred; other ambiguous cases, such as multiple LV models, are averaged.
evidence_quote: We prioritize polls as follows: likely voters > registered voters > all adults.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: State weighted averages in 2016 used pollster rating, sample size with diminishing returns, and recency, which matters less early and more later. Repeat polls by the same firm give the latest the most weight without discarding older ones.
evidence_quote: Recency, which is less important early in the campaign and becomes more important later on.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: Historically Republicans gain a net 1 to 2 points in likely-voter polls versus RV or adult polls. Polls-plus started with this default; polls-only and now-cast used zero. Both update from paired polls, and LV polls show fewer undecideds.
quantities: historical R gain in LV polls = 1 to 2 percentage points net (pre-2016)
evidence_quote: Historically, Republicans gain slightly in likely voter polls — a net of 1 to 2 percentage points

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: In 2016 polls-plus assumed a modern convention bounce of 3 to 4 points and subtracted it from a candidate's polls right after the convention. Polls-plus and polls-only also down-weighted polls taken immediately after conventions, while the now-cast weighted them fully.
quantities: modern convention bounce = 3 to 4 percentage points (2016 polls-plus)
rationale: Bounces are large but fleeting.
evidence_quote: Polls-plus assumes that a modern-day convention bounce is worth 3 to 4 percentage points.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: The omitted third-party ('missing Johnson') adjustment estimates how much support the third-party candidate draws from the major candidates rather than undecideds: relatively little from undecideds. It assumes he draws equally from both, and it varies by state, taking more where he is stronger.
evidence_quote: The adjustment assumes Johnson takes his support from Clinton and Trump equally.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: The 2016 trend-line adjustment detects movement by comparing successive editions of the same poll (same pollster and geography), separately for each candidate, then fits a loess regression trend line and adjusts older polls by the subsequent trend, scaled by state elasticity. Empirically, more smoothing early and less smoothing late works best.
rationale: Same-poll comparisons remove a lot of noise.
evidence_quote: Empirically, using more smoothing early in the race and less smoothing late in the race works best.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: House effects are found by comparing a firm's polls with others of the same state. A proportion is subtracted that depends on how many polls the firm has; for example, a 3-point lean might yield a 1-point adjustment with few polls and 2.8 with dozens. They are computed separately per candidate, so a firm with few undecideds can lean toward both. The reference 'average poll' is weighted by pollster rating.
quantities: example adjustment, few polls = 1 point of 3 (illustration); example adjustment, dozens of polls = 2.8 points of 3 (illustration)
evidence_quote: The model might subtract only 1 point from Clinton if the firm has conducted only a few polls. But it might subtract 2.8 points if the firm has conducted dozens of polls

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: Third-party candidates tend to underperform their early polls, though not necessarily their late ones, because some early third-party supporters are undecideds using them as placeholders. Polls-plus reallocated some early third-party support to undecided; polls-only and now-cast did not.
evidence_quote: Historically, third-party candidates tend to underperform their early polls.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: Undecided voters are split evenly between the major-party candidates, which empirically works better in presidential races than a proportional split. Late in the race the third-party candidate also gets a share, and a small 'other' share is reserved in states expected to have four or more candidates on the ballot.
evidence_quote: Undecided voters are split evenly between the major-party candidates. Empirically, an even split works better for presidential races than a proportional split.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: The national popular vote is projected from a blend of top-down (national polls) and bottom-up (state polls controlled for PVI) estimates, with considerably more weight on bottom-up, which has been more accurate. It is held constant when demographic regressions are applied, which are recalibrated so they only redistribute the vote across states.
rationale: Regressions should create a realistic distribution, not shift the national total.
evidence_quote: The model uses a blend of both approaches but puts considerably more weight on the state polls strategy, which has been more accurate historically.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: FiveThirtyEight's 2016 PVI weighted the most recent presidential election (2012) 75 percent and the prior (2008) 25 percent, unlike Cook's equal weights. It adjusted for home-state effects: presidential candidates historically perform a net 7 points better at home and VP candidates about 2 points.
quantities: recent election weight = 75 percent (2016 PVI); presidential home-state effect = 7 percentage points net (historical); VP home-state effect = about 2 percentage points (historical)
evidence_quote: Historically, presidential candidates perform a net of 7 percentage points better in their home states.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: Three regression strategies were blended. Strategy 1, pure PVI: national margin plus PVI. Strategy 2, a regional regression of the adjusted polling average on PVI plus four region dummies, with split states such as Maryland half South and half Northeast; historically the most effective. Strategy 3, a demographic regression on PVI plus shares Black, Hispanic, Asian, non-Christian, evangelical, Mormon and college graduates plus a 12-month state economic index, with spurious-variable removal. Polls-plus blended them 30/50/20; polls-only and now-cast used 70/30 of strategies 2 and 3.
quantities: polls-plus blend (PVI/regional/demographic) = 30/50/20 percent (2016); polls-only blend (regional/demographic) = 70/30 percent (2016)
rationale: Hedging complex methods with simpler ones reduces overfitting.
evidence_quote: The polls-plus model uses a 30/50/20 blend of strategies 1, 2 and 3.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: The state polling average is blended with the regression estimate, which gets more weight early and with less polling: 100 percent with no polls, while polls can get up to 95 percent late in an abundantly polled state. Polls-only and now-cast give the regression slightly less weight.
quantities: max poll weight late = 95 percent (2016)
evidence_quote: The polling average can get as much as 95 percent of the weight late in the race in a state with abundant polling.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: The 2016 economic index averaged six normalized, equally weighted variables over the past year: nonfarm payrolls, industrial production, real personal income, PCE, CPI and the S&P 500. In the fundamentals forecast, an index 0.5 standard deviations above average implied the incumbent party winning nationally by 4 to 5 points. An elected-incumbent variable was neutral in 2016.
quantities: national margin per 0.5 SD economy = 4 to 5 percentage points (2016 fundamentals)
evidence_quote: if the economic index was 0.5 standard deviations above average, it would have the incumbent party winning by 4 to 5 percentage points nationally.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: In late June 2016, polls-plus gave fundamentals 35 to 40 percent of the weight, declining to zero by Election Day. The fundamentals weight is constrained against overfitting using a calculation derived from Lauderdale and Linzer (2014).
quantities: fundamentals weight late June = 35-40 percent (2016 polls-plus)
rationale: Fundamentals forecasts are prone to overfitting.
evidence_quote: Because fundamentals forecasts are subject to overfitting, the weight assigned to the fundamentals is constrained, based on a calculation derived from a 2014 paper by Lauderdale and Linzer .)

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: In 2016, elasticity scores were calculated from 2012 CCES individual-level voting records and 2008 state exit polls. Swingy states like New Hampshire have homogeneous moderate voters; Mississippi is bifurcated and inelastic; one-party-dominant states also swing less. National shifts are applied scaled by elasticity.
evidence_quote: Elasticity scores are calculated from individual-level voting records from the Cooperative Congressional Election Study (2012) and state-by-state exit polls (2008).

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: The 2016 national error magnitude grew with time until the election, the number of undecided voters and the third-party vote. National error is applied to every state about equally, subject to elasticity.
evidence_quote: The magnitude of the national error is based upon: The amount of time until the election (more time = more error); the number of undecided voters (more undecideds = more error); and the number of third-party voters

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: Demographic and regional error in 2016 was simulated by randomly varying the vote among groups in a file of more than 100,000 voters built from exit polls and CCES, using religion, race, region, party ID and college education. This produces correlation matrices, for example a high Wisconsin-Minnesota correlation.
quantities: voter file size = more than 100,000 voters (exit polls + CCES)
evidence_quote: The simulations are conducted from a file of more than 100,000 voters, built from the exit polls and CCES.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: State-specific error is larger when a state has fewer polls, when polls and the demographic regression disagree (e.g. Utah 2016), and when the state has a smaller population, since small states are more idiosyncratic and harder to poll and model.
evidence_quote: And states have more state-specific error when they have smaller populations.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: National, regional and state-specific errors are drawn from a t-distribution with 10 degrees of freedom, which turns normal-distribution odds of 50-to-1 into about 30-to-1 and 1,000-to-1 into about 180-to-1. It is used because only 11 elections from 1972 to 2012 inform the tails.
quantities: t-distribution degrees of freedom = 10 df (2016)
rationale: Small sample of elections; conservative tail assumptions.
evidence_quote: Specifically, they’re drawn from a t -distribution (with 10 degrees of freedom).

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: In 2016 the model ran at least 20,000 simulations per version per day, so changes under one percentage point may be simulation noise. Maine and Nebraska were simulated by congressional district. An Electoral College deadlock was assigned to Trump half the time, since Republicans controlled most House delegations, and to the popular-vote winner the other half.
quantities: daily simulations per version = at least 20,000 simulations (2016)
evidence_quote: If no candidate receives a majority of electoral votes, the model assigns the election to Trump half the time

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: The third-party (Johnson) vote is regressed on his 2012 vote, the 1980-2008 third-party vote (Perot/Anderson) and PVI. It has national and state-specific error but no demographic/regional error, since third-party candidates tend to rise or fall everywhere together. It is simulated with a combination of beta and t distributions, producing right-tailed outcomes. Ballot access is assumed where already secured, or where it existed in 2012 and the deadline has not passed.
evidence_quote: The model uses a combination of a beta distribution and a t -distribution to model Johnson’s vote.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: Tipping-point chance: in each simulation where the popular vote is close enough for the Electoral College to matter, states are sorted by margin and electoral votes accumulated until one candidate reaches 270; that state is the tipping point, shared in a 269-269 tie. Voter Power Index is each state's tipping-point chance divided by its share of national turnout; for example, a VPI of 3.5 means a vote there is 3.5 times as powerful as the national average.
evidence_quote: Tipping-point chance is the probability that a state will provide the decisive vote in the Electoral College.

title: A User’s Guide To FiveThirtyEight’s 2016 General Election Forecast
statement: Be conservative early and aggressive late: summer poll fluctuations are often noise or short-term bounces, so the model reacts conservatively, while late fluctuations are more meaningful and the model reacts more aggressively.
evidence_quote: Fluctuations late in the race are more meaningful, and the model will be more aggressive.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: Version history: House model launched Aug. 16, 2018; top-two primaries and Pennsylvania redistricting handling added Aug. 20, 2018; race pages Aug. 26; Senate Sept. 12, 2018; governors Oct. 17, 2018; 2020 update Sept. 18, 2020 with a Senate-only forecast; 2022 update June 30, 2022. House and Senate forecasts are generated by the same program, with House data informing Senate and vice versa, while House and Senate data inform governors but not the reverse.
evidence_quote: In fact, they’re literally generated by the same program, with data from House races informing the Senate forecasts and vice versa.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: In 2022 the model began multiplying funds raised from within a candidate's state by 5 when assessing fundraising edge, because a dollar from in-state was found to be about five times as predictive as an out-of-state dollar.
quantities: in-state contribution multiplier = 5 x (2022 onward)
rationale: Empirically about five times as valuable in predicting outcomes.
evidence_quote: We found that a dollar received from within a candidate’s state is about five times as valuable as a dollar received outside of it

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: In 2022 the model began blending its complex fundamentals formula with a simple alternative of partisan lean plus generic ballot. Tested on 2018 and 2020, the complex version slightly outperformed the simple one, but a blend beat either alone, so partisanship and the generic ballot gained influence relative to other fundamentals.
rationale: High partisanship era.
evidence_quote: a blend of the complicated and simple formulas does better than either one taken alone.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: In 2022 FiveThirtyEight increased the assumed correlation of race-by-race errors in congressional races, because polling errors were becoming more correlated even though correlation remains considerably lower than across states in presidential races. It also reduced the emphasis on sample size in poll weighting, consistent with a pollster-ratings change, and removed 2020 COVID-specific tweaks.
evidence_quote: Therefore, we’ve increased the degree to which race-by-race errors are assumed to be correlated in the model.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: 2020 congressional changes: fundamentals formulas adjusted so higher partisanship makes partisan lean more predictive and candidate quality less; house effects computed mostly from polls in the same state or district; Election Day error raised 20 percent for COVID and mail voting; CANTOR similarity including expected mail-vote share; Cost of Voting Index; Deluxe became the interactive default.
quantities: Election Day error increase = 20 percent (2020)
evidence_quote: higher partisanship is associated with the partisan lean of a state or district being more predictive of election outcomes, while it makes candidate quality factors (such as the candidate’s level of experience) less predictive.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: About three-quarters of the uncertainty in the House and Senate forecasts comes from local, race-by-race factors, unlike the presidential model where outcomes are extremely correlated across states. Governor races are even more localized, with partisanship a much weaker factor.
quantities: share of uncertainty from local factors = about three-quarters share (House and Senate, 2018)
evidence_quote: Nonetheless, about three-quarters of the uncertainty in the House and Senate forecasts comes from local, race-by-race factors.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: Share of House races called correctly, 1998-2016 training data, 100 days out and on Election Day: Lite 94.2 and 96.2 percent; fundamentals alone 95.4 and 95.7; Classic 95.4 and 96.7; expert ratings alone 94.8 and 96.6; Deluxe 95.7 and 96.9. In training, Classic miscalled 3.3 percent of House races versus 3.8 for Lite.
quantities: Lite Election Day accuracy = 96.2 percent (House 1998-2016); Classic Election Day accuracy = 96.7 percent (House 1998-2016); Deluxe Election Day accuracy = 96.9 percent (House 1998-2016); fundamentals-only 100 days = 95.4 percent (House 1998-2016)
evidence_quote: In the training data, Classic miscalled 3.3 percent of House races, compared with 3.8 percent for Lite.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: In 2018 FiveThirtyEight considered Classic its preferred version despite Deluxe being slightly more accurate, because borrowing others' forecasts felt like cheating; from 2020 Deluxe became the default display.
rationale: Part of the point is testing a rigorous algorithm against subjective forecasts.
evidence_quote: Basically, because we think it’s kind of cheating to borrow other people’s forecasts and make them part of our own.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: The midterm models use almost all polls, including partisan and campaign polls, which make up about half of House district polling. Polls are excluded for veracity concerns or known fakers, DIY hobbyist polls on platforms like Google Surveys, subsamples of multistate polls unless conditions are met, and MRP or other blended or smoothed outputs, because FiveThirtyEight wants to do the blending itself.
quantities: partisan share of House district polling = something like half share (2018)
evidence_quote: We want to do the blending and smoothing ourselves rather than inputting other people’s models into ours.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: Poll weights are set algorithmically from sample size, recency and pollster rating, never case by case. The algorithm emphasizes diversity, insisting on an average from at least two or three distinct firms in a race even if some polls are less recent.
quantities: minimum distinct firms = two or three firms (per race average)
evidence_quote: it will insist on constructing an average of polls from at least two or three distinct polling firms even if some of the polls are less recent.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: The midterm likely-voter adjustment is dynamic: it starts with a prior that LV polls slightly help Republicans, smaller in midterms with a Republican president, and updates as pollsters publish paired LV/RV results. FLIPR later replaced this with a more neutral prior.
evidence_quote: it starts with a prior that likely voter polls slightly help Republicans, but this prior is updated as pollsters publish polls that directly compare likely and registered voter results.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: The congressional timeline adjustment shifts a race poll by roughly two-thirds of the subsequent generic ballot change in congressional races and about half in gubernatorial races, modulated by the state's or district's elasticity. It is much more conservative than the presidential model's timeline adjustment.
quantities: timeline factor, congressional = roughly two-thirds share (2018-2022); timeline factor, gubernatorial = half share (2018-2022)
evidence_quote: by roughly two-thirds that amount in congressional races and half that amount in gubernatorial races, depending on the elasticity score of the state or district

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: Polls are classified as partisan by sponsor, not by who conducts them: a candidate, party, campaign committee, or a PAC, super PAC or 501(c)(4/5/6) mostly active for one party. Partisan polls get lower weight and a house-effect prior of about 4 points toward the sponsor's side, overridden if the pollster's results match nonpartisan polls over time.
quantities: partisan poll bias prior = about 4 percentage points (toward sponsor)
rationale: Partisan-sponsored polls are historically less accurate.
evidence_quote: the house effects adjustment starts out with a prior that assumes these polls are biased by about 4 percentage points toward their preferred candidate or party.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: CANTOR uses a k-nearest neighbors algorithm on demographic, geographic and political factors to find similar districts and states; districts can be compared with states. Stage one guesses what polls would show from partisan lean and incumbency, e.g. Republican incumbents polling poorly where polled suggests vulnerability elsewhere. Stage two adjusts by similarity scores. Projections are corrected for selection bias, since unpolled districts tend to be less competitive. Governor races do not feed CANTOR for House and Senate, but House and Senate feed governors.
rationale: Impute polls for unpolled races.
evidence_quote: It uses a k-nearest neighbors algorithm to identify similar congressional districts and states based on a variety of demographic, geographic and political factors.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: In competitive House races with incumbents, the fundamentals that best predicted results, in roughly declining order, were: (1) the incumbent's previous margin, adjusted for the national environment and the prior opponent; (2) the generic ballot; (3) fundraising share of individual contributions; (4) partisan lean; (5) congressional approval; (6) scandals involving either candidate; (7) the incumbent's roll-call party loyalty over the past three Congresses, with mavericks outperforming; (8) the challenger's elected experience. The analysis focused on competitive races.
evidence_quote: In competitive House districts with incumbents, the following factors have historically best predicted election results, in roughly declining order of importance:

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: The 2018 FiveThirtyEight partisan lean formula gives 50 percent weight to the 2016 presidential election, 25 percent to 2012, and 25 percent to state legislative elections, the same structure Silver Bulletin used in 2026.
quantities: latest presidential weight = 50 percent (2018); prior presidential weight = 25 percent (2018); state legislative weight = 25 percent (2018)
evidence_quote: In our partisan lean formula, 50 percent of the weight is given to the 2016 presidential election, 25 percent to the 2012 presidential election and 25 percent to state legislative elections.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: Senate fundamentals differ from House ones: the previous margin is less reliable because six years have passed; incumbency advantage is larger in smaller, more demographically distinct states; the model accounts for changes in state partisanship since the seat was last contested; and it uses a more advanced candidate-experience measure.
evidence_quote: the Senate model uses more sophisticated data in calculating the effects of incumbency.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: Gubernatorial fundamentals use the Senate factors except roll-call ideology, which is not used, and fundraising based on all contributions from the Campaign Finance Institute. The generic ballot is about two-thirds as predictive as for Congress and partisan lean about one-third as predictive: a state 12 points Democratic for Congress projects only about 4 points Democratic for governor.
quantities: generic ballot predictiveness for governor = around two-thirds ratio vs Congress (2018); partisan lean predictiveness for governor = around one-third ratio vs Congress (2018)
evidence_quote: A state that leans toward the Democrats by 12 points in a race for Congress would be predicted to do so by only about 4 points in a race for governor, for example.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: Open-seat races use the non-incumbency factors (generic ballot, fundraising, partisan lean, scandals, experience, top-two primary results where applicable) plus the previous congressional result, which is much less reliable than with an incumbent. Previous results are not used in open governor races. In 2018, Pennsylvania redistricting was handled by population overlap, and California and Washington top-two primary results were used.
evidence_quote: Previous election results aren’t used at all in gubernatorial races without incumbents.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: Classic and Deluxe compare their current national environment to a prior based on congressional elections since 1946, accounting for historic midterm swings and presidential approval; the prior phases out completely by Election Day.
evidence_quote: The prior is designed in such a way that it phases it out completely by Election Day.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: Average margin of victory by expert rating in House races since 1998: Toss-up 0 points; Tilt 4; Lean 7; Likely 12; Solid or Safe 34. The rating database covers House and governor races since 1998 and Senate since 1990. Solid ratings barely move projections unless other factors suggest the race should be competitive.
quantities: Tilt margin = 4 points (House since 1998); Lean margin = 7 points (House since 1998); Likely margin = 12 points (House since 1998); Solid/Safe margin = 34 points (House since 1998)

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: Expert raters are excellent at micro conditions but lag on the macro environment; for example they shifted sharply toward Democrats in early 2018 while the generic ballot was steady. Deluxe therefore blends the experts' relative ordering of races with Classic's data-driven national estimate, so Deluxe and Classic usually agree on total seats while possibly disagreeing on individual races.
evidence_quote: they tend to be lagging indicators of the macro political environment.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: The midterm models account for four error types: (1) local error, larger with less polling, conflicting indicators, or high elasticity, such as New Hampshire versus the bifurcated South; (2) regional and demographic error simulated with CANTOR similarity; (3) incumbency-driven error, for instance polls systematically underestimating Republican incumbents; (4) a uniform national swing, smaller for governor races. Error shrinks as Election Day approaches.
evidence_quote: Third, there can be error driven by incumbency status.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: The midterm models project turnout in each race from the eligible population and past midterm and presidential turnout, with competitive races producing higher turnout. Turnout matters for translating the national popular vote into seats.
evidence_quote: Projecting turnout is important in understanding the relationship between the national popular vote and the number of seats that each party might gain or lose.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s House, Senate And Governor Models Work
statement: FiveThirtyEight does not make ad hoc adjustments to individual race forecasts; everything is done strictly by algorithm.
evidence_quote: I should emphasize that we do not make ad-hoc adjustments to the forecasts in individual races.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The 2020 FiveThirtyEight presidential model differs modestly from 2016: more uncertainty components (economic uncertainty, news volume); an economic index extended back to 1880, adjusted for partisanship and with an economic forecasting component; extra Election Day error for pandemic turnout; COVID severity and mail-vote share as covariance factors; half the usual convention bounce adjustment; revised polling averages; a Cost of Voting Index adjustment; event handling for debates; and a single version with no polls-only, polls-plus or now-cast.
rationale: COVID-19 rather than 2016 justified rethinking.
evidence_quote: We’re running only one version of the presidential model this year.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: Polls in the 2020 presidential averages are weighted by sample size and pollster rating, and when one firm releases many polls each poll's weight is discounted so no pollster dominates.
evidence_quote: if there are a large number of polls from one polling firm, the weight applied to each individual poll is discounted so no one pollster dominates the average.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The presidential polling averages blend a simple weighted average with a more aggressive trend-line method. Early in the campaign they rely mostly on the weighted average, and in the final weeks mostly on the trend line, so averages become more aggressive as Election Day nears.
evidence_quote: So early on in the campaign, we rely mostly on the more conservative weighted average method, while in the final few weeks, we mostly use the trend line method

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The 2020 likely-voter adjustment shifted registered-voter polls toward what LV polls would show. Historically Republicans gain under LV screens, mitigated when the Republican is an incumbent; in 2020 paired polls showed Trump gaining about 1 point in LV versions.
quantities: Trump LV gain = around 1 percentage point (2020 paired polls)
evidence_quote: Generally speaking, this means that Republicans (such as Trump) gain ground relative to Democrats when applying a likely voter screen, although this effect is mitigated when the Republican is an incumbent.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The 2020 house-effects adjustment corrects polls that consistently lean toward a party or report more or fewer undecideds than others in the same state. Polls keep part of their house effect, since a small number of polls may reflect noise. House effects are computed mostly from polls of the same state, so a firm can lean differently in different states.
evidence_quote: In calculating house effects, the model mostly uses polls from the same state, so a polling firm could theoretically have a Trump-leaning house effect in one state and a Biden-leaning house effect in another.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The timeline adjustment shifts older state polls for movement in the race since they were conducted, based on national polls and polls of similar states; for example, an older Arizona poll is shifted toward Trump if national and Nevada polls moved toward him.
evidence_quote: Finally, we apply a timeline adjustment , which is based on a poll’s recency, and adjusts “old” polls for shifts in the overall race since it was conducted.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: After major events such as debates, the forecast blends the post-event polling average with the pre-event average, moving fully to the post-event average only after a week or two depending on the event, because event-driven shifts often revert. Candidates must sustain post-event gains to get full credit.
quantities: event blending period = a week or two days (debates, etc.)
rationale: Event bounces often fade.
evidence_quote: After a week or two (depending on the event) though, the model will fully use the post-event polling average because it no longer necessarily expects a reversion to the mean.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: At 2020 levels of polarization, the model expects a party to poll about 5 points better at the peak of its convention bounce, the day after its convention ends, fading fairly quickly, down from double-digit bounces in the past. In 2020 only half the usual adjustment was applied (virtual conventions) and back-to-back conventions largely cancelled: polls between the conventions were adjusted about 2 to 2.5 points toward Trump, and polls in the 2 to 3 weeks after the RNC less than 1 point toward Biden.
quantities: peak convention bounce = about 5 points (current polarization); 2020 adjustment between conventions = 2-2.5 points (toward Trump); 2020 post-RNC adjustment = less than 1 point (toward Biden)
rationale: Fewer swing voters under polarization.
evidence_quote: we would expect a party to poll about 5 percentage points better at the peak of its convention bounce on the day just after the conclusion of its convention

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The 2020 partisan lean index weights the past two presidential elections relative to the nation at 75 percent for 2016 and 25 percent for 2012, so states that trended between them may revert somewhat to the mean.
quantities: weight on most recent election = 75 percent (2016); weight on prior election = 25 percent (2012)
evidence_quote: In our partisan lean index, 75 percent of the weight is assigned to 2016 and 25 percent to 2012.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The partisan lean index includes a home-state adjustment for presidential and vice-presidential candidates. It is much larger for presidential candidates, larger in smaller states, and split when a candidate has two home states, e.g. Biden primary Delaware and secondary Pennsylvania, Trump primary New York and secondary Florida.
evidence_quote: The size of the home-state adjustment is much larger for presidential candidates than for their running mates.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The partisan lean index also adjusts for state elasticity, using a blend of each state's elasticity in 2008, 2012 and 2016, and in 2020 for ease of voting via the Cost of Voting Index. The latter was removed in 2024.
rationale: Lower voting barriers yield higher turnout and more Democratic votes empirically.
evidence_quote: The elasticity scores we’re using for 2020 are based on a blend of each state's elasticity in 2008, 2012 and 2016.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The modeled state estimate is an ensemble of three methods. (1) The 'rigid method': the national margin, imputed mostly from state polls, plus the state's partisan lean, e.g. Biden +5 nationally plus D+10 lean gives Biden +15. (2) A demographic regression fitting current state polls on partisan lean plus combinations of race, income, education, urbanization, religiosity and a COVID severity index: up to 180 regressions with collinearity and size limits, averaged with weights by adjusted R-squared and every regression getting some weight. (3) A regional regression on partisan lean plus four region dummies. The rigid method, historically most accurate, gets the majority of the weight, then demographic, then regional.
quantities: number of demographic regressions = as many as 180 regressions (2020)
rationale: Infer what polls would say in sparsely polled states from better-polled ones.
evidence_quote: The rigid method, which is the most accurate historically, receives the majority of the weight, followed by the demographic regression and then the regional regression.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The 'enhanced snapshot' for each state blends the state's polling average with the ensemble estimate, with poll weight depending on polling volume and recency. At the 2020 launch (Aug. 12) about 55 percent of the weight went to polls in the average state; in well-polled states near the end, as much as 97 to 98 percent. States without polls use the ensemble alone.
quantities: poll weight in average state at launch = around 55 percent (Aug 12, 2020); poll weight late in well-polled states = 97-98 percent (end of campaign)
evidence_quote: As of the forecast launch (Aug. 12), around 55 percent of the weight goes to the polling average rather than to the ensemble in the average state.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: National polls play relatively little role in the 2020 FiveThirtyEight presidential forecast beyond the trend-line adjustment. The national snapshot is the sum of the state snapshots weighted by projected turnout, based on population growth since 2016, voting-ease changes and current closeness, since closer states have higher turnout. National polls are not used in it.
evidence_quote: National polls are not used in the national snapshot; it’s simply a summation of the snapshots in the 50 states and Washington, D.C.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The FiveThirtyEight economic index, used since 2012, has six variables: nonfarm payrolls (jobs), real personal consumption expenditures (spending), real disposable personal income (income), industrial production (manufacturing), CPI (inflation) and the S&P 500 (stock market). Each is standardized to roughly equal mean and standard deviation over data since 1946, measured over the two years before the election with much heavier weight on roughly the final six months, and calibrated on vintage real-time data where possible.
quantities: number of economic variables = 6 variables (2020 index); lookback window = 2 years (heavier weight on last ~6 months)
rationale: Equal-weighted blend avoids p-hacking among many economic measures.
evidence_quote: All variables are standardized so that they have roughly the same mean and standard deviation

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The economic index is a z-score (0 is an average economy) extended approximately to 1880. Election Day values include 1932 -2.34, 1980 -1.71, 2008 -1.34, 1920 -1.52, 1936 +1.55, 1880 +1.37, 1984 +0.86, 1964 +0.70, 2012 -0.10 and 2016 +0.08. The economy explains only about 30 percent of the variation in incumbent-party performance.
quantities: 1932 index = -2.34 z-score; 2008 index = -1.34 z-score; variance explained by economy = around 30 percent (incumbent party performance)
rationale: Expanding the sample matters even with less reliable early data.
evidence_quote: In fact, we found that the economy explains only around 30 percent of the variation in the incumbent party’s performance

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The 2020 fundamentals forecast also accounts for incumbency status: an elected incumbent (Trump 2020, Obama 2012), a successor incumbent (Ford 1976), or no incumbent (2008, 2016). It also accounts for polarization from House roll-call vote distance; greater polarization is associated with closer margins and smaller effects of the economy and incumbency.
evidence_quote: Periods of greater polarization (such as today in the U.S.) are associated with closer electoral margins and also smaller impacts of economic conditions and incumbency.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The model forecasts each of the six economic variables to Election Day with some mean reversion, using recent stock market performance, which has some predictive power, and surveys of professional economists.
rationale: Conditions at forecast time may not resemble November.
evidence_quote: the model makes a simple forecast for each of the six economic variables, which accounts for some mean-reversion

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: Published schedule of weight on polls versus fundamentals by days until the election: 0 days 100/0; 5 days 97/3; 10 days 94/6; 25 days 89/11; 50 days 84/16; 75 days 79/21; 100 days 74/26; 150 days 65/35; 200 days 57/43; 250 days 47/53. At the 2020 launch it was 77/23. Fundamentals help the trailing side at the margin, and higher-elasticity states are shifted slightly more.
quantities: poll weight at 100 days = 74 percent (2020 schedule); poll weight at 50 days = 84 percent (2020 schedule); poll weight at 25 days = 89 percent (2020 schedule); poll weight at 0 days = 100 percent (2020 schedule); poll weight at 250 days = 47 percent (2020 schedule)
rationale: Fundamentals have more misses once data before 1948 is included.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: Silver considers fundamentals-only presidential models overrated: with many ways to measure the economy and few elections, it is easy to p-hack. Their telltale failure is fitting past elections well and predicting unknown ones poorly; one Q2-GDP model implied Biden would win nearly 1,000 electoral votes in 2020.
evidence_quote: it’s easy to “p-hack” your way to glory with these models because there are so many ways to measure “the economy” but only a small sample size of elections

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The 2020 model distinguishes four error types: national drift (change in the national forecast before Election Day), national Election Day error (final forecast miss), correlated state error along demographic or geographic lines, and state-specific error.
evidence_quote: With that disclaimer out of the way, here are the four types of uncertainty that the model tries to account for:

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: National drift is calculated as Constant x (Days Until Election)^(1/3) x Uncertainty Index. The cube root implies polls do not become more accurate linearly but sharply toward the end.
quantities: drift exponent on days = 1/3 power (cube root)
rationale: August is still early as far as polling goes.
evidence_quote: Constant x (Days Until Election)^⅓ x Uncertainty Index

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The FiveThirtyEight Uncertainty Index is an equally weighted blend of eight measures: (1) undecided share in national polls; (2) undecided plus third-party share; (3) polarization from House roll-call distance, which lowers uncertainty; (4) volatility of the national polling average; (5) volume of national polling; (6) gap between the polling snapshot and the fundamentals forecast; (7) standard deviation of the economic index components; (8) news volume, measured by full-width New York Times headlines over the past 500 days with recent days weighted more. In 2020 the overall level was about average relative to elections since 1972.
quantities: index components = 8 measures (equal weights); news lookback = 500 days (NYT full-width headlines)
rationale: With small samples and correlated measures, use an equal-weight blend rather than picking one or two metrics.
evidence_quote: we think it is better to use an equally-weighted blend of all reasonable metrics rather than picking and choosing just one or two metrics.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: National Election Day error uses a version of the uncertainty index that de-emphasizes components 6 to 8, which relate to future movement, and is calibrated on final-poll errors in elections since 1936 for sample size. Fat-tailed distributions are used for many error components, including Election Day error.
quantities: calibration start = 1936 year (final-poll errors)
rationale: Conservative given small samples; very accurate 2004-2012 polls may not be replicable.
evidence_quote: the calculation is based on the error in final polls in elections since 1936 , rather than solely on more recent elections.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: For 2020 the model increased national Election Day error, correlated state error and state-specific error by 20 percent, since pandemic primaries showed about 50 percent higher turnout variability and a 50 percent rise in turnout error is estimated to raise vote-share error by 20 percent. This COVID adjustment was removed in 2024.
quantities: error inflation = 20 percent (2020 COVID); turnout variability increase = about 50 percent (pandemic primaries)
evidence_quote: we increase national Election Day error, correlated state error and state-specific error by 20 percent relative to their usual values

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: In each of 40,000 simulations per update, the model first draws national drift and national Election Day error and applies them roughly uniformly across states, scaled by elasticity. It then draws correlated state errors as random permutations over demographic and geographic variables, and finally residual state-specific error.
quantities: simulations = 40,000 simulations (each update)
evidence_quote: the model first picks two random numbers to reflect national drift (how much the national forecast could change) and national Election Day error

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: Correlated state error is simulated over these variables: race (white, Black, Hispanic, Asian); religion (evangelical, mainline Protestant, Catholic, Mormon, other, nonreligious); partisan lean in 2016 and 2012; latitude and longitude; region; urbanization; median household income; median age; gender; education (bachelor's share); immigration (share of the voting-eligible population); COVID severity; and expected mail-vote share. Most end-of-campaign state polling error is assumed correlated with other states.
rationale: A Michigan miss is likely reflected in Wisconsin and Ohio.
evidence_quote: we estimate that at the end of the campaign, most of the error associated with state polling is likely to be correlated with errors in other states.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: States demographically resembling the nation have less polling error under correlated-error simulation, while outlier states are harder to predict; for example, underestimating Mormons barely affects national or Florida polls but could cause a huge miss in Utah.
evidence_quote: states that are outliers based on some combination of the variables listed above tend to be harder to predict.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: Residual state-specific error is relatively small and mainly a function of polling volume, larger in states with no polling, which is why unpolled Oregon had higher Trump odds than expected at the 2020 launch.
evidence_quote: This tends to be relatively small, and is primarily a function of the volume of polling in each state, especially in states that have had no polling at all.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The presidential model forecasts 54 jurisdictions: 48 states, DC, Maine's two congressional districts and Nebraska's three, with Maine and Nebraska statewide forecasts mostly the sum of district forecasts but also informed by statewide polls. Electoral College ties of 269-269 are reported as ties in 2020 rather than broken. Faithless electors are not modeled.
quantities: jurisdictions forecast = 54 jurisdictions (2020)
evidence_quote: In total, the model calculates a forecast in 54 jurisdictions

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: A 'major' third-party candidate, modeled explicitly as with Gary Johnson in 2016 or Perot in backtests, must be on the ballot almost everywhere, included in most polls, and usually polling in the mid-to-high single digits. 'Other' votes are predicted per state from the number of third-party candidates on the ballot, write-in rules, historical third-party share and competitiveness, since swing states give third parties fewer votes.
evidence_quote: We defined major as (i) a candidate who is on the ballot almost everywhere, (ii) who is included in most polls and (iii) who usually polls in at least the mid-to-high single digits.

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: The model forecasts the vote as cast, assuming reasonable efforts to let eligible citizens vote and count legal ballots and that electors go to each state's popular-vote winner; it does not model extraconstitutional interference. Its probabilities can still serve as a benchmark for suspicious claims, such as a candidate claiming a state where it gave them 0.4 percent.
evidence_quote: It does not account for the possibility of extraconstitutional shenanigans by Trump or by anyone else

title: How FiveThirtyEight’s 2020 Presidential Forecast Works — And What’s Different Because Of COVID-19
statement: FiveThirtyEight reports its models, including election forecasts since 2008, have been well calibrated over time, and its 2016 forecast gave Trump about 30 percent, higher than other models and markets, partly by detecting his potential Electoral College overperformance.
quantities: 2016 Trump probability = around 30 percent (final)
evidence_quote: Candidates who our models claim have a 30 percent chance of winning really do win their races about 30 percent of the time

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: The pollster ratings database includes polls conducted in 1998 or later with a median field date within 21 days of the election, for presidential general elections, presidential primaries and caucuses, and Senate, House and governor general elections. Special elections, runoffs, instant-runoff rounds, all-party primaries, and national presidential and generic ballot polls are included, even if they were not used in forecasts.
quantities: start year = 1998 year; window = 21 days (median field date before election)
rationale: 1998 is when multiple comprehensive data sources begin.
evidence_quote: They have a median field date within 21 days of the election date.

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Collection rules: missing sample sizes are estimated from the reported margin of error or the firm's other polls, with 600 as a last-resort default; only the likely-voter version is kept when multiple populations are published; multiple versions of one survey (e.g. with and without a third-party candidate) are averaged; tracking polls are restricted to non-overlapping dates.
quantities: default sample size = 600 respondents (last resort)
evidence_quote: As a last resort, we use 600 as a default sample size.

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Presidential primary poll exclusions: New Hampshire polls before the Iowa caucus; polls of later states before New Hampshire; polls whose leader or runner-up dropped out before the primary; polls where any candidate at 15 percent or more, or any combination at 25 percent or more, dropped out before the primary.
quantities: single dropout threshold = 15 percent (exclude poll); combined dropout threshold = 25 percent (exclude poll)
evidence_quote: We exclude primary polls if any candidate receiving at least 15 percent in the poll dropped out before that primary was held.

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Polls are attributed to the firm that conducted them regardless of sponsor, or to partnerships (e.g. 'Fabrizio, Lee & Associates/Impact Research'). Media companies with in-house operations are credited when they contributed the most methodological IP, which is why NYT/Siena is separate from Siena. Companies run by the same team with the same methodology are evaluated together.
evidence_quote: Our policy is to classify polls based on the pollster that conducted them, regardless of sponsorship

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Simple error is the absolute difference between a poll's margin and the certified result's margin between the top two finishers in the election, not the top two in the poll. A pollster's simple average error is computed as a root-mean-square error.
evidence_quote: This average is calculated using root-mean-square error .

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Simple Plus-Minus equals a pollster's simple average error minus the error expected from a regression on election type, the poll's sampling margin of error and days between poll and election; for example, 4.6 actual against 5.3 expected gives -0.7, where negative is better. Presidential general polls are historically the most accurate, primaries the least.
rationale: Some elections are harder to poll.
evidence_quote: We run a regression analysis that predicts polling error based on the type of election surveyed, a poll’s margin of sampling error and the number of days between the poll and the election.

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Poll error decomposes as Total Error = sqrt(Sampling Error^2 + Temporal Error^2 + Pollster Error^2). A 1,000-voter poll misses the final margin by only about 2.5 points on average from sampling error alone. Even with no temporal or sampling error, the average poll would still miss the margin by about 2 points from pollster-induced error.
quantities: sampling error, n=1000 = about 2.5 points (margin) (average miss); irreducible pollster error = about 2 points (margin) (average miss)
evidence_quote: the average poll would still miss the final margin in the race by about 2 points.

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Ratings use all polls in the final three weeks rather than only each firm's last poll. Late game-changers are rare; herding increases in the final days; some late movement is artificial, from response bias or bad turnout models; much voting is early (over 80 percent in Arizona's 2022 Senate race); and a larger sample improves confidence. Three, four or five-week windows give no significant differences, and ratings adjust for the slight advantage of polling closer to Election Day.
quantities: early/mail share AZ 2022 Senate = over 80 percent (example)
evidence_quote: But we feel strongly that evaluating a polling firm’s accuracy based only on its very last poll before an election is a mistake.

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Advanced Plus-Minus blends Relative Plus-Minus (performance against other polls of the same race) with weight n, the number of other firms polling that race, and Simple Plus-Minus with weight 3; for example, with six other firms, Relative gets two-thirds. Strength of competition is handled by iteration, as in sports power ratings.
quantities: Simple Plus-Minus weight = 3 weight units (vs n for Relative)
rationale: With many polls, judge relative to peers; with few, judge on absolute error.
evidence_quote: Relative Plus-Minus gets the weight of n , and Simple Plus-Minus gets a weight of three.

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Advanced Plus-Minus also adjusts for how many other firms polled the same race, because polls are more accurate when more are in the field (herding or selection bias). It rewards firms that poll neglected races and penalizes those arriving after a dozen polls. It puts slightly more weight on recent polls and adjusts for the higher volatility of election types such as presidential primaries.
evidence_quote: This has the effect of rewarding polling firms that survey races few other pollsters do and penalizing those that swoop in only after there are already a dozen polls in the field.

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Predictive Plus-Minus formula: PPM = [max(-2, APM + herding_penalty) x disc_pollcount + prior x 18] / (18 + disc_pollcount), where disc_pollcount discounts older polls. In 2023 the prior was 0.66 - 0.57 x quality + min(18, disc_pollcount) x -0.03, with quality = 1 if the firm is in the AAPOR Transparency Initiative or contributes to the Roper Center archive, else 0. APM is floored at -2, and the prior gets an effective weight of 18 polls.
quantities: shrinkage weight on prior = 18 effective polls (PPM formula); APM floor = -2 points (PPM formula); prior intercept = 0.66 points (2023); quality bonus = -0.57 points (2023); poll count slope = -0.03 points per poll (capped at 18)
rationale: Mean reversion toward a methodology-dependent prior.
evidence_quote: it is currently calculated as 0.66 – quality ⋅ 0.57 + min (18, disc_pollcount ) ⋅ -0.03.

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Past performance reflects more noise than signal until a firm has about 30 polls; below that, methodological standards are the better guide, and above it past performance should be favored. In every cycle evaluated, pollsters in AAPOR Transparency or Roper performed significantly better.
quantities: polls needed for track record to dominate = about 30 polls
evidence_quote: Our finding is that past performance reflects more noise than signal until you have about 30 polls to evaluate

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Senate polls from 2006 to 2013 showed methodologically poor pollsters improving their accuracy by about 2 points when strong polls were also in the field, evidence of herding. The herding penalty is half the difference between a firm's actual ADPA (average distance from the average of previous polls with median field date at least three days earlier) and its theoretical minimum ADPA from sampling error of its polls and the comparison average.
quantities: herding accuracy gain for weak pollsters = roughly 2 points (Senate 2006-2013); herding penalty factor = 0.5 x (min ADPA - actual ADPA); ADPA comparison lag = 3 days (earlier median field date)
evidence_quote: The herding penalty for each pollster is one-half of the difference between a pollster’s actual ADPA and its theoretical minimum ADPA based on sampling error

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: Predictive Plus-Minus is converted to letter grades from A+ to D-, with about 83 percent of firms in the B or C range. Banned firms, for fabrication or for trading in betting markets affected by their own polls, get an F, which no PPM value can produce. Firms with fewer than roughly 20 recent polls get provisional grades of A/B, B/C or C/D.
quantities: share of firms graded B or C = about 83 percent (2023); polls for precise grade = roughly 20 recent polls
evidence_quote: It takes roughly 20 recent polls (or a larger number of older polls) for a pollster to get a precise pollster rating.

title: How Our Pollster Ratings Work
statement: For retrospective accuracy, Silver recommends Mean-Reverted Advanced Plus-Minus. For predicting future accuracy, as forecasting models need, Predictive Plus-Minus is used, and letter grades are based entirely on it.
evidence_quote: our letter grades are based entirely on Predictive Plus-Minus.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: Silver holds that pollsters should not be excluded from polling averages on the basis of an ideological or political litmus test, such as their relationships with partisan media outlets. Exclusion, if any, should rest on methodology or track record.
rationale: Many pollsters hold strong political opinions and are friendly with operatives, and some poll for campaigns. Applying a political-relationship standard would wipe out dozens of pollsters and would likely be applied asymmetrically.
evidence_quote: I strongly oppose subjecting pollsters to an ideological or political litmus test. Look, there might be good reasons to exclude Rasmussen based on their methodology

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: Silver argues that pollster partisanship should be judged empirically by testing polls against actual election results. Pollsters' track records hold them accountable for any political bias that makes their polls less accurate.
rationale: Unlike most pundits, pollsters have track records that can be tested against outcomes.
evidence_quote: pollsters have a track record that can be tested against actual results. They can be held accountable for political bias that might render their polls less accurate.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: A pollster with a strong, consistent partisan lean relative to the consensus, such as Rasmussen's Republican lean, should be handled statistically through a house effects adjustment in the polling average rather than through exclusion.
rationale: Statistical adjustment corrects the lean while keeping the information in the polls.
evidence_quote: there are ways to adjust for that — statistical ways like a house effects adjustment, not ways that involve acting like you're the House Un-American Activities Committee.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: Rasmussen Reports has had strongly Republican-leaning results relative to the polling consensus for many years. Even so, its overall accuracy in 538's pollster ratings is roughly average, not poor, because polls in general considerably understated Republican performance in 2014, 2016 and 2020.
quantities: elections where polls understated Republicans = 2014, 2016, 2020 election years (Reason Rasmussen's R-leaning house effect did not hurt its accuracy)
rationale: Silver describes this as 'two wrongs making a right': Rasmussen's bias offset the industry's Democratic bias.
evidence_quote: Despite that strong Republican house effect, however, they've had roughly average accuracy overall because polls have considerably understated Republican performance in several recent elections (2014, 2016, 2020).

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: An accuracy-only pollster rating can reward a biased pollster whose lean happens to offset a systematic industry-wide polling error in the same cycles. Rasmussen's average rating is partly a case of its Republican bias cancelling the field's Democratic bias.
rationale: Two wrongs making a right.
evidence_quote: Rasmussen has had a Republican bias, but other polls have had a Democratic bias, so they come out of the wash looking OK? Yeah, probably.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: The FiveThirtyEight pollster ratings page shown in the article grades a pollster using polls conducted within 21 days of an election, based on each poll's median field date. The page offers views of accuracy across all polls and of directional error (overestimating Democrats vs. Republicans).
quantities: window for polls used in pollster grades = 21 days before election (Based on the poll's median date, FiveThirtyEight pollster ratings)

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: The FiveThirtyEight chart of Rasmussen Reports' polls (directional view) shows the distribution of poll errors skewed toward overestimating Republicans. Most dots sit right of the center line, with a long right tail including a couple of large outliers, while a meaningful minority overestimated Democrats.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: Silver argues it is bad practice to retroactively revise already-published data, such as removing a later-banned pollster from historical polling averages and pollster ratings, based on decisions made long after publication.
rationale: Retroactive revision makes the numbers less reliable as a historical record.
evidence_quote: It's bad practice to revise data that's already been published, based on decisions you made long after that data was published.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: Training or calibrating forecasting models on historical data cleaned with hindsight leads to overconfidence. Real-time data will contain edge cases and minor errors that would have been removed in hindsight but cannot be caught in advance, so error estimates from cleaned data understate live uncertainty.
rationale: Cleaned data neglects the challenges of handling new, messy data as it arrives.
evidence_quote: it can lead to overconfidence when using that data to train or build models. If you clean up a past data set based on information that wouldn't have been available to you at the time

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: A polling average needs a consistent, legible set of inclusion rules that can be applied to the hundreds of pollsters encountered over an election campaign. Silver includes pollsters he subjectively dislikes, politically or methodologically, for the sake of consistency.
quantities: number of pollsters encountered = hundreds pollsters (Over the course of a US election campaign); Silver's experience = 15 years (Years running polling averages and models)
rationale: Case-by-case decisions are extremely time-consuming mid-campaign. They are also highly likely to introduce the modeler's own biases, whether rooting for a political outcome or wanting the model to look smart.
evidence_quote: you need a consistent and legible set of rules that be applied to hundreds of pollsters you'll encounter over the course of an election campaign.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: Ad hoc, case-by-case exclusion of pollsters risks the modeler injecting bias, either toward a preferred political outcome or toward whatever will make the model look smart.
rationale: Subjective judgments are not consistent across pollsters.
evidence_quote: highly likely to result in introducing your own biases, whether it's the political outcome you're rooting for or whatever you think will make your model look smart.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: Silver criticizes the post-2023 ABC News/FiveThirtyEight approach under G. Elliott Morris. It threatened to ban Rasmussen from all aggregation and forecasting models, the polls page, historical averages and pollster ratings unless Rasmussen answered questions about its political relationships and detailed methodology. Silver calls this an ad hoc exclusion effort rather than a consistent standard.
quantities: response window given to Rasmussen = a day-and-a-half days (Just before a four-day summer weekend)
rationale: The methodological questions were nitpicks that could be asked of almost any pollster, such as Quinnipiac. They demanded more disclosure than pollsters typically provide.
evidence_quote: I think it's clear that the letter is an ad hoc exercise to exclude Rasmussen, not an effort to develop a consistent set of standards.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
statement: Silver views vague pollster methodology statements as normal and benign, such as weighting by 'age, race, gender, political party, and other factors'. Commercial pollsters may legitimately keep weighting algorithms proprietary, so missing detailed disclosure of randomization or weighting should not by itself justify exclusion.
rationale: Such disclosure goes well beyond what pollsters typically provide.
evidence_quote: a commercial polling organization would be within its rights to keep some of the details of its weighting algorithms proprietary.

title: Polling averages shouldn't be political litmus tests
