rationale: There is no point duplicating the work, but inclusion standards differ.
evidence_quote: we maintain a supplementary polling database of polls that we use that they don't, as well as a strike list of polls we delete from their data

title: How the election model handles a candidate swap
statement: Silver Bulletin removed SoCal Research polls, which 538 uses, under a longstanding Silver-era FiveThirtyEight rule against amateur/DIY polling.
rationale: Longstanding rule.
evidence_quote: We're now removing one pollster that 538 uses because it violates a longstanding rule from the Nate days of FiveThirtyEight of not using amateur/DIY polling.

title: How the election model handles a candidate swap
statement: The model includes placeholder dates for future debates, at that point one more presidential and one more VP debate. Scheduled future debates slightly increase model uncertainty because they are landmark events that can swing polls.
quantities: placeholder debates = 1 presidential, 1 VP debates (as of July 31, 2024)
evidence_quote: the presence of future debates slightly increases the amount of uncertainty in the model because debates are landmark events that can cause polling swings

title: How the election model handles a candidate swap
statement: Silver used Polymarket traders' confidence that a Harris-Trump debate would occur as a reason to keep the debate placeholders in the model.
evidence_quote: Polymarket traders are confident the debate will eventually occur

title: How the election model handles a candidate swap
statement: Model output on relaunch: Harris had a 43% chance of winning the Electoral College, up from 38% the day before on strong swing-state polls. Biden had been at 27% in the last pre-swap run, which Silver called probably generous.
quantities: Harris EC win probability = 43 percent (July 31, 2024); Harris prior day = 38 percent (July 30, 2024 relaunch); Biden last run = 27 percent (before dropout)
evidence_quote: a 43 percent chance of winning the Electoral College — that's already up from 38 percent yesterday

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: In its final step, after adjustments that turn polling averages into Election Day predictions, the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model simulates 40,000 election outcomes. These simulations produce the national and state topline predictions.
quantities: number of simulations = 40,000 simulations (each model run, 2024 presidential)
evidence_quote: we simulate 40,000 election outcomes. These simulations give us our topline predictions nationally and in each state

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: Conditional probabilities in the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model are computed empirically from the simulations. Among all simulations where a candidate wins a given state, the model counts the share in which that candidate also wins the Electoral College. For example, Harris won Pennsylvania in 22,448 of 40,000 simulations and the Electoral College in 20,539 of those, giving 91.5%.
quantities: Harris PA wins = 22,448 simulations (Aug 8, 2024 run; about 56%); Harris EC wins given PA win = 20,539 simulations (Aug 8, 2024 run); Harris P(win EC | win PA) = 91.5 percent (Aug 8, 2024); Trump PA wins = 17,552 simulations (Aug 8, 2024 run)
evidence_quote: We just look at all of the simulations where a candidate wins a certain state, and check how often that candidate won the Electoral College in that set of simulations.

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: The same counting approach extends to conditioning on several states at once. In the Aug 8, 2024 run, Harris wins the election 95% of the time when she wins both Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, and loses only 2% of the time when she wins all three Blue Wall states (PA, WI, MI).
quantities: P(Harris wins | PA and WI) = 95 percent (Aug 8, 2024); P(Harris loses | wins PA, WI, MI) = 2 percent (Aug 8, 2024)
evidence_quote: We can even extend this logic to get conditional predictions for multiple states.

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: The Silver Bulletin defines a contest's tipping-point chance as the probability that it gives the Electoral College winner their 270th electoral vote. Its Voter Power Index (VPI) is the relative likelihood that an individual voter in a state determines the Electoral College winner. A missing conditional probability means the candidate won that state in 0 of 40,000 simulations.
quantities: electoral vote threshold = 270 electoral votes (tipping-point definition)

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: Aug 8, 2024 tipping-point chances, with VPI in parentheses: PA 34% (8.1), WI 14% (6.7), MI 12% (3.5), GA 10% (3.1), AZ 8% (3.4), NC 6% (1.8), NV 3% (3.2), TX 2% (0.3), FL 2% (0.2), VA 2% (0.6), NM 1% (2.0), NE-2 1% (4.3), NH 1% (1.6), CO 1% (0.3). The model treats Maine and Nebraska's congressional districts (e.g., NE-2) as separate contests.
quantities: PA tipping chance = 34 percent (Aug 8, 2024); PA VPI = 8.1 index (Aug 8, 2024); NE-2 VPI = 4.3 index (Aug 8, 2024)

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: In the Aug 8, 2024 run, Trump's 46% overall chance of winning the Electoral College rose to 95.5% (reported as 96%) when he wins Pennsylvania. Harris has less than a 10% chance of winning if she loses any Blue Wall state. If Harris wins Michigan, Trump still has 17%, reflecting his additional Sunbelt paths.
quantities: Trump EC chance = 46 percent (Aug 8, 2024); Trump P(win | PA) = 96 percent (Aug 8, 2024); Trump P(win | Harris wins MI) = 17 percent (Aug 8, 2024)
evidence_quote: Harris has a less than 10 percent chance of winning the election if she loses any of them.

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: State outcomes in the Silver Bulletin model are correlated rather than independent, with stronger correlation between geographically and demographically similar states.
evidence_quote: Candidates' performances across states aren't independent, so if someone wins Pennsylvania, they're much more likely to win other battleground states — especially geographically and demographically similar states.

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement:
Swing-state win probabilities conditional on Pennsylvania (Aug 8, 2024), shown as unconditional / if Harris wins PA / if Trump wins PA:
- Wisconsin: 57% Harris / 90% Harris / 85% Trump
- Michigan: 63% Harris / 94% Harris / 77% Trump
- Georgia: 57% Trump / 70% Harris / 91% Trump
- Arizona: 55% Trump / 74% Harris / 93% Trump
- North Carolina: 63% Trump / 63% Harris / 97% Trump
- Nevada: 51% Harris / 79% Harris / 86% Trump
quantities: WI Harris | Harris wins PA = 90 percent (Aug 8, 2024); NC Harris | Harris wins PA = 63 percent (Aug 8, 2024); NC Trump | Trump wins PA = 97 percent (Aug 8, 2024)
rationale: Shows the implied strength of correlation between Pennsylvania and other swing states.

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: Correlated polling error in the simulations, as described for the 2020 FiveThirtyEight model and cited as still applying, comes from random permutations along demographic and geographic characteristics. For example, in one simulation Trump overperforms with Hispanic voters and so does better in heavily Hispanic states; in another, Biden overperforms in states with many Catholics.
evidence_quote: to calculate correlated polling error, the model creates random permutations based on different demographic and geographic characteristics.

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: Conditional probabilities for very unlikely state outcomes (e.g., Trump wins California in 143 of 40,000 simulations, about 0.4%, and wins the EC in 123 of those, 86.0%) should be read cautiously. They rest on small simulation samples. More importantly, by Bayesian reasoning they mix two routes: a national landslide and a state-specific freak shock. The model treats the freak-shock route as only about 6 times less likely than the landslide route.
quantities: Trump CA wins = 143 simulations (out of 40,000, Aug 8, 2024); Trump P(EC | CA) = 86.0 percent (Aug 8, 2024); freak vs landslide odds ratio = 6:1 ratio (freak accident less likely than landslide)
evidence_quote: The freak accident scenario is more unlikely, but by "only" by about a 6:1 ratio, the model thinks.

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: The authors say the model probably overstates outlier outcomes. One reason is that fat-tailed state-specific errors can produce six-sigma results. Another is that noncompetitive states are rarely polled, and the model is very uncertain about states with little or no polling.
quantities: tail outcome size = six sigma standard deviations (state-specific error)
evidence_quote: our model is probably too generous about accounting for these outlier occurrences, i.e. it overstates their likelihood.

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: Simulated errors in the Silver Bulletin model, including state-specific error, are drawn from a t-distribution, which is fat-tailed.
rationale: There are few elections with reliable polling (national polls since about 1936, material swing-state polling since about 1976), so the long-run error distribution is uncertain and catastrophic polling errors are possible.
evidence_quote: the reason we use fat-tailed distributions at all — specifically, a t-distribution — is because we don't actually have have all that many elections with reliable polling data

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: Starting with the Aug 9, 2024 run, the Silver Bulletin model reduces the fat-tailedness of state-specific error (state relative to national) to cut freak outcomes somewhat. It keeps fat tails motivated by limited data on the overall polling error.
quantities: data points per year on state-vs-national alignment = 51 data points (50 states plus DC); national polls start = 1936 year (approximate); swing state polls start = 1976 year (approximate)
rationale: There is far more data (51 points per election) on how states line up relative to the national result than on national polling error, so state-specific error needs less fat-tailing.
evidence_quote: we'll be reducing the degree to which the simulations assume that state-specific error is fat-tailed.

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: Extreme tail probabilities (e.g., whether Trump's chance of winning California is 0.4% or 0.04%) cannot be validated empirically, because doing so would require hundreds of elections.
quantities: model CA probability = 0.4 percent (Trump wins CA); alternative = 0.04 percent (hypothetical)
evidence_quote: we'd need a sample of hundreds of elections to test that, and we'll never get that in our lifetimes.

title: Welcome to the bizarre world of conditional probability
statement: The model projects polling averages forward to Election Day (November 5) through a series of adjustments before running the simulations.
evidence_quote: after making a bunch of fancy adjustments to go from our polling averages to predictions for November 5th

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: The Silver Bulletin presidential model has a special 'named third-party candidate' (N3PC) mode. For a designated N3PC the model explicitly forecasts the candidate's vote share, and the candidate is eligible to win electoral votes in the simulations.
evidence_quote: N3PC's receive special handling in the model: we explicitly forecast their vote share, and they're eligible to receive electoral votes.

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: Past examples of candidates treated as N3PCs include Ross Perot in 1992 and 1996 and Gary Johnson in 2016. RFK Jr. was an N3PC in 2024 until his withdrawal.
evidence_quote: examples from past elections include Ross Perot in 1992 and 1996 or Gary Johnson in 2016

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: Poll version selection: when a designated N3PC is in the race, the Silver Bulletin presidential model defaults toward the multiway-ballot version of a poll rather than the head-to-head version.
evidence_quote: When there's an N3PC in the race, the model defaults toward using the multiway version

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: Third-party adjustment: in N3PC mode, when a poll does not list the N3PC as an option, the Silver Bulletin presidential model extrapolates (imputes) the N3PC's vote share for that poll, allocating votes to him.
evidence_quote: extrapolates the N3PC's vote share in cases where a poll doesn't list him as an option

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: When there is no designated N3PC, the Silver Bulletin presidential model averages all available versions of a poll (head-to-head and multiway) together instead of preferring one version.
evidence_quote: If there isn't a designated N3PC, it averages all available versions of the survey together instead.

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: N3PC designation criterion 1 (described by Silver as admittedly somewhat arbitrary): the candidate is generally polling in the mid-single digits or higher.
quantities: polling threshold for N3PC = mid-single digits or higher percent (general polling level required for N3PC status)
evidence_quote: Whether a candidate is generally polling in the mid-single digits or higher

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: N3PC designation criterion 2: the candidate is expected to qualify for the ballot in enough states that he could theoretically reach 270 electoral votes. Silver applies this by its spirit, so a candidate who exits swing-state ballots and endorses a rival fails it even if he technically meets it.
quantities: electoral votes needed = 270 electoral votes (ballot access must make this theoretically reachable)
rationale: You don't endorse another candidate and take yourself off swing-state ballots if you seriously want to contest the Electoral College.
evidence_quote: Whether the candidate is expected to qualify for the ballot in most states, enough that he could theoretically reach 270 electoral votes.

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: On Aug 24, 2024, the Silver Bulletin presidential model dropped RFK Jr. from N3PC status and lumped him in with 'other' candidates. This was implemented by changing a single cell in one spreadsheet, which implies N3PC status is a configuration flag.
rationale: Simple is best under these circumstances. He no longer meets the N3PC criteria, and the change uses existing model logic.
evidence_quote: we've changed RFK's status in the model by changing a single cell in one spreadsheet

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: After Kennedy's removal from N3PC status, the Silver Bulletin presidential model expects all candidates other than Harris and Trump combined, including Kennedy where he remains on the ballot, to get 1 to 2 percent of the vote on Nov. 5, 2024.
quantities: projected combined 'other' vote = 1 to 2 percent (2024 general election, post-RFK withdrawal)
rationale: Minor-party support in polls often doesn't translate to ballots.
evidence_quote: to get 1 to 2 percent of the vote combined on Nov. 5

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: Third-party candidates typically poll higher than their eventual vote share. In polls they might get 2 or 3 percent combined, but that support often doesn't materialize. Undecided voters park there, then stay home or switch to a major-party candidate in the booth. The model therefore projects 'other' below its polled level.
quantities: typical combined third-party polling = 2 or 3 percent (when included in polls, 2024)
rationale: Third-party options act as a 'Free Parking space' for actually undecided voters.
evidence_quote: empirically, support for minor parties in polls often doesn't translate to support on the ballot. Instead, they serve as a Free Parking space for voters who are actually undecided.

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: The Silver Bulletin presidential model gives minor candidates a lower vote projection in battleground states, reflecting tactical voting.
rationale: Third-party candidates do worse in close elections, especially in swing states, because voters avoid protest votes when their ballot could matter.
evidence_quote: The model accounts for this: if you look carefully, minor candidates get a lower projection in battleground states.

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: Data from Silver's presidential primary model show that candidates who suspend their campaigns after ballot deadlines typically lose half their vote or more. Applied to RFK Jr., this implied he would poll at 1 or 2 percent instead of 3 or 4.
quantities: vote loss after suspension = half or more share of prior support (candidates suspending after ballot deadlines, from primary model data); expected RFK polling after suspension = 1 or 2 percent (if pollsters still include him); RFK prior polling = 3 or 4 percent (before suspension; about 4 in polling average)
model_version: primary model data applied to 2024 presidential
evidence_quote: Typically they lose half their vote or more.

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: Ballot access for an N3PC is simulated probabilistically in the Silver Bulletin presidential model. In states where RFK's ballot status was uncertain, he randomly appeared on the ballot in some simulations but not others. Where he was off the ballot, his votes were reallocated to the major-party candidates.
evidence_quote: he'd randomly make the ballot in some simulations but not others

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: Rejected alternative 1 for handling RFK's withdrawal: keep Kennedy as an N3PC and remove him only in the states where he withdraws. This would have meant the model first allocated votes to him in polls that didn't list him, then subtracted them back out. It would also have overprojected his vote share, since he no longer met the N3PC standards.
rationale: Continuity benefit, but internally inconsistent.
evidence_quote: the model would first have been allocating votes to Kennedy in polls where he wasn't listed as part of its third-party adjustment and then subtracting them back out again

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: Rejected alternative 2, originally planned: run the third-party adjustment in reverse, imputing what polls that included Kennedy would show without him. Silver rejected it for three reasons. It created ambiguity about how other third-party candidates (Stein, Oliver) were treated. It would wrongly zero out RFK when he remains on most ballots. It would have required election-specific new code.
rationale: Avoid ad-hoc fixes when the model's existing logic offers an alternative.
evidence_quote: Another approach would be to adjust polls that did include Kennedy to impute what they'd say without him — basically, the reverse of the third-party adjustment.

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: Mid-campaign changes to a model should be minimally invasive. Ad-hoc, election-specific fixes should be avoided when the model's preexisting logic offers a solution. Silver frames this partly as a critique of competitors.
evidence_quote: changes to a model in the midst of a campaign should be minimally invasive.

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: Effect of removing RFK on the Silver Bulletin national polling average (Aug 23 to Aug 24, 2024): Harris rose from 48.0 to 48.8 (+0.8) and Trump from 43.7 to 44.8 (+1.1). The net shift was 0.3 points toward Trump, which means Kennedy drew slightly more from Trump.
quantities: Harris average change = 48.0 to 48.8 (+0.8) percent (national average, RFK removal); Trump average change = 43.7 to 44.8 (+1.1) percent (national average, RFK removal); net shift to Trump = 0.3 percentage points (RFK removal)
evidence_quote: Harris's polling average has improved from 48.0 percent yesterday to 48.8 percent today (+0.8), while Trump's has increased from 43.7 to 44.8 (+1.1).

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: The Silver Bulletin national polling average accounts for each poll's quality, sample size and recency, and is adjusted based on trends in both state and national polls.

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: The Silver Bulletin presidential model applies a convention bounce adjustment that discounts post-convention poll gains. Harris's post-DNC poll gains were just enough to roughly offset both this adjustment and the RFK change, leaving her win probability flat. Without those gains she would have declined slightly.
quantities: Harris national lead = 4.0 percentage points (Aug 24, 2024); Harris lead at DNC start = 2.3 percentage points (start of DNC)
evidence_quote: her improvement is just enough to roughly offset both the convention bounce adjustment that the model makes and the RFK Jr. fix

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: The Silver Bulletin presidential model designates certain news events as 'landmark events', such as the DNC and RFK's withdrawal. After a landmark event, the model is more aggressive about accounting for polling shifts in the following days.
evidence_quote: Since the DNC and RFK's withdrawal are both what the model considers "landmark events," it will be aggressive about accounting for any polling shifts it sees in the coming days.

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.
statement: With an N3PC in the race, the Silver Bulletin presidential model in about 2 percent of simulations had RFK winning some electoral votes, which could produce an Electoral College deadlock with no one reaching 270. With no N3PC, the only deadlock is an exact 269-269 tie, at about a 0.3 percent chance. Removing these deadlock scenarios slightly helped Harris.

evidence_quote: Now the only deadlock scenario is an exact 269-269 tie, which is only a 0.3 percent chance given how the states line up combinatorially.

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.

evidence_quote: When there's a news event so recently that there hasn't yet been time for it to be accounted for in the polling, it may be worth looking toward alternatives like prediction markets

title: We removed RFK Jr. from our model. But it didn’t hurt Kamala.

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model applies a convention bounce adjustment that shaves some support off a candidate's post-convention polls. The adjustment is applied regardless of what the polls actually show.
rationale: Convention bounces are typically short-term and are expected to fade.
evidence_quote: no matter what the polls look like, our model will apply a convention bounce adjustment that shaves some support off of Harris’ post-DNC polls

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: In 2024 the Silver Bulletin model expects a net convention bounce of only 2 to 2.5 points in margin immediately after the convention. In the worked example, the adjustment shaves off about 2 points.
quantities: expected net convention bounce = 2 or 2.5 percentage points (net margin) (immediately after the convention, 2024 model); bounce adjustment in example = 2 percentage points (amount shaved off Harris's post-DNC polls in scenario 3)
rationale: Conventions matter less in a polarized environment with a 24/7 news cycle.
evidence_quote: our model still expects a pretty modest bounce – a net gain of only 2 or 2.5 points immediately after the convention

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: For 2024 the Silver Bulletin model rolled back COVID-era (2020) adjustments to the convention bounce, because bounces were expected to be larger than during the height of COVID-19 in 2020.
rationale: The expectation was that 2024 convention bounces would exceed the muted 2020 bounces.
evidence_quote: Our expectation was that convention bounces this year would be larger than they were during the height of COVID-19 in 2020 — and we rolled back COVID-era adjustments to the model accordingly.

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: Under the convention bounce adjustment, a bounce of the expected size leaves the forecast roughly unchanged. In the 2024 example, an expected bounce meant Harris ending up 4 or 5 points ahead of Trump after the DNC.
quantities: post-DNC margin consistent with expected bounce = 4 or 5 percentage points (Harris lead over Trump)
rationale: Gains are offset by the adjustment.
evidence_quote: her gains will be offset by our convention bounce adjustment and she’ll stay right around where she is in the forecast

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: If a candidate gets little or no bounce, or declines in the polls, during the post-convention window, the Silver Bulletin model lowers that candidate's win probability. The model expects a bounce, so missing it is treated as a bad sign; for example, Harris still being up only 2 points at a likely polling high point.
quantities: example weak post-DNC lead = 2 percentage points (Harris margin that would cause decline in forecast)
rationale: The model expects a bounce, so not getting one is read as underlying weakness.
evidence_quote: Basically, the model expects a bounce, so not getting one is seen as a bad thing.

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: The convention bounce adjustment is temporary. If a candidate keeps leading for a few weeks after the convention, the model becomes more convinced that the numbers are durable and the candidate rises in the forecast again. This implies the adjustment decays over time after the convention.
rationale: Sustained post-convention polling indicates real rather than illusory gains.
evidence_quote: if Harris continued to lead Trump a few weeks from now, the model would become more convinced that her numbers were durable and she’d begin to rise in our forecast again

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: If a candidate's post-convention bounce exceeds the expected size, the candidate gains in the forecast even after the adjustment. Example: Harris up 6 points post-DNC, minus the 2-point adjustment, still puts her ahead of her pre-convention position.
quantities: example large post-DNC lead = 6 percentage points (Harris national margin)
evidence_quote: if she’s up 6 points in the average post-DNC, shaving off 2 points from her polls still puts her ahead of where she was going in

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: Convention bounces tend to peak a few days after the convention ends.
evidence_quote: Bounces tend to peak about a few days after the convention ends

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: From 1964 to 2020, a candidate's polling standing rose by an average of 5 percentage points after their party's convention. Bounce is measured as the change in the candidate's polling average from one week before to one week after the convention, using American Presidency Project data.
quantities: average convention bounce 1964-2020 = 5 percentage points (candidate's own vote share); measurement window = one week before to one week after (definition of bounce)
evidence_quote: On average, candidates’ standing in the polls increased by 5 percentage points after their party’s convention.

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: Most convention bounce gains come from undecided voters or voters who planned to vote third-party. The opponent's standing typically declines only slightly, so the net margin bounce is smaller than the gain in own vote share.
evidence_quote: Most of these gains came from the undecided column or from voters who’d said they planned to vote for third parties: the opponent’s standing typically declines too, but only slightly.

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: Convention bounces have shrunk over time. They averaged just over 6 points from 1964 to 2000 and only 1.8 points after 2000. The largest post-2000 bounce was Trump's 3 points after the 2016 RNC.
quantities: average bounce 1964-2000 = just over 6 percentage points; average bounce post-2000 = 1.8 percentage points; largest post-2000 bounce = 3 percentage points (Trump 2016 RNC)
rationale: High polarization and a 24/7 news cycle make conventions matter less.
evidence_quote: The average post-2000 convention bounce was only 1.8 points

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: The historical convention bounce table (1964-2020) lists bounces by nominee: 2020 Biden ±0, Trump +1; 2016 Clinton +2, Trump +3; 2012 Obama +2, Romney −1; 2008 Obama +4, McCain +6; 2004 Kerry −1, Bush +2; 2000 Gore +8, Bush +8; 1996 Clinton +5, Dole +3; 1992 Clinton +16, Bush +5; 1988 Dukakis +7, Bush +6; 1984 Mondale +9, Reagan +4; 1980 Carter +10, Reagan +8; 1976 Carter +9, Ford +5; 1972 McGovern ±0, Nixon +7; 1968 Humphrey +2, Nixon +5; 1964 Johnson +3, Goldwater +5.
quantities: largest bounce in table = +16 percent (Bill Clinton 1992); table average = +5 percent (1964-2020)

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: Greater recent volatility in the polls makes a meaningful convention bounce more likely. In a stable race like the pre-debate Biden-Trump contest, a large or sustained bounce would be unlikely. A caveat: a candidate's bounce may already have occurred during an earlier surge, as with Harris's post-launch surge.
rationale: When support is less set in stone, events move polls more.
evidence_quote: In a vacuum, I’d expect more variation in the polls to make a meaningful bounce more likely.

title: How big will the bounce be?
statement: Trump's apparent 2024 RNC bounce cannot be cleanly attributed to the convention. In the Biden-Trump average, Trump went from 42.6% to 45.2% (+2.6) and Biden from 39.9% to 41.2% (+1.3), so the margin moved from R+2.7 to R+4.0 between July 8 and July 21. That window overlapped the June 27 debate aftermath, the July 13 assassination attempt, the July 15 VP pick and Biden's July 21 withdrawal. The 'after' value is 6 days post-convention because Biden dropped out on day 6.
quantities: Trump before RNC = 42.6 % (July 8, 2024); Trump after RNC = 45.2 % (July 21, 2024); Biden before RNC = 39.9 % (July 8); Biden after RNC = 41.2 % (July 21); margin change = R+1.3 percentage points (R+2.7 to R+4.0)

evidence_quote: Her win probability still would increase in our model in that instance because of the convention bounce adjustment wearing off, but not by as much.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
statement: As of September 2024, the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model estimates an Electoral College bias of around 2.5 points against Democrats. Under this estimate, Harris needs roughly a 3-point national lead to be a slight favorite.
quantities: Electoral College bias = Around 2.5 percentage points (against Democrats, model estimate as of September 2024); National lead needed to be a slight favorite = 3 percentage points (Harris)
evidence_quote: Around 2.5 points against Democrats.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
statement: In the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model, state polls have more influence than national polls once the model has enough state data.
evidence_quote: ultimately state polls have more influence on the model than national polls once it has enough state data to go on.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
statement: The Silver Bulletin trendline adjustment extrapolates movement in national polls to state estimates when fresh state polls are lacking. For example, if Harris gains 2 points nationally, the model assumes she has gained about 2 points in Pennsylvania. This suggests a uniform-swing-style trend transfer.
quantities: Example national gain transferred to state = 2 percentage points (Pennsylvania example)
rationale: Without fresh state data, national movement is the best available signal. Actual state data can later produce surprises.
evidence_quote: it will assume that if Harris has gained 2 points in national polls, she's probably gained 2 points in Pennsylvania as well.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
statement: The Silver Bulletin polling averages respond aggressively to highly rated pollsters such as NYT/Siena, which suggests that weight depends on pollster rating.
evidence_quote: They also tend to be highly-rated polls, and the polling averages will respond aggressively to them.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
statement: In the Silver Bulletin pollster ratings, most quick overnight IVR polls have relatively low ratings and ought to be viewed with skepticism. Morning Consult and YouGov are rated as good pollsters.
evidence_quote: Most of these polls have relatively low ratings and ought to be looked at with some skepticism.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
statement: Online panel pollsters such as Morning Consult and YouGov weight heavily on past vote or party identification to counter partisan response bias in their non-probability samples. As a result, their polls typically show little movement after events, and they sometimes miss real shifts.
rationale: Enthusiastic partisans respond more eagerly to surveys after good events for their side, which can bias results.
evidence_quote: these firms tend to weight heavily on past voting patterns or party identification to minimize problems with partisan response bias in their non-probability samples.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
statement: Phase 0 of the typical post-debate poll pattern (days 0-1, the 'fakeout phase'): most changes to the forecast reflect pre-debate polls that are only now being released. They reveal nothing about the debate's impact.
quantities: Fakeout phase = 0-1 days after debate (post-debate phase 0)
evidence_quote: Most changes in the model that occur today and tomorrow will reflect pre-debate polling that wasn't released until now.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
statement: Phase 1 of the typical post-debate poll pattern (days 2-3): the first fully post-debate polls come from online panels and quick-and-dirty IVR polls. Traditional telephone pollsters stay in the field for 3-4 days and then take another 1-2 days to release.
quantities: Phase 1 timing = 2-3 days after debate (online/IVR polls); Phone poll field time = 3-4 days (traditional pollsters); Phone poll finalization time = a day or two days (after fieldwork ends)
evidence_quote: traditional telephone pollsters like to be in the field for 3-4 days, then they might want another day or two to finalize the poll and release the numbers.

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
statement: Phase 2 of the typical post-debate poll pattern (days 4-7): traditional high-quality phone polls arrive, national before state. These polls can show bigger bounces because they massage the data less.
quantities: Phase 2 timing = 4-7 days after debate
rationale: Pollsters gauge the overall national effect before polling individual states.
evidence_quote: Usually, you'll get national polls before state polls at this stage

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
statement: Phase 3 of the typical post-debate poll pattern (days 8-13): state polls arrive, and the Silver Bulletin averages and forecast settle into a 'new normal' with less volatility.
quantities: Phase 3 timing = 8-13 days after debate
evidence_quote: This is about when our polling averages and the forecast lock into the "new normal".

title: A guide to post-debate poll-watching
statement: Phase 4 of the typical post-debate poll pattern (14+ days): this is about the most reliable read of the debate's impact that will ever be available. Changes after this point mostly reflect later campaign developments.
quantities: Phase 4 timing = 14+ days after debate
rationale: The news cycle moves on.
evidence_quote: By two weeks from today — roughly September 25 — we'll have about as reliable a gauge of the impact of the debate as we're ever going to get.

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you

evidence_quote: putting the probabilistic component of the model behind a paywall

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
statement: A typical state poll has about 800 respondents. Its theoretical margin of error is about ±3.5 points on one candidate's vote share.
quantities: typical poll sample size = about 800 respondents (typical poll, e.g. Wisconsin 2024); margin of error, single candidate share = ±3.5 percentage points (800-person poll, 95% confidence)
evidence_quote: A typical poll has about 800 respondents. Well, the margin of error in an 800-person poll is plus or minus 3.5 points.

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
statement: In a two-way race with negligible third-party vote, the margin of error on the gap between the candidates is roughly twice the margin of error on one candidate's share. For an 800-person poll this is about ±7 points.
quantities: margin of error on the margin = about 7 percentage points (800-person poll, two-candidate race); multiplier = roughly 2 x (margin-of-error on the gap vs. on one candidate's share)
rationale: Nearly every vote that is not a Harris vote is a Trump vote, so errors in the two shares are perfectly negatively correlated.
evidence_quote: So the margin of error on the difference separating the candidates is roughly twice that: about 7 points.

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
statement: With a true margin of Harris +1, sampling error alone will produce some polls ranging from Trump +5 to Harris +7. About 1 poll in 20 will be an outlier beyond the 95% interval, such as Harris +10 or Trump +8.
quantities: margin-of-error coverage = 95 percent (share of polls expected inside the stated margin of error); outlier frequency = 1 in 20 polls (polls outside the margin of error if pollsters are honest)
evidence_quote: about 1 time in 20, you'll get a true outlier — a Harris +10 or a Trump +8 — provided that pollsters are being honest

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
statement: In practice, pollsters herd toward the consensus and suppress outlier results. As a result, the published spread of polls is narrower than pure sampling error would produce.
evidence_quote: In practice, pollsters tend to herd toward the consensus and suppress outlier results.

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
statement: Averaging polls reduces sampling error only partially. Four 800-person polls are equivalent to a 3,200-voter sample, which still has a margin of error on the margin of 3 or 4 points. A true Harris +1 race could therefore show an average anywhere from Trump +2 to Harris +4.
quantities: number of polls averaged = 4 polls (Wisconsin example); pooled sample size = 3200 voters (four 800-person polls combined); margin of error on the margin = 3 or 4 percentage points (pooled sample of 3,200)
evidence_quote: The margin of error on the difference separating the candidates is still 3 or 4 points

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
statement: The Silver Bulletin model makes inferences about a state's polling from polls of other states, borrowing strength across states.
rationale: This is described as part of the model's value beyond simple averaging.
evidence_quote: making inferences about what the polls in one state say based on polls of other states

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
statement: The Silver Bulletin model's more important function is to account for systematic polling error that affects polls collectively. An example is the error that substantially underestimated Trump in both 2016 and 2020.
rationale: Sampling error understates real-world uncertainty.
evidence_quote: their more important function is by accounting for another possibility: the chance of a systematic polling error

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you
statement: The Silver Bulletin model calibrates its win probabilities to the historical empirical accuracy of polls, not to theoretical sampling margins of error. Empirical error is considerably wider than theoretical error.
rationale: Real-world margins of error are considerably wider than theoretical ones.
evidence_quote: they're derived from how accurate the polls really have been, in practice — and in practice, the margins of error are considerably wider than they are in theory

title: Don't let randomness make a fool of you

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
statement: The model should enumerate even unlikely scenarios, such as weird regional shifts like those in 2022. One example is Harris losing the Blue Wall plus New Hampshire and Minnesota while sweeping Florida, Georgia and North Carolina. The simulation therefore must allow region-specific (non-uniform) error components.
rationale: Elections like 2022 had a lot of weird regional shifts.
evidence_quote: there are sometimes elections like 2022 with a lot of weird regional shifts, and the model's job is to enumerate even the unlikely scenarios.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
statement: Demographic correlation drives joint state outcomes. Florida becomes part of a Harris winning map mainly in scenarios where her vote collapses among the white working class but she overperforms among Hispanics or voters of color. In that case she can lose all three Blue Wall states and win via Florida, Arizona and Nevada.
evidence_quote: The particular scenario where Florida creates winning maps for Harris is if her vote collapses among the white working class — but she overperforms among Hispanics or voters of color generally.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
statement: Silver thinks the model is probably overly cautious in giving Iowa any tipping-point probability. Iowa is strongly correlated with the Blue Wall, so a Harris win in Iowa almost always comes with Blue Wall wins and a non-close electoral outcome.
rationale: If Harris wins Iowa, she'll almost certainly also win the Blue Wall states.
evidence_quote: it's probably being overly cautious in thinking that Iowa could ever be the tipping point.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
statement: For lightly polled, safe-ish states (Minnesota, New Mexico, Virginia), the model assigns a 0 to 1 percent tipping-point probability out of an abundance of caution. Sparse polling leaves more uncertainty.
quantities: MN/NM/VA tipping-point probability = 0 to 1 percent (Sept 21, 2024)
rationale: There hasn't been a ton of polling in these states.
evidence_quote: where there hasn't been a ton of polling and the model assigns a 0 to 1 percent tipping-point probability out of an abundance of caution.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states
statement: The model simulates Nebraska and Maine congressional-district electoral votes separately (NE-2, ME-2). In 610 of 40,000 simulations (about 1.5%), Harris won exactly the Blue Wall states plus NE-2 and lost the other battlegrounds, giving a 270-268 win. Without NE-2 that map would be a 269-269 tie, probably resolved for Trump in the House.
quantities: Blue Wall + NE-2 exact scenario = 610 simulations (out of 40,000, Sept 21, 2024); share of simulations = about 1.5 percent (Sept 21, 2024)
evidence_quote: Without that extra vote in Omaha, though, it's a 269-269 tie, which would probably be resolved for Trump in the U.S. House.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states

evidence_quote: it's a 269-269 tie, which would probably be resolved for Trump in the U.S. House.

title: A tour of the 7½ key swing states

evidence_quote: I generally don't believe in "reverse coattails" — the top-of-the-ticket can effect down-ballot races, but usually not the other way around.

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model ran 40,000 simulations in its run on the morning of September 23, 2024.
quantities: number of simulations = 40,000 simulations (model run on Monday morning, Sep 23, 2024)
evidence_quote: Out of the 40,000 simulations we ran on Monday morning

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: Because the Silver Bulletin 2024 model correlates states, it rarely produces outcomes where Arizona and Wisconsin diverge sharply. Only 147 of 40,000 simulations (about 0.37%) had Harris losing Arizona by at least 5 points while winning Wisconsin by at least 6.
quantities: simulations with Harris losing AZ by ≥5 and winning WI by ≥6 = 147 simulations (out of 40,000, Sep 23, 2024 run); AZ loss threshold = 5 percentage points (matches Times/Siena Arizona result); WI win threshold = 6 percentage points (matches MassINC Wisconsin result)
rationale: You would bet heavily against Democratic overperformance in Wisconsin combined with underperformance in Arizona, so at least one of the two polls is almost certainly wrong.
evidence_quote: there were only 147 cases where Harris both lost Arizona by at least 5 points, matching the Times result, and won Wisconsin by at least 6

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: The Silver Bulletin presidential model does not take individual state polls at face value. It averages each new poll with other surveys of that state and with a demographics-based prior for the state.
rationale: Shrinks the influence of any single possibly-outlying poll.
evidence_quote: the model isn't taking any of these numbers quite at face value, instead averaging them with other surveys of these states as well as its priors based on their demographics

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: State-level priors in the Silver Bulletin presidential model are based on state demographics and are blended with state polling.
evidence_quote: its priors based on their demographics

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: Several strong Times/Siena Sunbelt polls (Trump +2 to +5) and a MassINC Wisconsin poll (Harris +6 to 7) produced only incremental moves in state win probabilities. Harris moved from 40% to 37% in NC, 37% to 34% in GA, 37% to 32% in AZ, and 57% to 60% in WI.
quantities: NC Harris win prob before/after = 40 -> 37 percent (after Times/Siena poll, Sep 23, 2024); GA Harris win prob before/after = 37 -> 34 percent (after Times/Siena poll); AZ Harris win prob before/after = 37 -> 32 percent (after Times/Siena poll); WI Harris win prob before/after = 57 -> 60 percent (after MassINC poll)
rationale: Polls are averaged with other polls and with priors.
evidence_quote: Harris's win probability in North Carolina fell from 40 percent to 37 percent, in Georgia from 37 percent to 34 percent and in Arizona from 37 percent to 32 percent

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: Changes in the Silver Bulletin model are usually incremental. The exceptions are inflection points after major events such as debates.
evidence_quote: Outside of inflection points following major events like debates, changes in the model tend to be incremental.

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: New polls showing a candidate behind in states where the model already had that candidate narrowly behind, and which are not on the candidate's minimum path to 270, move the overall forecast less than expected. Conflicting high-quality polls in other states (e.g., Sunbelt vs. Wisconsin) also partly offset each other.
rationale: Harris's minimum viable path ran through PA, MI, WI and NE-2.
evidence_quote: The polls had less of an effect on our model than I'd expected.

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin and Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District together give Harris exactly 270 electoral votes. Nebraska's split allocation of electoral votes was assumed to remain after a Republican push to revert to winner-take-all appeared to fail.

evidence_quote: Those states, plus the 2nd Congressional District of Nebraska ... would suffice to give Harris 270 electoral votes.

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: Silver Bulletin pollster ratings penalize polling firms that show clear signs of herding, meaning hedging published results toward the polling averages.
rationale: Polling averages like Silver Bulletin's potentially contribute to herding, so the ratings counteract it.
evidence_quote: our pollster ratings actually punish polling firms that show clear signs of doing this

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: In the 2024 Silver Bulletin pollster ratings, Selzer & Co. is the highest-rated pollster and NYT/Siena is second. MassINC is described as highly rated.
quantities: Selzer rank = 1 rank (Silver Bulletin pollster ratings, Sep 2024); NYT/Siena rank = 2 rank (Silver Bulletin pollster ratings, Sep 2024)
rationale: Pollsters that stand behind seeming outliers are usually more accurate over the long run.
evidence_quote: That's why Selzer is our highest-rated pollster — the only one to rank higher than the Times.

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: Surprising or outlier polls should be included in the polling average as-is, not excluded, unskewed, or second-guessed through crosstabs. The average itself handles the discounting.
rationale: Outliers sometimes turn out right, and excluding them lets conventional wisdom contaminate the average.
evidence_quote: Just toss it in the averages.

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: Anyone building a polling average must publicly specify the inclusion and weighting rules ahead of time, so that choices are consistent rather than driven by ad hoc vibes or partisan preference.
rationale: Consistency prevents cherry-picking.
evidence_quote: you have to publicly specify the rules ahead of time

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: When a pollster publishes results that defy conventional wisdom, treat it as a sign that the pollster is doing good and honest work.
rationale: Many pollsters file-drawer outliers or massage data toward socially acceptable numbers.
evidence_quote: when pollsters publish results like these, you should take that as a sign that they're doing good and honest work

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: Herding (file-drawering outliers, weighting toward priors, peeking at other polls) can make the average individual poll more accurate while making the polling average worse. In particular, averages may then miss genuine large demographic shifts. Silver describes this as a tragedy-of-the-commons problem.
rationale: Herded polls do not add independent information.
evidence_quote: herding can make the average poll more accurate even as it makes the polling average worse

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: The margin of error on the gap between two candidates is roughly double the margin of error on one candidate's vote share. The Times polls of GA, AZ and NC had a combined MoE of 2.5 points on vote share, about 5 points on the margin. A Trump +3 average is therefore consistent with anything from Harris +2 to Trump +8.
quantities: combined MoE on vote share = 2.5 percentage points (Times/Siena GA, AZ, NC polls combined); MoE on margin = ~5 percentage points (same polls); plausible range around Trump +3 = Harris +2 to Trump +8 margin (Sunbelt)
evidence_quote: the margin of error is closer to 5 points on the difference separating the candidates

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: One in 20 polls will fall outside its margin of error, which corresponds to a 95% confidence interval.
quantities: share of polls outside MoE = 1 in 20 (sampling error)
evidence_quote: one in 20 polls will fall outside the margin of error

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: Subgroup crosstabs carry huge sampling error. The Times Arizona poll's 149 Hispanic respondents imply about a 16-point margin of error on the Trump-Harris gap. Using crosstabs to debunk polls is therefore misguided, since every honest poll will show some odd subgroup results.
quantities: Hispanic subsample = 149 respondents (Times/Siena Arizona poll); subgroup MoE on margin = 16 percentage points (same subsample)
rationale: Only polls that over-massage their data avoid odd subgroup results.
evidence_quote: the Times poll of Arizona surveyed 149 Hispanic voters. That translates to a margin of error of 16 points

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: Some pollsters import so many priors through weighting and massaging that their surveys are de facto closer to models than to polls.
evidence_quote: Some surveys are de facto closer to models than polls

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”
statement: Conventional wisdom almost always assumes that what happened last time will happen again. It was wrong about Trump campaigning in WI and MI in 2016 and about the 2022 red wave. Signs of realignment should be sought in polls, not in narrative.
evidence_quote: the place to look for hints of it will be in the polls — not the conventional wisdom about the race

title: Trust a pollster more when it publishes “outliers”

quantities: KS-3 poll margin = 13 percentage points (NYT/Siena, Oct 2022); KS-3 actual margin = 12.1 percentage points (2022 result); districts polled/won by Dems = 4/4 (NYT/Siena Oct 2022)
evidence_quote: Democrats won all four districts, including Davids by a 12.1-point margin.

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
statement: The Silver Bulletin presidential model's national popular vote forecast is not based directly on national polls. It is the sum of projected results in 56 contests: 50 states, DC, Nebraska's three congressional districts and Maine's two. National polls play only an indirect role, such as helping infer results in sparsely polled states.
quantities: contests projected = 56 contests (50 states + DC + 3 NE CDs + 2 ME CDs)
rationale: This bottom-up method is sometimes more accurate than national polls alone.
evidence_quote: our popular vote forecast isn’t actually based on national polls. Rather, it’s based on summing up the results from the 56 contests the model projects

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
statement: In 2012, Silver's bottom-up (sum of states) popular vote method correctly showed Obama winning the popular vote by a wider margin than national polls projected.
rationale: Cited as evidence supporting the bottom-up approach.
evidence_quote: like in 2012 when it correctly had Barack Obama winning the popular vote by a wider margin than national polls projected

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
statement: The Silver Bulletin forecast differs from its polling average in two ways. It incorporates a 'fundamentals' prior based on the economy and incumbency. It also blends the polling average with a regression that infers each state's result from national polls and polls of other states.
evidence_quote: incorporating a “fundamentals” prior based on the economy and incumbency, and blending our polling averages with a regression analysis that makes inferences about the race from national polls and polls of other states

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
statement: The fundamentals prior and the regression component get less weight as Election Day approaches. By Election Day the model defaults toward being more 'polls-only'.
evidence_quote: Those factors play less and less of a role as the model defaults toward being more “polls-only” by Election Day

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
statement: The weight on the state polling average versus the regression depends on how much recent polling a state has. With heavy recent polling in Pennsylvania, 93% of the weight went to the polling average and 7% to the regression.
quantities: PA weight on polling average = 93 percent (Sept 26, 2024); PA weight on regression = 7 percent (Sept 26, 2024)
rationale: More recent state polling means more trust in the state's own average.
evidence_quote: with a lot of recent polling in Pennsylvania, 93 percent of the weight goes to the polling average and just 7 percent to the regression

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
statement: The Silver Bulletin Pennsylvania forecast table lists 10 steps from polling average to win probability: (1) polling average; (2) adjust for bounces and recent events; (3) adjusted polling average; (4) reallocate undecided and third-party votes; (5) reallocated vote share; (6) blend with regression; (7) snapshot; (8) blend with economic fundamentals; (9) projected vote share; (10) chance of winning.

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
statement: In the Sept 26 Pennsylvania forecast table, the inputs and outputs were as follows. The polling average was Harris 48.8 / Trump 47.3, and the bounce adjustment was about zero. Reallocating undecided and third-party votes added +1.6 to each candidate (50.4 / 48.9). The regression estimate was 49.6 / 49.7, blended at weight 0.06. The snapshot was 50.3 / 48.9. The economic fundamentals estimate was 48.9 / 50.3, blended at weight 0.14. The final projection was 50.1 / 49.1, with a Harris win probability of 59.1%.
quantities: regression blend weight = 0.06 weight (PA, Sept 26 2024 (text says 7%)); fundamentals blend weight = 0.14 weight (PA, Sept 26 2024, roughly 6 weeks before election); undecided/third-party reallocation = +1.6 each percentage points (PA, applied equally to both candidates); PA Harris win probability = 59.1 percent (Sept 26 2024); PA projected vote = 50.1 vs 49.1 percent (Harris vs Trump)

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
statement: The Silver Bulletin forecast reallocates undecided and third-party votes to the major candidates. In Pennsylvania on Sept 26 the reallocation was equal, +1.6 points each.
quantities: reallocation = +1.6/+1.6 percentage points (PA Sept 26 2024)

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?

rationale: Silver says the imputations are usually pretty reasonable.
evidence_quote: Whether through imputation or by directly looking at the polling, the model does expect Harris’s margins in some of the bluest states to be down from Biden’s numbers

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?

evidence_quote: Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin are correlated, but not perfectly so, and as any sports bettor will tell you, correlated parlays are still hard to win

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
statement: Of the 102 simulations in which Harris won the Electoral College but lost the popular vote, Harris won MI in 90%, PA in 88%, WI in 81% and NE-2 in 82%. She won NC in 31%, GA in 21% and AZ in 3%, averaging 277 electoral votes. A few of these were extreme-tail outcomes.

evidence_quote: Harris won Michigan in 90 percent of these simulations

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
statement: On Sept 26, 2024 the model gave a 20% chance that Harris wins the popular vote but loses the Electoral College, versus 0.3% for the reverse split. Harris was a 3:1 favorite in the popular vote while the Electoral College was roughly a toss-up.
quantities: P(Harris wins PV, loses EC) = 20 percent (Sept 26 2024); P(Trump wins PV, loses EC) = 0.3 percent (Sept 26 2024 (~300:1)); Harris PV odds = 3:1 odds (favorite)
evidence_quote: there’s a 20 percent chance that Harris wins the popular but loses the Electoral College, but only a 0.3 percent chance of the same thing happening to Donald Trump

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?
statement: The model projected Harris +2.5 nationally and +1.0 in Pennsylvania (the tipping point), a point-estimate Electoral College gap of 1.5 points. Averaged across simulations, the gap is about 2 points. Splits can occur at popular vote margins anywhere from about Trump +1 to Harris +5.
quantities: projected national margin = Harris +2.5 percentage points (forecast); projected PA margin = Harris +1.0 percentage points (forecast); point-estimate EC gap = 1.5 percentage points (forecast); average simulated EC gap = about 2 percentage points (after uncertainty; about half the 2020 gap); split range = Trump +1 to Harris +5 popular vote margin (range where splits occur)
rationale: Because outcomes are probabilistic, small misses in PA, MI or WI widen the effective gap.
evidence_quote: in our average simulation after accounting for this uncertainty, the Electoral College / popular vote winds up being about 2 points, not 1.5

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?

Harris's win probability is 10.5% at D+0 to +1, 32.8% at D+1 to +2, 63.3% at D+2 to +3, 87.0% at D+3 to +4, 96.7% at D+4 to +5 and 99.5% at D+5 to +6. quantities: Harris win prob D+0-1 = 10.5 percent (Sept 26 2024); Harris win prob D+1-2 = 32.8 percent; Harris win prob D+2-3 = 63.3 percent; Harris win prob D+3-4 = 87.0 percent; Harris win prob D+4-5 = 96.7 percent; Harris win prob R+0-1 = 3.0 percent; Harris win prob R+1-2 = 0.6 percent; Harris EV D+6-7 = 337.5 electoral votes; Harris EV R+6-7 = 186.5 electoral votes

title: Pigs fly. Hell freezes over. The Electoral College favors ... Democrats?

title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?
statement: Silver Bulletin polling averages are 'aggressive': they put a big premium on newer data, i.e. heavy recency weighting. Other good models use less aggressive recency weighting.
rationale: Acknowledged as a legitimate design choice that others make differently.

title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?
statement: In the Silver Bulletin model, sample size is a major factor in a poll's influence (weight) score.

title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?
statement: When a firm frequently polls the same race (national or the same state), as YouGov and Morning Consult do, the Silver Bulletin model spreads a total firm-level weight across that firm's surveys rather than giving each poll full weight.

title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?

title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?

title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?

title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?
statement: Published house effects are mean-reverted estimates, meant to approximate a pollster's long-run house effect if it surveyed the race every day. Firms with only a handful of polls are shrunk heavily toward the mean; prolific firms such as Morning Consult get more precise, less-shrunk estimates.

title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?

title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?

title: Which polls are biased toward Harris or Trump?

title: The 128 paths to the White House

title: When you should panic about the polls
statement: The Silver Bulletin polling averages treat certain campaign set pieces as 'landmark events': debates, conventions, VP picks and candidates wrapping up their nominations. The averages are designed to become more aggressive (more responsive to new polls) after one of these occurs.
rationale: Polling movement is more likely to be real after campaign set pieces.
evidence_quote: the model accounts for this latter group of circumstances, which we call "landmark events": our polling averages are designed to be more aggressive after one of them occurs.

title: When you should panic about the polls

evidence_quote: polling movement is more likely to be "real" after surprises like the James Comey letter

title: When you should panic about the polls
statement: The Silver Bulletin polling averages 'draw curves'. They fit a set of trendlines to recent polling movements, ranging from more conservative to more aggressive. The resulting curves can have inflection points, sometimes sharp ones.
evidence_quote: we fit a bunch of trendlines from recent polling movements that range from more conservative to more aggressive. And curves can be — well, curvy. They can have inflection points

title: When you should panic about the polls
statement: When a candidate has moved sharply (e.g., gained 2 points nationally in a week), the next several polls are high-leverage. The polling average is effectively testing whether the aggressive trendline is correct, much as with exponential data series such as early COVID case counts.
quantities: example steep national shift = 2 percentage points (gain over the past week, described as relatively steep given recent stable elections)
rationale: With multiple trendlines fitted, new data during a trend strongly discriminates between conservative and aggressive fits.
evidence_quote: the next several polls that come in are high-leverage as the model essentially tries to determine whether the aggressive curve is correct

title: When you should panic about the polls
statement: When polls have been steady for several weeks, the Silver Bulletin average resists change. It usually takes several polls telling a consistent story to convince the model that something has changed.
rationale: Stable data favors the conservative trendlines.
evidence_quote: It usually takes several polls telling a consistent story to convince the model that something has changed.

title: When you should panic about the polls
statement: The Silver Bulletin model is designed to be more aggressive toward the very end of the race, specifically in the last week or week-and-a-half. Four weeks out is too soon for this.
quantities: late-aggressiveness window = 1-1.5 weeks (before Election Day); too early = 4 weeks (not yet in aggressive window)
rationale: There is no time left for mean reversion, and some voters decide at the very end.
evidence_quote: the model is designed to be more aggressive toward the very end of the race. But by this I mean specifically the last week or week-and-a-half: four weeks out is a little too soon.

title: When you should panic about the polls
statement: Earlier in the race, the Silver Bulletin model assumes temporary disruptions to polling tend to mean-revert toward the fundamentals. Late in the race there is no time for this reversion, so shocks are taken more at face value.
rationale: A temporary shock at the top of voters' minds on Election Day can decide the outcome.
evidence_quote: there's no longer time for any mean reversion

title: When you should panic about the polls
statement: The Silver Bulletin forecast simulates many permutations of state outcomes and counts who comes up with more winning maps, given correlations between states and the uncertainties in the outlook.

title: When you should panic about the polls
statement: The Silver Bulletin state polling averages account for each poll's quality, sample size and recency, and are adjusted based on trends in both state and national polls.

title: When you should panic about the polls

title: Why you should mostly ignore "internal polls"

Silver gives three reasons: campaigns poll for resource allocation and message testing rather than prediction; principal-agent problems and optimism bias discourage delivering bad news to the boss; and staff are partisan true believers prone to motivated reasoning.

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment
statement: After the 2016 and 2020 misses, many pollsters in 2024 weight samples by recalled past vote, which had been an uncommon technique. Pollsters traditionally avoided it because respondents misremember or misstate their vote, overclaiming a vote for the previous winner.
rationale: Recall bias toward the winner (Biden) could make samples look artificially shifted toward Trump.
evidence_quote: many pollsters are applying what until now had been a relatively uncommon technique: weighting their samples based on how people say they voted in the last election

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment

evidence_quote: it will look like there's been a shift toward Trump when there actually hasn't been

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment

title: New York Times polls are betting on a political realignment

title: Does Trump have momentum?
statement: The Silver Bulletin election forecasts are explicitly designed to be 'momentumless'. The best prediction of what the forecast will say tomorrow is what it says today, so the forecast avoids autocorrelation and behaves like a martingale.
rationale: Predictable future movement would mean the forecast is leaving information on the table.
evidence_quote: The Silver Bulletin election forecasts are explicitly designed to be momentumless. In other words, the best prediction of what the forecast says tomorrow is what it says today

title: Does Trump have momentum?
statement: The sensitivity parameters of the Silver Bulletin polling averages were tuned with minimizing autocorrelation, both positive and negative, as one of the most important objectives.
rationale: Averages that are too sensitive produce mean reversion (negative autocorrelation). Averages that are too sluggish produce positive autocorrelation, leaving predictable trend information unused.
evidence_quote: one of the most important factors I sought to optimize for when tuning their parameters was minimizing autocorrelation — that is, having neither positive autocorrelation nor negative autocorrelation

title: Does Trump have momentum?
statement: Silver defines negative autocorrelation as an over-sensitive average whose moves predictably reverse: a candidate going from +1 to +2 implies a reversion to +1.5 next week. He defines positive autocorrelation as an over-sluggish average whose moves predictably continue: +1 to +2 implies +3 next week.
quantities: example margin path = +1 to +2 percentage points (Hypothetical Trump margin in Arizona used to illustrate autocorrelation)
evidence_quote: If Trump rising from +1 to +2 implies that the polling average next week will be +3, this is positive autocorrelation

title: Does Trump have momentum?
statement: The Silver Bulletin polling averages tend to be more sensitive to new polls than most other averages.
rationale: This follows from tuning to minimize autocorrelation rather than to minimize visible volatility.
evidence_quote: the Silver Bulletin polling averages tend to be more sensitive than most

title: Does Trump have momentum?
statement: Silver says professional model builders tend to make their models too sluggish, 'easing into' changes more than is optimal for predictive accuracy, because they fear looking silly if the forecast bounces around. Laypeople make the opposite error and overreact to new information.
rationale: The reluctance to show volatility comes from reputational concerns rather than accuracy.
evidence_quote: They think it makes them look silly if their forecast is bouncing around a lot, so they build models that “ease into” changes more than is optimal

title: Does Trump have momentum?
statement: The Silver Bulletin polling averages are designed to look two weeks out: today's average should optimally predict what new polls will say two weeks from now. This is a middle ground between a short-term focus, which calls for an aggressive average, and a 30-day focus, which calls for a conservative one.
quantities: prediction horizon of polling average = 2 weeks (Target horizon used in tuning, except at the end of the race)
rationale: The best short-term prediction may extend a bounce, while the best long-term prediction may revert, because bounces from debates and conventions can be short-lived.
evidence_quote: our polling averages are designed to look two weeks out — that is, the polling average today should optimally predict what new polls will say two weeks from now

title: Does Trump have momentum?
statement: At the end of the race, the Silver Bulletin polling averages switch to a more aggressive (more sensitive) setting, because there is no time left for reversion to the mean.
rationale: Near election day, the short-term and final-outcome horizons converge.
evidence_quote: except at the end of the race when there’s no time left for reversion to the mean, and we use a more aggressive setting

title: Does Trump have momentum?

title: Does Trump have momentum?

title: Does Trump have momentum?
