title: Likability isn't enough
statement: Silver treats a candidate's advantage in favorability ratings as, at most, a minor factor that might suggest room for late growth among undecided voters. He does not expect a gap between favorability and head-to-head polls to close. The 2016 precedent (Clinton led more in favorability than in head-to-head polls and still lost) argues against using the favorability gap as a predictor.
rationale: In 2016 Clinton had a similar favorability-vs-head-to-head gap and lost. Favorability measures likability, while votes depend on perceived policy and who 'fights for you'.
evidence_quote: I don't particularly think there's any reason to expect that gap to close.

title: Likability isn't enough
statement: Silver cites 538's favorability averages for Harris (46.5% favorable, 47.2% unfavorable) and Trump (43.3% favorable, 52.4% unfavorable) as of Oct 22, 2024. Harris led by 3.2 points on favorable share and 5.2 points on unfavorable share.
quantities: Harris favorable = 46.5 percent (538 average, Oct 2024); Harris unfavorable = 47.2 percent (538 average, Oct 2024); Trump favorable = 43.3 percent (538 average, Oct 2024); Trump unfavorable = 52.4 percent (538 average, Oct 2024); favorable gap = 3.2 percentage points (Harris advantage); unfavorable gap = 5.2 percentage points (Harris advantage)
evidence_quote: Harris's favorability rating is 46.5 percent, according to 538. Donald Trump's is 43.3 percent.

title: Likability isn't enough
statement: The RealClearPolitics favorability chart for 2016 shows Clinton's net favorability at about -12.6 and Trump's at about -21.0 near election time. Clinton's net favorability advantage over Trump (roughly 8 points) exceeded her head-to-head polling lead.
quantities: Clinton net favorability = -12.6 percentage points (RCP average, late 2016); Trump net favorability = -21.0 percentage points (RCP average, late 2016)

title: Likability isn't enough
statement: In 2016, Clinton underperformed her polls, but the errors were mostly at the state level. National polls were quite accurate.
evidence_quote: Clinton underperformed her polls in 2016 — but the errors were mostly at the state level. National polls were quite accurate.

title: Likability isn't enough
statement: Silver cautions against overstating the importance of campaign tactics, which are largely constrained by underlying conditions of the race outside the candidates' control. Messaging matters only at the margin.
rationale: Fundamentals constrain campaigns.
evidence_quote: I don't want to overstate the importance of campaign tactics, a lot of which are constrained by the underlying conditions of the race that are outside of the candidates' control.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: Silver states that polls are typically off by around 3 points in one direction or the other. He treats this as a 'normal-sized' polling error.
quantities: typical polling error = around 3 points (typical polling miss in presidential elections)
evidence_quote: polls are typically off by around 3 points in one direction or the other

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model's simulations account for correlated polling error across states. As a result, a normal-sized error can push all 7 key battleground states toward the same candidate.
quantities: number of key battleground states = 7 states (AZ, GA, MI, NC, NV, PA, WI)
rationale: Polling errors are correlated across states, so a sweep is a natural outcome.
evidence_quote: In our simulations yesterday, which account for the possibility of a correlated polling error, the most common outcome was Trump winning all 7 swing states

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: In the Silver Bulletin simulations of October 22, 2024, the most common single outcome was Trump winning all 7 swing states (24%, or 24.4% in the table). The next most common was a Harris sweep of all 7 (15%, or 15.3% in the table).
quantities: Trump sweep probability = 24.4 percent (simulations, Oct 22, 2024); Harris sweep probability = 15.3 percent (simulations, Oct 22, 2024)
evidence_quote: the most common outcome was Trump winning all 7 swing states: this happened 24 percent of the time. And the next most common was a Harris sweep, which occurred in 15 percent of simulations

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: The 'paths to victory' table is built from 40,000 simulations of the Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model. It enumerates all 128 (2^7) win/loss permutations of the 7 likeliest tipping-point states, with each permutation's probability and Harris's Electoral College win probability in that scenario.
quantities: simulations = 40,000 simulations (model run underlying the table, Oct 22, 2024); permutations = 128 scenarios (2^7 combinations of 7 tipping-point states)

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: In the paths-to-victory table, Harris is given a default number of electoral votes in each scenario. Each state other than the 7 tipping-point states is assigned to whichever candidate currently leads that state's forecast. Harris's win probability within a scenario can still fall between 0 and 100%, which suggests the probabilities are computed from simulations in which non-battleground states also vary.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: Scenario rows from the October 22, 2024 table, listed as AZ, GA, MI, NC, NV, PA, WI: (1) R R R R D R R (only Nevada to Harris) 4.6%, 232 Harris EVs, 0.2% Harris win. (2) R D D D D D D 3.4%, 308 EVs, 100%. (3) R R D R D D D (Harris wins MI, NV, PA, WI) 2.9%, 276 EVs, 98.7%. (4) D R D D D D D 2.8%, 303 EVs, 100%. (5) D R D R D D D 2.6%, 287 EVs, 99.8%. (6) R R R R R R D 2.6%, 236 EVs, 0.0%. (7) R R D R R D D (Harris wins the Blue Wall only) 2.2%, 270 EVs, 85.4%. (8) R R D R R R R 1.9%, 241 EVs, 0.1%. (9) R D D D R D D 1.9%, 302 EVs, 99.6%. (10) R R D R R R D 1.9%, 251 EVs, 0.7%. (11) R R D R D R D 1.6%, 257 EVs, 1.6%. (12) R R D D D D D 1.6%, 292 EVs, 99.8%. (13) R D R R R R R 1.3%, 242 EVs, 0.6%. Harris's base is 226 EVs if she loses all 7 and 319 if she sweeps.
quantities: Harris EVs with all 7 lost = 226 electoral votes (default allocation); Harris EVs with all 7 won = 319 electoral votes (default allocation); Blue Wall-only scenario probability = 2.2 percent (Harris wins MI, PA, WI only); Harris win probability in Blue Wall-only scenario = 85.4 percent (270 EVs at default allocation)

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: In the 270-EV Blue Wall-only scenario, Harris wins only 85.4% of the time rather than 100%. This implies the model also varies non-battleground states (e.g., NE-2, or other states) within simulations, and that ties or other-state flips matter.
quantities: Harris win probability at 270 default EVs = 85.4 percent (scenario R R D R R D D)

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: The baseline assumption of the Silver Bulletin model is that the polls will probably be wrong to some degree, but the direction of the error is extremely hard to predict. The model therefore does not build in a directional bias correction for Trump's past overperformance.
rationale: Empirically there is basically no correlation in polling error from one cycle to the next.
evidence_quote: the baseline assumption of the Silver Bulletin model is that while the polls could be wrong again — and in fact, they probably will be wrong to some degree — it's extremely hard to predict the direction of the error.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: Empirically, there is basically no correlation in the direction of polling error from one election cycle to the next.
evidence_quote: Empirically, there's basically no correlation in polling error from one cycle to the next one.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: Forecasters should assume a pro-Trump polling error is roughly as likely as a pro-Harris one, i.e., the error distribution is centered on zero.
rationale: Pollsters changing their methods, possible overcompensation, and possible herding cut in different directions.
evidence_quote: you should probably assume that a pro-Trump polling error is roughly as likely as a pro-Harris one.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: A Trump sweep of the 7 swing states is more likely than a Harris sweep in the simulations not because of any directional error assumption. Trump has clearer leads in Georgia and Arizona, which tilt toward him, while the other 5 states are basically toss-ups, so a Trump sweep is a slightly less heavy lift.
evidence_quote: he has clearer "leads" in Georgia and Arizona than Harris has in any state — the other 5 states are basically toss-ups

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: Trump's polling overperformance in 2016 and 2020 was likely caused by nonresponse bias rather than 'shy Trump voters' lying to pollsters. Democrats are more likely to respond to political surveys, so pollsters weren't reaching enough Trump voters.
rationale: There is little evidence for the shy-voter theory, there is no persistent worldwide right-wing overperformance, and there is less stigma than ever to supporting Trump.
evidence_quote: It's not that Trump voters are lying to pollsters; it's that in 2016 and 2020, pollsters weren't reaching enough of them.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: Pollsters have changed their methods in response to 2016 and 2020 nonresponse bias. Silver estimates that if they still used their 2016/2020 techniques, polls would probably show a Harris lead in the Electoral College instead of a rough toss-up.
evidence_quote: If polling firms were still applying the same techniques they did in 2016 and 2020, we'd probably be seeing a Harris lead in the Electoral College right now.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: Pollsters may overcompensate for past misses on Trump, consciously or unconsciously making assumptions that favor him. The 2017 UK election is an example: pollsters adjusted for 'shy Tories' and Labour beat its polls instead.
rationale: Polls are increasingly like mini-models with many subjective decision points.
evidence_quote: If pollsters are terrified of missing low on Mr. Trump again, they may consciously or unconsciously make assumptions that favor him.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: One possible cause of the 2020 polling error was COVID: Democrats were more likely to socially distance and had more time to respond to polls. If that was the main cause, the bias may not recur, and corrections for it could overcompensate.
evidence_quote: if the 2020 polling error was primarily caused by COVID: Democrats being more likely to "socially distance" and having more time to respond to polls

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: Pollsters may herd toward other polls or decline to publish outliers. In 2024 a conspicuously large number of swing-state polls showed margins within 2 points either way, and almost nobody except maybe NYT/Siena published results like Trump +5 or Harris +6.
quantities: herding band = 2 points (conspicuously many swing-state polls within ±2)
rationale: Pollsters are influenced by vibes and the media narrative.
evidence_quote: a conspicuously large number of polls in this race show the swing states within 2 points in either direction

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: Silver speculates that if pollsters had published unadjusted, unherded numbers, the results might be a hair more favorable to Harris than the public record, which has been influenced by recent Trumpy vibes. He explicitly does not try to predict the direction of polling bias.
evidence_quote: it would be a hair more favorable to Harris than the numbers we're seeing in the public record

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: Gut instinct and media 'vibes' should not override models or other relatively objective indicators. Elections are too infrequent to calibrate intuition, and guts tend to extrapolate the last election or echo the media.
rationale: Gut can be calibrated in poker over thousands of hands, but elections occur once every four years.
evidence_quote: Basically, you should stick to the models or other relatively objective indicators.

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: Conventional wisdom is wrong more often than the polls are. Examples are dismissing Trump's chances in 2016 despite a fairly close race and misjudging 2022. Silver sees a case for mild contrarianism, shading slightly against conventional wisdom.
rationale: Media echo chambers exaggerate small shifts in 'momentum' because saying 'toss-up' repeatedly is boring.
evidence_quote: The conventional wisdom is very often wrong — it's wrong more often than the polls are

title: Why Harris could beat her polls
statement: Media coverage of polls, including headlines and which polls get discussed, swings more than the underlying data as accounted for by models. The figure orders sources from least to most vibes-distorted: 'virginal' polls, polls as published and fed into models, polls as discussed by the media, and vibes/conventional wisdom.
evidence_quote: Media coverage of polls — how articles are headlined or which polls generate more discussion — often swings around more than the underlying data as accounted for by models like ours.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: In the Silver Bulletin polling average and presidential model, when a firm releases both a likely voter (LV) and a registered voter (RV) version of the same poll, the LV version is used instead of the RV version.
rationale: LV polls are theoretically more accurate than RV polls.
evidence_quote: When a firm releases two versions of a poll, we use the LV version instead of the RV version.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: The Silver Bulletin polling average and forecast give LV polls a higher weight than RV polls.
rationale: LV polls are theoretically more accurate.
evidence_quote: we weight polls of likely voters higher than polls of registered voters in our polling average and forecast.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: When a poll publishes only RV numbers, the Silver Bulletin model adjusts it to an LV basis. The size of the adjustment is estimated from polls that release both LV and RV versions of the same survey.
rationale: Puts RV-only polls on the same footing as the more accurate LV polls.
evidence_quote: when a poll only publishes RV numbers, we adjust it to essentially transform it to an LV basis. The adjustment is based on polls that release both likely-voter and registered-voter versions of the same survey

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: The authors call the LV/RV difference something they 'carefully track' as one factor the model accounts for. This implies the RV-to-LV adjustment is estimated from current-cycle data rather than fixed.
evidence_quote: We carefully track the differences between likely voter (LV) and registered voter (RV) polls because this is one factor our model accounts for.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: Historically, LV screens helped Republicans. Pollsters traditionally switched from RV to LV polls after Labor Day, which often boosted GOP candidates, for example Bush in 2004. Part of Bush's September 2004 surge was also due to the timing of the Republican convention.
quantities: Example year = 2004 (Bush-Kerry polling, RV-to-LV switch after Labor Day)
rationale: Republicans were historically the more regular, reliable voters.
evidence_quote: Traditionally, pollsters began switching from registered voter polls to likely voter polls after Labor Day, which often boosted Republican candidates.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: Before his debate and exit from the race, Biden did better in LV polls than in RV polls in 2024, a reversal of the historical pattern of LV screens helping Republicans.
evidence_quote: Joe Biden was doing better in LV polls than in RV polls — a reversal of the historical trend.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: In 2024 national polls that released both versions, Harris averaged D+2.3 among RVs versus D+2.8 among LVs, so LV screens helped her by 0.5 points nationally.
quantities: National RV margin = D +2.3 percentage points (Paired LV/RV national polls since Harris entered the race); National LV margin = D +2.8 percentage points (Paired LV/RV national polls since Harris entered the race); National LV-RV difference = 0.5 percentage points (In Harris's favor)
evidence_quote: The average margin in these polls is D +2.3 among RVs as compared to a D +2.8 margin in LV polls — a 0.5-point difference in Harris' favor.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: In state-level battleground polls, LV versions were on average 0.5 points more favorable to Trump than RV versions (state average D+0.6 RV vs D+0.1 LV). By state (RV margin, LV margin, LV shift): Arizona R+0.7 to R+1.0 (R+0.3); Georgia R+0.2 to R+1.4 (R+1.2); Michigan D+2.0 to D+3.2 (D+1.2); Nevada D+3.3 to D+2.0 (R+1.3); North Carolina EVEN to R+0.9 (R+0.9); Pennsylvania D+2.6 to D+1.7 (R+0.9); Wisconsin D+3.8 to D+3.4 (R+0.4).
quantities: State average RV margin = D +0.6 percentage points (Paired polls, battleground states); State average LV margin = D +0.1 percentage points (Paired polls, battleground states); State average LV shift = R +0.5 percentage points (LV relative to RV); Arizona LV shift = R +0.3 percentage points (RV R+0.7, LV R+1.0); Georgia LV shift = R +1.2 percentage points (RV R+0.2, LV R+1.4); Michigan LV shift = D +1.2 percentage points (RV D+2.0, LV D+3.2); Nevada LV shift = R +1.3 percentage points (RV D+3.3, LV D+2.0); North Carolina LV shift = R +0.9 percentage points (RV EVEN, LV R+0.9); Pennsylvania LV shift = R +0.9 percentage points (RV D+2.6, LV D+1.7); Wisconsin LV shift = R +0.4 percentage points (RV D+3.8, LV D+3.4)
evidence_quote: If you average across all states, you end up with LV polls being 0.5 points more favorable to Trump.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: State-level LV/RV comparisons rest on small samples. For example, the Silver Bulletin database had only 10 Michigan polls that published both LV and RV numbers, so state-specific gaps should not be over-interpreted.
quantities: Michigan paired LV/RV polls = 10 polls (Silver Bulletin database as of Oct 24, 2024)
evidence_quote: in Michigan, there are 10 polls in our database that published both LV and RV numbers. That isn't nothing, but it isn't a huge sample either.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: The state-level LV shift toward Trump grew steadily through the 2024 campaign: 0.1 points in July, about 0.3 in August, about 0.65 in September and about 0.7 in October. The national LV shift toward Harris was about 0.45 in July, about 0.7 in August, about 0.35 in September and about 0.2 in October.
quantities: State LV shift, July = 0.1 percentage points (R) (State polls, LV vs RV); State LV shift, October = 0.7 percentage points (R) (State polls, LV vs RV); State LV shift, Aug/Sep = ~0.33 / ~0.65 percentage points (R) (Read from chart); National LV shift, Jul/Aug/Sep/Oct = ~-0.44 / ~-0.68 / ~-0.36 / ~-0.22 percentage points (negative = D) (Read from chart)
evidence_quote: In July, LV polls at the state level were only 0.1 points more favorable to Trump than RV polls. Three months later? Trump does 0.7 points better in state-level LV polls.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: Calibrating the Silver Bulletin model on RV rather than LV polls would narrow its Electoral College/popular vote gap and slightly raise Harris's win probability, resembling the universe of NYT/Siena polls. The model's LV preference therefore contributes to its estimated Electoral College bias.
rationale: State LV polls favor Trump while national LV polls favor Harris.
evidence_quote: If we calibrated our model based on RV rather than LV polls, it would show a narrower Electoral College / popular vote gap, with Harris's overall win probability slightly improving.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: Pollsters differ in the direction of their LV/RV gap. Nationally, Harris does better in the LV version for nearly all firms: NYT/Siena +0.8, YouGov +0.3, Marist +0.5. Harris Insights is the only exception.
quantities: NYT/Siena national LV gain for Harris = 0.8 percentage points (2024); YouGov national LV gain for Harris = 0.3 percentage points (2024); Marist national LV gain for Harris = 0.5 percentage points (2024)
evidence_quote: Harris does 0.8 points better in the LV versions of national New York Times/Siena polls, 0.3 points better in LV YouGov polls, and 0.5 points better in LV Marist polls.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: State-level LV-minus-RV margin shifts by pollster (positive = Republican), among firms with at least two state polls: NYT/Siena -0.5, Marquette -0.5, Washington Post -0.4, Morning Consult -0.2, YouGov +0.4, Florida Atlantic +0.4, Marist +0.6, Beacon/Shaw (Fox) +1.6, TIPP +2.0, Focaldata +2.5, Noble Predictive +3.0.
quantities: NYT/Siena = -0.5 percentage points (State LV-RV shift); Marquette = -0.5 percentage points (State LV-RV shift); Washington Post = -0.4 percentage points (State LV-RV shift); Morning Consult = -0.2 percentage points (State LV-RV shift); YouGov = +0.4 percentage points (State LV-RV shift); Florida Atlantic = +0.4 percentage points (State LV-RV shift); Marist = +0.6 percentage points (State LV-RV shift); Beacon/Shaw (Fox) = +1.6 percentage points (State LV-RV shift); TIPP = +2.0 percentage points (State LV-RV shift); Focaldata = +2.5 percentage points (State LV-RV shift); Noble Predictive = +3.0 percentage points (State LV-RV shift)

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: The direction of a pollster's LV/RV gap does not track pollster quality. A+ pollsters NYT/Siena and Washington Post show Harris better among LVs, while A-rated Marist and Fox News show the opposite.
evidence_quote: It isn't a quality issue. Some of our highest-rated pollsters like NYT and The Washington Post (both A+) show Harris doing better among LVs.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: LV screens involve subjective pollster decisions. They are one source of uncertainty that makes a polling error in either direction highly plausible, possibly including aggressive swing-state screens or herding toward a toss-up.
evidence_quote: They're one of the factors that makes the polling situation uncertain and a polling error in either direction highly plausible.

title: A mystery in likely voter polls
statement: In the Washington Post North Carolina example, Trump led by 4 among RVs and by 3 among LVs. Both candidates gained from third-party and undecided voters in the LV version.
quantities: Trump RV lead = 4 percentage points (WaPo NC poll); Trump LV lead = 3 percentage points (WaPo NC poll)
evidence_quote: And both Trump and Harris gain ground from third-party candidates and the undecided column.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model does not use early-vote data (party breakdowns of early ballots) as an input to its vote-share forecast. Silver doubts that early voting could add much value even with a lot of effort.
rationale: There are no good baselines, polls already capture early voting, vote choice is unknown, and early-vote-based predictions have a poor track record.
evidence_quote: when people ask me how early voting is incorporated into the model, the answer is that (with one extremely minor exception) it isn't

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: The only use of early-vote data in the Silver Bulletin 2024 model is this: if the total number of votes already counted in a state exceeds the model's turnout prediction, the model raises its turnout projection for that state.
evidence_quote: we'll up our turnout projections in a state if the total number of votes already counted exceeds our model's prediction.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: In 2016, across 13 states with partisan early-vote breakdowns compiled by Michael McDonald, the D-minus-R early-vote margin missed the final Clinton-minus-Trump margin by an average of 14 points.
quantities: average early vote misprediction = 14 percentage points (2016, 13 states); states with data = 13 states (2016)
rationale: Early voters are not a representative sample of the electorate.
evidence_quote: On average, the D less R margin in the early vote mispredicted the final Clinton/Trump margin by 14 points!

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: The 2016 table (University of Florida Election Lab) shows the gap between the D-R early-vote margin and the final margin in each state. It is smallest in Oregon (1.1), Florida (2.6), Arizona (2.9) and Nevada (3.5). It is largest in West Virginia (53.5), Louisiana (25.5) and Nebraska (22.3). In West Virginia, Democrats led the early vote by 12 points while Trump won by 41.7.
quantities: Arizona error = 2.9 percentage points (early vote -6.4, final -3.5); Colorado early vote margin = -0.8 percentage points (final +4.9); Florida error = 2.6 percentage points (early +1.4, final -1.2); Iowa error = 16.1 percentage points (early +6.7); Louisiana error = 25.5 percentage points (early +5.9); Maryland error = 15.2 percentage points (early +41.6, final +26.4); Nebraska error = 22.3 percentage points (early -2.8, final -25.1); Nevada error = 3.5 percentage points (early +5.9, final +2.4); North Carolina error = 13.5 percentage points (final -3.7); California error = 15.4 percentage points (final +30.0); Oregon error = 1.1 percentage points (2016); West Virginia error = 53.5 percentage points (final -41.7)

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: As a benchmark for polling error, pollsters are criticized when off by 3 points, and larger misses are considered disasters. A 14-point miss, like the average early-vote misprediction, would be unacceptable for a poll.
quantities: criticized poll error threshold = 3 points (pollster accuracy norms)
evidence_quote: Pollsters get yelled at when their polls are off by even 3 points, and anything more than that is considered an absolute disaster.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: Sample size does not fix a biased sample. The 1936 Literary Digest poll of almost 2.3 million voters showed Landon beating Roosevelt 57-43, but Roosevelt won by 24, a 38-point error. Its sample was drawn from lists of telephone and automobile owners, who skewed rich and Republican.
quantities: Literary Digest sample = almost 2.3 million voters (1936); polling error = 38 points (1936 Literary Digest); Roosevelt margin = 24 points (1936)
rationale: If you're aiming at the wrong target, more respondents don't improve accuracy.
evidence_quote: If you're aiming at the wrong target, it doesn't matter how many people you poll — it won't get any more accurate.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: Early-vote baselines are unstable for several reasons: early-voting rules change, states made one-off COVID provisions in 2020, voters take time to adopt new methods, and parties change their emphasis. Trump discouraged early voting in 2020 but encouraged it in 2024, and Democrats shifted heavily to mail in 2020.
rationale: You are aiming at a moving target, so comparisons across cycles are unreliable.
evidence_quote: But you're aiming at a moving target.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: Silver's preferred likely-voter approach for a pollster is probabilistic: each respondent gets a probability of voting, and respondents who have already voted get 100 percent.
quantities: likely voter score for already-voted respondents = 100 percent (Silver's preferred LV method)
evidence_quote: if I were running a poll, I'd treat likely voters probabilistically, and anyone who had already voted would get a score of 100 percent.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: Early-vote information is already captured by polls, because pollsters ask respondents whether they have already voted and combine early voters with likely voters who have yet to vote. A poll-based model therefore implicitly includes it. CNN's 2024 polls illustrate this. In Nevada, Trump led early voters by 6 but the topline was Trump +1. In Arizona, Harris led early voters by 9 but the topline was Harris +1.
quantities: CNN Nevada topline = Trump +1 points (Oct 2024); CNN Nevada early voters = Trump +6 points (Oct 2024); CNN Arizona early voters = Harris +9 points (Oct 2024); CNN Arizona topline = Harris +1 points (Oct 2024)
evidence_quote: pollsters, who are fully aware of what the early voting data says in Nevada and ask respondents if they already voted, continue to show the race tied.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: Vote method shifts without vote choice shifting. Early voting mostly cannibalizes enthusiastic voters who would have voted on Election Day anyway. In Maryland, the in-person early vote was purple in 2020 and blue in 2022, and the Election Day vote was red in 2020 and blue in 2022, yet Biden in 2020 and Moore in 2022 both won 67-33. Split Ticket's chart puts mail at 53% of ballots in 2020 versus 29% in 2022, and Election Day at 14% versus 52%.
quantities: MD 2020 mail share = 53 percent of ballots (83% D); MD 2020 in-person early share = 32 percent of ballots (53% D); MD 2020 Election Day share = 14 percent of ballots (41% D); MD 2022 mail share = 29 percent of ballots (83% D); MD 2022 early share = 19 percent of ballots (67% D); MD 2022 Election Day share = 52 percent of ballots (57% D); final margin = 67-33 percent (both elections)
rationale: It's much easier to change how someone votes than who they vote for.
evidence_quote: it's much easier to get someone to change how they vote than who they vote for.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: Party-registration early-vote counts do not reveal vote shares, which depend on crossover rates and independents. Silver's worked example: Harris wins 6% of Republicans, Trump wins 3.5% of Democrats, and Harris wins independents by 4. Under those rates, a 38-40-22 D-R-I early-vote breakdown, which looks like R+2, is actually Harris +1.
quantities: Harris share of Republicans = 6 percent (October 2024 national polls); Trump share of Democrats = 3.5 percent (October 2024 national polls); independent margin = 4 points (hypothetical Harris); D-R-I breakdown = 38-40-22 percent (hypothetical early vote); implied result = Harris +1 points (hypothetical)
evidence_quote: a 38-40-22 D-R-I breakdown in the early vote, which looks like a 2-point Republican lead, would actually be Harris +1.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: Independents typically make up a smaller share of early voters than of the overall electorate. They are generally less enthusiastic and more likely to decide late.
evidence_quote: Independent voters are generally less enthusiastic and more likely to make a decision late in the race.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: Early-vote analysis has too many free parameters to be reliable: trend since 2020 versus since 2016, absolute numbers, demographic subgroups, and voter propensity breakdowns. This invites cherry-picking. It also has a bad track record; in 2016 it helped convince the media and Democrats that Clinton was certain to win. Silver calls it a gateway to poll unskewing that adds more noise than signal.
evidence_quote: there are too many floating parameters — too many ways to cherry-pick to tell yourself the narrative you like.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: Nevada is a partial exception where early vote matters more, because the state traditionally has little Election Day vote, and Jon Ralston's analysis is worth reading. Ambiguities remain even there: Democrats do well in mail early voting, Republicans win in-person early voting, and mail ballots are reported with a lag of several days.
evidence_quote: the early vote in Nevada matters more than elsewhere because it traditionally has little election-day vote.

title: The early vote doesn't reliably predict results
statement: Early-vote partisan patterns vary idiosyncratically across similar states. In 2016, North Carolina's early vote was blue while Florida's was purple, because Republicans in Florida traditionally emphasize early voting to older voters. More Republicans than Democrats voted early in Colorado, yet Clinton won the state.
evidence_quote: Similar states can produce surprisingly different patterns.

title: There’s more herding in swing state polls than at a sheep farm in the Scottish Highlands
statement: The Silver Bulletin 2024 presidential model ran 40,000 simulations in its Friday-afternoon run of Nov 1, 2024.

title: There’s more herding in swing state polls than at a sheep farm in the Scottish Highlands
statement: Silver's herding test works in three steps. First, for each poll, compute from its sample size the probability that it shows a margin within ±2.5 points if the race is truly tied, using the margin-of-error formula for the difference between candidates. Second, sum these probabilities to get the expected number of close polls. Third, use a binomial distribution, assuming independent polls, to get the probability of at least the observed number of close polls.
quantities: closeness threshold = 2.5 percentage points (non-integer chosen because averaged poll versions produce half-point margins); P(within 2.5) for n=400 = about 40 percent (tied race); P(within 2.5) for n=5686 = almost 95 percent (tied race)
rationale: Honest polls should produce more apparent outliers than observed.
evidence_quote: Based on a binomial distribution — which assumes that all polls are independent of one another, which theoretically they should be

statement: Bonica and Grumbach's supplementary specifications found moderation effects under 3 points of vote share. quantities: B&G max effect = under 3 percentage points vote share (supplementary analyses); margin equivalent = up to 6 points of margin (Silver's conversion)
evidence_quote: So in terms of vote margin, the effects of moderation are up to 6 points in some of the models they tried out. That's huge!

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
statement: Marginal candidate effects matter more when control of government is expected to come down to a couple of points in a few key races. A 2-point moderation bonus matters little if incumbents usually win by 10 points, but it matters a lot in nail-biters. Morris's estimate that moderation raises win probability by 'just' 10 percent is also large when multiplied across dozens of races.
quantities: moderation bonus example = 2 points (illustrative); typical incumbent margin example = 10 points (illustrative); win probability increase = 10 percent (Morris estimate)
evidence_quote: A 2-point moderation "bonus" might not matter much if incumbents usually win by 10 points, but if everything is a nail-biter, it matters more.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
statement: Strong prior regularities such as the median voter theorem should inform model checking. If a model finds that a well-established factor like moderation hardly matters at all, Silver says that result should be regarded with suspicion ('basic Bayesian reasoning').
rationale: Exercise-is-good-for-health analogy.
evidence_quote: it's a strong enough regularity that if your model finds that exercise hardly matters at all, it should be regarded with suspicion. This is basic Bayesian reasoning.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
statement: Running a model under many specifications is good practice. Good model-builders learn which factors are robust across specifications, and this is the 'art' of statistical inference.
evidence_quote: What street smart model-builders do is develop a sense for which factors are most robust once they've tested out a variety of specifications.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
statement: If a factor matters a lot in some specifications but not in others, the underlying data may be dubious. The remedy is to quality-check the data, collect more, or develop a more rigorous processing algorithm.
evidence_quote: sometimes the issue is that your underlying data is dubious and you need to go back and QC the data, collect more of it, or go back to the lab

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
statement: Domain knowledge, such as forecasting every congressional district, helps vet model specifications and catch mismeasured inputs. Jain found enough candidates with apparently misspecified ideology scores to conclude that CFScores and B&G's other measures add a lot of noise.
evidence_quote: Domain knowledge — for instance, making forecasts of every Congressional district, as Split Ticket does — can help greatly for vetting different model specifications.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
statement: Silver argues that machine learning is inappropriate for election modeling except under three conditions: (a) very large data, millions of observations or more, versus the dozens to thousands typical of elections; (b) ambiguous relationships among variables, whereas politics has a finite list of well-specified factors such as incumbency, moderation and presidential vote; and (c) priority on prediction over causal explanation.
quantities: data size suited to ML = millions or more observations (threshold for ML); typical election data size = dozens to thousands observations (election analysis)
rationale: Small, structured datasets favor classical inference guided by domain knowledge.
evidence_quote: not the dozens or hundreds or at best thousands of observations that you're usually limited to in election analysis

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
statement: Silver describes B&G's glmnet approach as essentially lasso regression, which on small datasets is a close cousin of stepwise regression. He says automated variable selection is unsophisticated and generally inferior to choices made by an experienced researcher with domain knowledge.
evidence_quote: it's a form of lasso regression, which when applied to a small dataset like this, is a kissing cousin of the much-derided stepwise regression.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority
statement: High explained variance, such as B&G's claimed 92% of congressional vote-share variation, is not impressive because district partisanship explains most of it. Implausibly accurate fit to past elections is a sign of overfitting ('the Allan Lichtman problem').
quantities: BG-WAR R² claim = 92 % of variance (congressional vote shares)
evidence_quote: If you claim to have "predicted" every past election with implausible accuracy, that's usually a sign that you've tortured the past data until it fit.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority

Holdout or out-of-sample testing cannot remove the 'original sin' of knowing the results while designing the model, because knowledge of outcomes shapes which specifications and variables the researcher considers plausible.
evidence_quote: There's no technique that can overcome the "original sin" of knowing what the results were before you started designing your model.

title: Real talk on models, moderation, and the misuse of academic authority

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: Silver Bulletin polling averages aim to include all professionally conducted surveys, listing them under the polling firm rather than the media sponsor.
quantities: update frequency = ~6 updates per week (polling averages)
rationale: Inclusivity is the general aim; reliability is handled through weighting rather than exclusion.
evidence_quote: Our general aim is for inclusivity. We seek to include all professionally-conducted surveys.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: Silver Bulletin excludes four kinds of polls: those from pollsters banned for known or suspected faked data, DIY polls by non-professional hobbyists on platforms like Google Surveys, 'polls' that blend or smooth data with methods such as MRP, and polls that ask vote choice only after revealing leading information about candidates.
rationale: These are not genuine, independent, neutrally worded measurements of opinion.
evidence_quote: We don't use "polls" that blend or smooth their data using methods such as MRP.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: Internal and campaign polls are included if they meet the other standards. For approval averages they are treated like any other poll; for the generic ballot they get a different house-effect prior. Nominally nonpartisan pollsters with undisclosed histories of partisan work, currently Trafalgar Group and Rasmussen Reports, are automatically classified as partisan.
rationale: Undisclosed campaign relationships make a firm's polls behave like partisan polls.
evidence_quote: Internal or campaign polls are included, provided they meet these other standards.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: When a pollster publishes several versions of one survey, the generic ballot average prefers likely voters over registered voters over all adults, while approval averages prefer the reverse order (with a separate likely-voter-only approval average). All averages prefer versions that include leaners. When a survey has several turnout models or methods, all applicable versions are averaged.
rationale: Election-oriented measures should reflect the electorate; approval measures the whole public.
evidence_quote: we prioritize polls of likely voters > registered voters > all adults. For approval ratings, the opposite is true

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: The generic ballot average pools two question wordings: which party's candidate the voter will support for Congress, and which party they would prefer to control Congress.
evidence_quote: two slightly distinct questions are included in the average

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: Each poll gets an influence score from three factors: the Silver Bulletin pollster rating (historical accuracy plus membership in transparency initiatives), sample size with strong diminishing returns, and recency. The sample-size and recency settings are set empirically.
rationale: Sample size matters less in practice than in theory, possibly because pollsters' complex weighting reduces the effective sample size.
evidence_quote: sample size makes less difference than it does in theory, and there are considerable diminishing returns from adding additional voters to the sample.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: Recency weights are tuned to best predict new polls over the following two weeks. They are more aggressive for presidential approval than for the generic ballot or Musk favorability, and the generic ballot's recency weighting becomes more aggressive as Election Day approaches.
quantities: validation horizon for recency settings = 2 weeks (settings chosen to predict polls in the subsequent two weeks)
rationale: Approval ratings stabilize more quickly, so shifts are more likely to be signal than noise.
evidence_quote: based on which settings best predict new polls over the subsequent two weeks.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: To stop one firm 'flooding the zone', weights are based on the total number of voters a pollster contacted in a time window. A firm that polls daily or weekly maxes out its total weight, which is divided among its surveys in that window. Tracking polls with overlapping sample dates get an additional adjustment.
rationale: Prevents prolific pollsters from dominating the average through volume alone.
evidence_quote: it essentially "maxes out" the total weight assigned to the firm, and this weight is divided among all instances of the survey in a given window.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: The polling average on each date is a local polynomial regression using a blend of more aggressive and more conservative smoothing settings. The settings are chosen empirically so the average is stable, free of autoregression, and minimizes error in predicting the next new survey.
rationale: The current average should be the best predictor of forthcoming polls.
evidence_quote: the current polling average should be the best predictor of forthcoming surveys.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: Too little smoothing overfits and makes the curve jumpy, while too much smoothing lags new trends. Empirically the generic ballot tends to be under-smoothed and too bouncy, which is less true for approval ratings, so approval settings are more aggressive.
rationale: Bias-variance trade-off in smoothing.
evidence_quote: we've found that generic ballot can suffer from under-smoothing, making the average too "bouncy,"

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: A house effect is a firm's persistent difference from other polls of the same race at the same time. Only a proportion of it is removed, and that proportion grows with the firm's total sample size on that question, from a small fraction for a firm with one or two polls to nearly 100 percent for very frequent pollsters.
quantities: share of house effect removed = close to 100 percent (firms that poll a question extremely often)
rationale: Shrinkage: confidence in a firm's house effect grows with how much it has polled.
evidence_quote: The proportion subject to the house effects adjustment is based on the aggregate sample size of polling conducted by the firm.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: The generic ballot uses a newer house-effect formula that starts with a smaller adjustment but ramps up faster as sample size grows. Silver Bulletin considers it slightly more accurate and expects to move approval averages to it, though it only changes results in the decimal places.
rationale: Slightly more accurate.
evidence_quote: starts out with a lower adjustment but ramps it up more quickly as the aggregate sample size increases.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: House effects are estimated separately for each side, approve and disapprove or Democrat and Republican, rather than only on the margin. The model also adjusts for firms that persistently report more or fewer undecided voters than the average.
rationale: Firms differ systematically in how many undecideds they report.
evidence_quote: Certain firms persistently include more or fewer undecided voters than the polling average, and so we adjust for this, too.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: The 'true north' that polls are adjusted toward is weighted toward higher-rated pollsters. For the generic ballot, partisan-sponsored polls are excluded from the true-north calculation.
rationale: The reference point for bias should come from the most reliable, non-partisan sources.
evidence_quote: Firms with higher pollster ratings have more influence on what our model considers to be "true north"

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: House effects are found iteratively. First compute an average without adjustments, then estimate each firm's house effect against the polynomial curve, recompute the average with adjusted polls, re-estimate house effects, and repeat several times until there is no further improvement.
rationale: House effects and the average depend on each other, so they are solved jointly.
evidence_quote: The model loops through the process several times until there are no further gains to be had.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: For the generic ballot and the horse-race averages used in forecasts, explicitly partisan polls start with a prior that they are biased toward the sponsor by a net of about 1.7 points. Nonpartisan polls start with a zero prior. Both priors are eventually overridden by the firm's actual track record against other polls. The prior is not used for presidential approval.
quantities: partisan poll prior bias = ~1.7 points (net margin) (toward the sponsoring party, generic ballot and forecast horse-race averages)
rationale: Default to assuming nonpartisan polls are unbiased and partisan polls lean toward their sponsor until data says otherwise.
model_version: Silver Bulletin generic ballot and forecast averages (2026)
evidence_quote: we assume they're slightly biased toward the sponsoring candidate or party. (More specifically, by a net of about 1.7 points.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: The approval and generic ballot averages display shaded bands showing where 90 percent of new polls are projected to fall, based on historical analysis of such averages over several decades. The bands widen when there are fewer polls and when polls disagree more.
quantities: band coverage = 90 percent of new polls (shaded error region on charts)
evidence_quote: The shaded areas indicate where we project 90 percent of new polls to fall

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: For each state, the generic ballot benchmark equals the state's partisan lean plus the national generic ballot multiplied by the state's elasticity.
evidence_quote: Benchmark = partisan lean score + generic ballot * elasticity

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: A state's partisan lean weights its vote relative to the nation 50 percent on the 2024 presidential election, 25 percent on 2020, and 25 percent on a rolling average of the last five state legislative elections. The legislative figure estimates the lower-chamber popular vote as if all seats were contested, using regression to handle uncontested seats.
quantities: weight on 2024 presidential = 50 percent (partisan lean); weight on 2020 presidential = 25 percent (partisan lean); weight on state legislative average = 25 percent (rolling average of past five state legislative elections)
rationale: Blends recent presidential results with down-ballot partisanship.
evidence_quote: the formula gives 50 percent of the weight to the 2024 presidential election, 25 percent to the 2020 presidential election, and 25 percent to a rolling average

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: Elasticity measures how strongly a state swings with the national environment. It is estimated from 2022 and 2024 Cooperative Election Study microdata by giving each voter a probability of voting D or R and treating voters near 50/50 as more swingable. Current values run from 0.90 in Mississippi to 1.23 in Alaska and 1.25 in Hawaii.
quantities: CES sample size = 60,000 voters per survey (2022 and 2024 Cooperative Election Studies); minimum elasticity = 0.90 (Mississippi); elasticity = 1.23 (Alaska); maximum elasticity = 1.25 (Hawaii)
rationale: Polarized electorates move little with the national tide, while states with more cross-pressured swing voters move more.
model_version: Silver Bulletin / FiveThirtyEight elasticity concept, 2026 values
evidence_quote: range from 0.90 in Mississippi to 1.23 in Alaska and 1.25 in Hawaii.

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages
statement: Each voter's vote probability for the elasticity calculation is an average of two models. One uses political variables, namely party identification strength and liberal-conservative self-placement. The other uses demographics only. Cross-pressured voters therefore start closer to 50/50.
rationale: Combining attitudinal and demographic predictors identifies cross-pressured voters.
evidence_quote: these probabilities are based on an average of two formulas

title: How Silver Bulletin calculates our polling averages

evidence_quote: leverage the larger volume of polling data available (such as the ability to infer information from both state and national polls).

title: Midterm polls have good news, great news, and bad news for Democrats. Wait, what?
statement: Republicans historically gained when pollsters switched from registered-voter to likely-voter screens. title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: FLIPR applies a likely-voter adjustment to generic ballot polls conducted among registered voters. Following longstanding practice, the adjustment is estimated mainly from polls that publish both LV and RV versions of the same survey. In August 2026 the LV versions were better for Democrats, so FLIPR's generic ballot was D+8.1 versus D+6.7 in the raw average.
quantities: raw generic ballot = D+6.7 points (Aug 11, 2026); FLIPR LV-adjusted generic ballot = D+8.1 points (Aug 11, 2026)
rationale: Registered-voter polls do not account for turnout.
evidence_quote: the adjustment is based mostly on polls that release both likely and registered voter versions of the same survey.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: FLIPR computes a historical 'prior' for the national House popular vote from all congressional elections since 1946, using the president's approval rating, the previous election's result, and whether the election is a midterm, adjusted for increasing partisan polarization. In August 2026 the prior was D+8.7.
quantities: historical prior = D+8.7 points (House popular vote, Aug 2026); data start = 1946 year (congressional elections used for prior)
evidence_quote: We estimate a “prior” based on all congressional elections since 1946, calibrated based on the president’s approval rating, the result of the previous election, and whether the election was a midterm

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: FLIPR comes in three versions: Lite, an attempt at a polls-only forecast; Classic, which adds fundamentals; and Deluxe, which adds expert ratings. At launch, Democrats' House chances were 83 percent in Lite, 87 in Classic and 87 in Deluxe. Senate chances were 57, 56 and 57 percent.
quantities: House D win prob, Deluxe = 87 percent (Aug 11, 2026); House D win prob, Classic = 87 percent (Aug 11, 2026); House D win prob, Lite = 83 percent (Aug 11, 2026); Senate D win prob, Deluxe = 57 percent (Aug 11, 2026)
evidence_quote: the Deluxe version of FLIPR, which accounts for polls, “fundamentals”, and expert ratings, has Democrats with a 87 percent chance of winning the House.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: The Lite (polls-only) version of FLIPR carries considerably greater uncertainty than Classic and Deluxe. It can be more optimistic about expected seat gains yet give a lower win probability, because its error bars are much wider when only polls are used.
rationale: Adding fundamentals reduces forecast error.
evidence_quote: if you’re only allowed to look at polls, the error bars are much wider.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: FLIPR finds the House tipping point at a national environment of about D+3 to D+3.5 after mid-decade redistricting, so Republicans are effectively spotted about a field goal. The Senate threshold for a Democratic majority is around D+6 or better.
quantities: House cut point = 3-3.5 points (D national margin) (2026 maps); Senate cut point = about 6 points (D national margin) (2026 map)
evidence_quote: FLIPR, in line with other models, finds that the cut point is somewhere around 3 or 3.5 percentage points.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: Extremely partisan maps drawn by both parties have greatly reduced the number of competitive House districts, so even a D+9 House popular vote would struggle to match the 41-seat gain of 2018.
quantities: 2018 Democratic House gain = 41 seats (reference)
evidence_quote: extremely partisan maps drawn by both parties have greatly reduced the number of competitive districts in the House.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: Work on FLIPR found the political climate more stable than ever in forecasting-relevant ways: opinions are baked in, voters tune in early, and recent elections have not had the late shifts in the national environment that used to be common in midterms.
evidence_quote: recent elections haven’t featured the late shifts in the political climate that used to be common in midterms.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: FLIPR's analysis finds candidate-quality factors matter only about half as much as when Silver published his first midterm forecast in 2010.
quantities: candidate quality effect relative to 2010 = about half ratio (FLIPR 2026 analysis)
rationale: Rising partisanship and less ticket-splitting.
evidence_quote: candidate quality factors matter only about half as much as when I published my first midterms forecast in 2010.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: Classic and Deluxe expect candidates who trail in polls during or just after contentious primaries to recover toward the state's partisan baseline. In Michigan, Lite had Republican Rogers as a 60 percent favorite, while Classic and Deluxe projected El-Sayed to win by about 3 points against a D+7 to D+8 baseline.
quantities: Lite Rogers win prob = 60 percent (Michigan Senate, Aug 2026); Classic/Deluxe projected El-Sayed margin = about 3 points (Michigan Senate); Michigan baseline = D+7 to D+8 points (projected November baseline)
rationale: Candidates often poll poorly amid contentious primaries.
evidence_quote: candidates often struggle in the polls when they’re in the midst of contentious primaries.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: Gubernatorial races are considerably less partisan than congressional races, so FLIPR is much less confident that a weak gubernatorial candidate will revert to the partisan mean.
evidence_quote: gubernatorial races are still considerably less partisan than races for Congress.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: Polling and forecasting errors are correlated across Senate races, but much less than across states in a presidential race where the same two candidates are on every ballot. Congressional races are also more correlated with one another in presidential years than in midterms, and FLIPR now accounts for this.
rationale: 2018 and 2022 midterm maps were patchy and regionalized.
evidence_quote: congressional races are more correlated with one another in presidential years than in midterms, and FLIPR now accounts for this.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: FLIPR explicitly simulates ranked-choice voting and Alaska's top-four primary system, which may make its Alaska forecast more volatile than other states.
evidence_quote: FLIPR now explicitly simulates ranked-choice voting and Alaska’s unique top-four primary

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: Silver judges that the 2022 race-level polls were largely accurate and unbiased, contrary to a narrative that polls underestimated Democrats; Democrats lost only 9 House seats and gained a Senate seat.
quantities: 2022 Democratic House losses = 9 seats (2022 midterm)
evidence_quote: The polls were largely accurate and unbiased.

title: Everything is breaking Democrats’ way. Is it enough to win the Senate?
statement: Silver's subjective views about candidates are not factored into the model, and he expects to be occasionally surprised by its outputs.
rationale: If you are never surprised by your model, there is no point in building one.
evidence_quote: Though my subjective feelings aren’t factored into the model.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR forecasts House, Senate and governor races and is trained on both midterm and presidential years. Some of its code dates to Silver's first midterm forecast at FiveThirtyEight in 2010; it was nearly completely refit in 2018, when Lite/Classic/Deluxe was introduced, changed again in 2022 to reflect polarization, and every line of the 2022 code was audited and often improved for 2026 with help from AI coding tools. No congressional forecast was run in 2024.
quantities: age of oldest code = 16 years (since 2010)
rationale: Changes execute the original design with more precision, robustness and internal consistency rather than changing its philosophy.
evidence_quote: The model underwent a near-complete refit in 2018 when the Lite/Classic/Deluxe concept was introduced.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR stacks three layers, each defining a version: Lite derives as much as possible from polls alone; Classic adds non-polling leading indicators ('fundamentals'); Deluxe adds expert race ratings. Deluxe is the default, and expert ratings are described as the least important layer.
evidence_quote: Lite derives as much information as possible from polls alone;

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR runs 40,000 simulations every time the model is updated and uses variance-reduction techniques so the effective sample size is larger than 40,000.
quantities: simulations per update = 40,000 simulations (FLIPR 2026)
rationale: Simulations are needed because of complex correlations between races.
evidence_quote: we run 40,000 simulations every time the model is updated.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: For 2026, FLIPR increases the relative weight on fundamentals versus polls because elections have become more predictable from partisanship with less ticket-splitting, while polls have had some rough years. It also accounts for the national environment 'locking in' earlier, so the generic ballot is more predictive months ahead than it once was.
rationale: Empirical tests on historical data.
evidence_quote: should our model increase the relative weight on “fundamentals” as opposed to polls? The answer is basically yes

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR is fit primarily on Senate races since 1990 and on House and gubernatorial races since 1998.
quantities: Senate training start = 1990 year (FLIPR fit); House and governor training start = 1998 year (FLIPR fit)
evidence_quote: The model is fit primarily based on Senate races since 1990, and House and gubernatorial races since 1998.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Unlike the presidential model, which defaults toward polls-only by Election Day, FLIPR is a more even blend of polls and fundamentals even at the end, because non-polling data is richer for about 500 races and polling is sparse, with many House races getting little or no nonpartisan polling.
quantities: races per cycle = around 500 races (House + Senate + governor)
evidence_quote: FLIPR is more of an even blend between polls and fundamentals

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR distinguishes 'micro' indicators that apply to one race (race polls, candidate fundraising) from 'macro' indicators that affect all races (generic ballot, polarization). Races cannot be forecast independently and then simulated, because outcomes are correlated, as in 2016 when Republicans beat their polls across the board.
rationale: Systematic error versus independent race variance.
evidence_quote: You can’t just forecast each race individually and apply some sort of Monte Carlo simulation on top because race outcomes are somewhat correlated.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Step 1: FLIPR's race-level polling averages use the shared Silver Bulletin algorithm. Polls are weighted by recency, sample size and pollster rating, adjusted for house effects, and smoothed by averaging more aggressive and more conservative LOWESS regression curves.
rationale: Balance responsiveness against bounciness.
evidence_quote: we’ve found the best way to do this is to calculate what are essentially various LOWESS regression curves, and then average more aggressive and more conservative versions.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR's house effects are estimated from both generic ballot and individual race polls, and are more punitive to partisan or internal campaign polls released publicly, which start with a prior that they are biased. Historically that bias averages about 4 points toward the preferred candidate.
quantities: historical bias of partisan/internal polls = about 4 points (toward sponsor's candidate)
evidence_quote: On average in the historical data, this bias is about 4 points toward their preferred candidate.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR adjusts every registered-voter or all-adult poll toward what it would show among likely voters, estimated from surveys that publish both versions. The shift is shrunk toward a prior until enough paired polls exist to phase the prior out. In 2026 most paired surveys favored Democrats in the LV version.
evidence_quote: the magnitude of the shift is shrunken toward a prior

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR dropped its old prior that the RV-to-LV shift favors Republicans, because Democrats' college-educated coalition now turns out at high rates. It uses a more neutral prior that is overridden more quickly as paired LV/RV polls arrive.
rationale: Turnout patterns changed.
evidence_quote: the model has discarded its prior that the shift from registered voters to likely voters typically favors Republicans.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR applies a timeline adjustment: if the generic ballot has moved since a race was last polled, a fraction of that movement is added to the race's margin, since a partial correction works better than a full one empirically. Race averages can therefore shift without new polls.
rationale: Avoid relying on stale polling.
evidence_quote: We’ve found empirically that a partial correction works better than a full correction.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR also applies the likely-voter adjustment to its own versions of the generic ballot and presidential approval, which Silver Bulletin's regular averages do not. In early August 2026 this moved the generic ballot from about D+6.5 to about D+8.
quantities: default generic ballot = about D+6.5 points (early August 2026); LV-adjusted generic ballot = around D+8 points (early August 2026)
evidence_quote: FLIPR also applies the likely voter adjustment to its averages of the generic ballot and presidential approval, which our regular averages do not.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Presidential approval averages tolerate more aggressive smoothing settings, while the generic ballot average must be fairly conservative or it bounces around too much; Silver says he tried it the other way.
evidence_quote: the generic ballot average needs to be fairly conservative or will bounce around too much

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Step 2: FLIPR estimates the national environment as a weighted average of the generic ballot and a 'bottom-up' estimate implied by polls of individual Senate and House races relative to each race's partisan lean. Weights depend on the relative amount of generic ballot versus race polling. Gubernatorial polls are excluded from this calculation because they correlate less with state partisanship. Example: generic ballot D+8 and race polls implying D+4 give about D+6.
evidence_quote: FLIPR will basically take an average of these

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: New in 2026, the bottom-up national estimate gives more weight to states and districts that resemble most others nationally, so a poll of a Pennsylvania swing district counts more than one in Hawaii or rural Alabama. It also corrects for selection bias in which races get polled.
rationale: Competitive-looking races in lopsided seats get polled more, which biases naive estimates.
evidence_quote: a poll of a swing district in Pennsylvania will have more impact on the calculation than a race in Hawaii or rural Alabama.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Partisan lean scores for each state and district are based on the past two presidential elections relative to the nation and on recent state legislative elections, and reflect new boundaries after redistricting. They are denominated in margin: R+10 means 10 points more Republican in margin than the nation, which Cook PVI would call R+5 because PVI uses one party's vote share. Texas was about R+11 in 2026.
quantities: Texas partisan lean = around R+11 points (margin) (2026); Cook PVI equivalent ratio = about 2x ratio (margin vs share)
evidence_quote: If we say a district is R +10, that means the vote margin in that district is 10 points more Republican than in the country overall.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Elasticity, each state's or district's sensitivity to national swings, is estimated from Cooperative Election Study voter-level microdata for 2016 through 2025. It is applied at various points in FLIPR, including scaling national error shifts, but mostly has a minor impact.
quantities: CES waves used = 2016-2025 years (elasticity microdata)
rationale: Cross-pressured electorates swing more.
evidence_quote: This elasticity calculation, which is derived from voter-level microdata

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: CANTOR (Congressional Algorithm using Neighboring Typologies to Optimize Regression) computes pairwise similarity scores among all 485 units, 435 districts plus 50 states. It uses political traits (partisan lean), demographics (race, religion, education) and geography (region with Silver's own definitions and some split states, distance, urbanization). It then imputes polling-like estimates for unpolled races from how polls in similar places over- or under-perform their baselines.
quantities: CANTOR units = 485 states+districts (485 x 484 pairwise comparisons)
rationale: Overperformance tends to cluster in similar places.
evidence_quote: it calculates similarity scores between any given combination of states or districts

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: For 2026, CANTOR accounts for a wider array of demographics, notably separating religious groups such as Jewish and Muslim voters that were previously lumped with others.
evidence_quote: A wider array of demographics are now accounted for by CANTOR, particularly including religious groups

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Step 3: FLIPR computes two fundamentals estimates. 'Simple fundamentals' are the generic ballot plus partisan lean. 'Fancy fundamentals' come from a large regression on races since 1990 including candidate-quality factors. Before 2022 only fancy fundamentals were used. For congressional races, simple fundamentals now get almost half the weight in many cases, implying candidate-quality factors including incumbency are about half as important as over the period since 1990.
quantities: simple fundamentals weight, congressional = almost half share (2026)
rationale: Polarization crowds out everything but partisanship.
evidence_quote: For Congressional races, “simple fundamentals” now get almost half the weight in many cases.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: The ratio of simple to fancy fundamentals is now tied to a polarization coefficient instead of a fixed ratio. Polarization is measured as the difference in party means from Voteview. Fancy fundamentals now use FLIPR's full national-environment estimate; simple fundamentals use the generic ballot alone.
evidence_quote: Our indicator for polarization is the difference in party means from Voteview.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: New in 2026: when simple and fancy fundamentals disagree, as for popular Republican Gov. Phil Scott in Vermont, FLIPR trusts fundamentals less, puts more weight on polls and expert ratings, and increases the race's uncertainty. When they agree, it increases the weight on fundamentals.
evidence_quote: In cases where “simple fundamentals” and “fancy fundamentals” are not aligned, the model trusts fundamentals less in general.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Fancy fundamentals fit separate regressions for incumbent and open-seat races; races with appointed incumbents count as open seats. Incumbency handling uses congressional approval polls to gauge the climate for incumbents, a larger incumbency advantage in small or idiosyncratic states and districts with low CANTOR similarity, the incumbent's margin in their last competitive race adjusted for that year's environment and redistricting, whether the incumbent is in a first elected term or beat an incumbent last time (both treated as strengths), and a smaller advantage when new and old districts overlap little.
rationale: First-termers lacked incumbency last time, so their last margin understates strength.
evidence_quote: we technically fit separate regressions for incumbent and open-seat races.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Fancy fundamentals include fundraising from individual contributions only, excluding party and PAC money, with in-state contributions weighted 5x. They also include elected experience on a 0-3 scale, from never elected to current or former senator or governor; party-loyalty scores from congressional votes for incumbents only, since defectors outperform; and scandals, with new scandals counting more than ones a candidate has already survived. The scandal list was compiled by Nathaniel Rakich and is one of the more subjective parts of the model.
quantities: home-state contribution weight = 5x multiplier (fundraising); elected experience scale = 0-3 points (0 never elected, 3 senator/governor)
evidence_quote: Home-state contributions get a 5x weight.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR now estimates the in-state share of contributions from donors whose state is known and extrapolates it to all individual contributions, including small-donor money the FEC does not itemize by state, fixing a clumsy 2022 implementation. Late replacement candidates and candidates who eschew individual contributions, such as JB Pritzker, now have fundraising treated as missing and estimated by proxy instead of zero; FLIPR does not account for self-funding.
evidence_quote: Because FLIPR does not account for self-funding, these candidates would previously have been treated as raising zero money

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Classic uses a small weight on CANTOR's imputed polling proxies, because CANTOR is generally less accurate than either fundamentals or actual race polls.
evidence_quote: While CANTOR is a cool system, it’s generally less accurate than either fundamentals or polls directly from the state or district.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: In recent elections the Deluxe forecast typically calls only one or two additional races correctly out of about 500 compared with Classic. Expert ratings are good at ranking races relative to each other but persistently assume a neutral national environment (generic ballot near zero) until late in the cycle: in early August 2026 they implied about D+2 versus FLIPR Classic's D+7.
quantities: extra correct calls, Deluxe vs Classic = one or two races (per cycle of ~500); experts' implied environment = around D+2 points (early Aug 2026); FLIPR Classic environment = roughly D+7 points (early Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: expert raters tend to implicitly assume a neutral political environment (i.e., a generic ballot of about zero) until quite late in the cycle.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Step 4 (Deluxe): (1) translate ratings from Cook Political Report, Inside Elections and Sabato's Crystal Ball into implied margins, using a Bayesian treatment for Solid/Safe ratings, which are informative only when Classic puts the race near a category boundary; (2) estimate each outlet's implied national environment; (3) shift the ratings to FLIPR's national environment to de-bias them; (4) blend with Classic.
rationale: Experts' value is in rank-ordering races, not in the national environment.
evidence_quote: De-bias the expert ratings by shifting them to FLIPR’s estimate of the national environment.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Expert ratings now get about one-sixth of the forecast for polled congressional races and about one-quarter for polled governor races, with more weight in unpolled races and wherever FLIPR judges fundamentals and polls less reliable. Previously they got about one-third across the board.
quantities: expert weight, polled congressional = about 1/6 share (Deluxe 2026); expert weight, polled gubernatorial = one-quarter share (Deluxe 2026); previous expert weight = closer to 1/3 share (earlier Deluxe)
rationale: Use experts as a fallback where other indicators are unreliable.
evidence_quote: It’s typically about one-sixth of the forecast for Congressional races with polling and one-quarter of the forecast for gubernatorial races with polling

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: The 2026 code audit found that earlier de-biasing of expert ratings leaked some of the experts' neutral-environment assumption into Deluxe; FLIPR now removes that bias completely so experts cannot affect the national picture.
evidence_quote: there was a bit of leakage from the experts’ implicit assumptions about the national environment

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Step 5: a prior for the House popular vote is fit on macro factors since 1946: presidential approval, the previous House popular vote adjusted for uncontested 'blank districts', polarization, and midterm status. Classic and Deluxe nudge the current snapshot toward this prior, with an effect that is gentle and fades to zero by Election Day; Lite uses the snapshot with wider uncertainty. In August 2026 the prior was about D+8.5 versus a snapshot near D+7.
quantities: prior = around D+8.5 points (early Aug 2026); snapshot = closer to D+7 points (early Aug 2026)
rationale: As the generic ballot became more stable, the prior is less useful than it used to be.
evidence_quote: the effect of this adjustment is relatively gentle, and essentially fades out by Election Day.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR's prior now distinguishes presidential years from midterms more sharply, because midterms tend to produce more lopsided outcomes.
