evidence_quote: Midterms tend to produce more lopsided outcomes than are typically seen in congressional elections in presidential years.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Illustration of FLIPR's uncertainty logic: a candidate leading by 3 points with a 5-point margin of error wins 88 percent of the time; if the margin of error doubles to 10 points, 72 percent.
quantities: win prob, 3-pt lead, 5-pt MoE = 88 percent (illustration); win prob, 3-pt lead, 10-pt MoE = 72 percent (illustration)
evidence_quote: A candidate with a 3-point lead in a race where the margin of error is 5 points will win her race 88 percent of the time.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Step 6: race-level uncertainty in FLIPR is higher when there is less polling, more undecided voters, more time until the election, and more disagreement between model subcomponents such as fundamentals versus polls. Primary polls often miss by double digits.
rationale: The degree of uncertainty is itself predictable.
evidence_quote: There’s more time to go until the election;

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR splits error into layers. National error shifts all races together, scaled by each unit's elasticity, and has two parts: 'drift', the change in the national environment before Election Day, which is smaller under high polarization and goes to zero by Election Day, and Election Day systematic polling error. Local error has a statewide draw shared by all races in a state (new in 2026) and a race-specific draw. Correlated demographic error uses CANTOR's variables to simulate over- or underperformance among subgroups such as Hispanics, Catholics or the Northeast, producing clustered regional errors like those of 2018 and 2022.
rationale: Errors are more correlated across similar places.
evidence_quote: Finally, correlated demographic error is an intermediate layer that sits between these and is the most complex layer.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR now calibrates drift separately from Election Day error, where it previously blended them; the new specification is more consistent with the presidential forecast. The recalibration showed the national picture locks in earlier than it used to.
evidence_quote: Previously, the model blended drift and Election Day uncertainty together.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR now assumes congressional and gubernatorial races are slightly more correlated with one another in presidential years than in midterms, because the presidential race anchors everything.
evidence_quote: The model now assumes that races are slightly more correlated with one another in presidential years than they are in midterms.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: Step 7: FLIPR's simulations use slightly fat-tailed distributions for rare out-of-sample events, but the fat tails are less severe than in past years because recent cycles lacked huge outliers.
evidence_quote: Fat tails are less severe than in past years, as we now have more cycles without huge outlier outcomes.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: For races with prominent independent candidates, FLIPR simulates the independent's vote share with a right-tailed distribution: usually not close, with an outside chance of real momentum. Independents who are de facto partisans, such as Dan Osborn in Nebraska or Bernie Sanders, are treated as members of that party.
evidence_quote: FLIPR simulates the independent’s vote share using a right-tailed statistical distribution

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR's simulations handle ranked-choice voting in Maine and Alaska, Alaska's top-four primary, Georgia-style runoffs when no candidate reaches 50 percent, and Louisiana's House jungle primary, used for the last time in 2026.
evidence_quote: In states like Georgia where elections go to runoffs if no candidate gets 50 percent of the vote, FLIPR simulates this too;

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR simulates turnout probabilistically as a post-processing step that does not affect vote shares or win probabilities. Local turnout is benchmarked on race competitiveness, whether a Senate or governor race is on the ballot, past turnout, and estimated voting-eligible population adjusted for growth. National turnout comes from polls asking whether voters are more or less excited than usual. Turnout within a state must be consistent across House, Senate and governor races within bounds, gets a capped correction for differential party turnout, and district totals are scaled to match the authoritative national estimate.
evidence_quote: The turnout simulations are essentially a post-processing step

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR treats gubernatorial races as less partisan than congressional races more completely in 2026: fundamentals are considerably upweighted for congressional forecasts and slightly downweighted for governors relative to the 2022 build, because partisan lean and fundraising data are less reliable for governor races.
evidence_quote: fundamentals are considerably upweighted in our congressional forecasts but slightly downweighted for governors.

title: How FLIPR forecasts the midterm elections
statement: FLIPR now calculates its own native presidential approval rating with a likely-voter adjustment.
evidence_quote: The model now calculates its own native version of presidential approval ratings that makes a likely-voter adjustment.

title: Prediction markets aren't magic
statement: Before a state's primary, FLIPR uses 'educated guesses' of each party's nominee, based simply on polls and prediction markets with no attempt at value-added prediction, and replaces them with actual winners after the primary. FLIPR is a general-election model, not a primary model.
evidence_quote: We usually just go by polls and prediction markets and these very much aren’t intended as any sort of value-added prediction; FLIPR is a general election model, not a primary model.

title: Prediction markets aren't magic
statement: FLIPR is updated almost every day with no fixed time, usually around 9-11 AM or 5-6 PM Eastern following poll release patterns, and multiple updates per day are avoided unless there is big news.
rationale: Polls tend to come out early morning or late afternoon.
evidence_quote: We do try to avoid multiple updates in a day unless there’s really big news.

title: Prediction markets aren't magic
statement: FLIPR does not use prediction market prices as inputs; Silver strongly objects to doing so in election models, for the reasons given in SBSQ #30: independence, recursivity, collinearity and markets being a moving target.
evidence_quote: I voiced a strong objection to using prediction markets as inputs in forecasting models. FLIPR does not do this

title: Prediction markets aren't magic
statement: Historically, presidential primary polls have an average error of 9 points on the margin between the top two finishers, which implies a 95 percent margin of error of about 22 points. Silver suspects down-ballot primaries, with lower turnout, have effective margins of error of 25 to 30 points.
quantities: average presidential primary poll error = 9 points (margin) (historical); 95% margin of error, presidential primaries = 22 points (historical); suspected MoE, gubernatorial/Senate primaries = 25-30 points (Silver's estimate)
rationale: Lower turnout makes primaries harder to poll.
evidence_quote: Historically, the average error of presidential primary polls is 9 points in predicting the margin between the top two finishers

title: Prediction markets aren't magic
statement: For a model or market to be well calibrated, 5 percent chances must happen about 5 percent of the time, not zero; quantifying uncertainty is described as most of the work in a model like FLIPR.
evidence_quote: for a model or a market to be well-calibrated, 5 percent chances are supposed to happen 5 percent of the time, not zero percent.

title: Prediction markets aren't magic
statement: Silver looks at prediction markets daily and finds them useful for diagnosing potential problems with a model and for honing in on outcomes as election-night results arrive, but not as a source of information beyond what is public, except sometimes for the wrong reason (insider trading).
evidence_quote: they’re very useful, for instance, in diagnosing potential problems with your model

title: Prediction markets aren't magic
statement: In the 2026 Wisconsin Democratic governor primary, three candidates dropped out within weeks for reasons unrelated to frontrunner Francesca Hong's strength, and one later re-entered and won. Silver argues such fluid fields warrant extra caution beyond what the polls imply.
evidence_quote: Wisconsin, in particular, ought to have been a case where traders were more cautious

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: As of August 15, 2026, FLIPR's forecast for the national House popular vote was D+7.2. If the national popular vote is under about D+6, Republicans are clear favorites to retain the Senate.
quantities: forecast national popular vote = D+7.2 points (Aug 15, 2026); Senate threshold = D+6 points (2026)
evidence_quote: As of today, our forecast for the popular vote is D +7.2.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: FLIPR collapses all of a candidate's scandals into a single line, essentially keeping only the most recent one, which is lenient to candidates like Ken Paxton who have several.
evidence_quote: it collapses all scandals, however many there are, into a single line, essentially keeping only the most recent one.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: Worked example from Texas: simple fundamentals (generic ballot plus Texas partisan lean) gave R+3.4, versus R+14 in 2024. Fancy fundamentals, driven by Paxton's scandals and Talarico's fundraising edge ($65M vs $9M by mid-July), gave D+9.2. The blended fundamentals were D+3.1, with the polling average at Talarico +1.9.
quantities: Texas simple fundamentals = R+3.4 points (Aug 2026); Texas fancy fundamentals = D+9.2 points (Aug 2026); Texas blended fundamentals = D+3.1 points (Aug 2026); Talarico fundraising = 65 million USD (mid-July); Paxton fundraising = 9 million USD (mid-July)
rationale: The more partisan the climate, the more FLIPR leans on simple fundamentals.
evidence_quote: The more partisan the background climate, the more FLIPR takes advantage of the simple fundamentals hedge.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: FLIPR gives incumbency and the full experience bonus only to elected officeholders. An appointed senator such as Jon Husted in Ohio gets no credit for being a senator, and races with appointed incumbents are treated as open seats.
evidence_quote: the model only gives incumbency and the full candidate experience bonus to elected incumbents

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: Ohio example: simple fundamentals R+3, fancy fundamentals D+1.6 (Sherrod Brown as a strong former senator who ran 8 points ahead of Harris in 2024, against an appointed incumbent), final fundamentals R+0.6, polling average Brown +3.2, Democratic win probability 62 percent.
quantities: Ohio fancy fundamentals = D+1.6 points (Aug 2026); Ohio final fundamentals = R+0.6 points (Aug 2026); Ohio D win prob = 62 percent (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: Our final fundamentals estimate thus shows an essentially neutral environment in Ohio: R +0.6.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: FLIPR uses a candidate's past election margin only for incumbents, not challengers.
evidence_quote: FLIPR uses the past election margin only for incumbents and not challengers.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: Maine example: simple fundamentals D+15; candidate-specific fancy fundamentals R+11, reflecting Collins's cash advantage, history of overperformance and incumbency; final fundamentals D+1.8; polls Jackson +3; Democratic win probability 70 percent.
quantities: Maine simple fundamentals = D+15 points (Aug 2026); Maine fancy fundamentals = R+11 points (Aug 2026); Maine final fundamentals = D+1.8 points (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: adding in candidate-specific information takes Maine all the way to R +11, and the model’s final fundamentals estimate is a tight D +1.8.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: Candidates who enter on an emergency basis, such as Troy Jackson in Maine or Darline Graham in South Carolina, get a partial mulligan: they are treated as having below-average but nonzero fundraising until they file reports.
evidence_quote: the model essentially gives a partial mulligan to candidates who enter the race on an emergency basis

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: FLIPR uses party-loyalty scores (a bonus for breaking with one's party, usually moderates) only for congressional incumbents, and does not estimate subjective ideology scores for the hundreds of non-incumbents. Candidate ideology, such as Abdul El-Sayed's progressivism, is therefore a known gap that shows up only implicitly through polls and expert ratings.
rationale: Subjective ideology scoring for hundreds of challengers is impractical.
evidence_quote: So this is a known limitation of the system

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: Michigan example: baseline D+8 from Trump's 1.4-point 2024 win plus the national environment; fancy fundamentals D+11, since El-Sayed's individual fundraising offsets his lack of elected experience; polling average R+1, with a Democratic super PAC poll among inputs; Democratic win probability 68 percent, betting that Haley Stevens supporters return.
quantities: Michigan simple fundamentals = D+8 points (Aug 2026); Michigan fancy fundamentals = D+11 points (Aug 2026); Michigan polling average = R+1 points (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: our model’s fancy fundamentals actually give Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed the edge and push the environment to D +11.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: FLIPR's elected-experience variable counts only elected positions; appointed posts such as El-Sayed's Wayne County Health Director role do not count.
evidence_quote: El-Sayed’s previous positions like Wayne County Health Director were appointed, not elected ones

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: FLIPR is described as consensus-driven: in Florida, simple fundamentals were competitive (R+2.5) but polls (Moody +6) and expert ratings both favored the Republican, so two of three layers outweighed the equivocal fundamentals, giving Democrats 22 percent.
quantities: Florida simple fundamentals = R+2.5 points (Aug 2026); Florida D win prob = 22 percent (Deluxe, Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: FLIPR is a consensus-driven model, and with two of the three layers (polls and experts) clearly favoring Moody, that outweighs the more equivocal fundamentals.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: FLIPR race ratings are based on win probability; a party with more than 75 percent but less than 95 percent is rated 'likely'.
quantities: 'likely' rating range = 75-95 percent win probability (FLIPR ratings)
evidence_quote: When one party has more than a 75 percent chance of winning a race but less than 95 percent, we rate it as “likely”.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: FLIPR computes a tipping-point probability for each Senate race: the chance it decides chamber control. In August 2026 the top seven had a combined 71 percent; Texas 13, Ohio 12, Iowa 11, Maine 11, Michigan 11, Alaska 9 and North Carolina 4 percent. Because Senate races are less correlated than a presidential ticket, the tipping point is spread over more states.
quantities: combined tipping-point probability, top 7 = 71 percent (Aug 15, 2026)
evidence_quote: Precisely because Senate races are less correlated with one another than the presidential ticket, these states aren’t quite comprehensive in covering possible tipping point states.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: FLIPR treats Dan Osborn in Nebraska, technically an independent but the only major candidate against Republican Pete Ricketts, as a de facto Democrat.
evidence_quote: FLIPR treats him as a de facto Democrat

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: Contradictory polls across Senate races, such as Brown +8 in Ohio and El-Sayed -4 in bluer Michigan, are plausible because congressional outcomes are correlated much less than presidential ones. The advanced FLIPR versions still expect such divergences to narrow toward fundamentals over the coming months.
evidence_quote: Outcomes in congressional races are correlated with one another, although considerably less so than in presidential races.

title: A tour of the 7 key Senate races
statement: In Alaska, FLIPR was a bit more bearish on Democrat Mary Peltola than prediction markets, possibly because it does not credit her history of overperformance (Split Ticket WAR scores of D+9 and D+22) or her moderate record, since she is not an incumbent. Such subjective misses are expected to cancel out across many races.
quantities: Alaska baseline = R+7 points (Aug 2026); Alaska D win prob = 42 percent (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: FLIPR accounts for a lot of things, but not everything.

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: FLIPR assumes correlated polling errors are fairly common, so one party may sweep most toss-ups as Trump did the 2024 swing states. It also assumes these systematic errors are unpredictable and symmetric, equally likely to favor either party over the long run. Silver calls this a big but deliberate assumption.
evidence_quote: It also assumes, however, that these errors are equally likely to benefit Republicans or Democrats.

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: Classic and Deluxe treat August polls as not being an unbiased estimator of the November result: they take a weighted average of polls and fundamentals, so a race at R+3 in polls and D+7 in fundamentals might be projected around D+1. The forecast is not a 'now-cast'; reversion toward partisan fundamentals is expected.
rationale: August reflects a different information environment, with fewer ads and partisan cues.
evidence_quote: Classic and Deluxe FLIPR assume that summer polling can be predictably biased.

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: In mid-August 2026 FLIPR's national environment was about D+7.5, and its historical regression prior predicted about D+8.5, consistent with a midterm against a president at 38 percent approval and with lame-duck presidents' history.
quantities: national environment = around D+7.5 points (Aug 19, 2026); historical regression prior = around D+8.5 points (Aug 2026); Trump approval = 38 percent (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: FLIPR thinks the current national environment is around D +7.5

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: Poll-error datasets spanning many polls but few cycles are effectively small samples, because errors are heavily correlated within a cycle; Ruffini's summer-bias data is closer to n=4 than n=hundreds.
quantities: effective sample = 4 cycles (2018-2024 summer Senate polls)
evidence_quote: So in some ways, this is closer to n=4 than n=hundreds.

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: Polls considerably overestimated Democrats in 2020 and 2024 but were accurate and unbiased by historical standards in the 2018 and 2022 midterms. The generic ballot has historically overstated Democrats early in cycles but also understated the opposition party, so long-term trends conflict.
quantities: Ruffini summer Senate poll bias = about 5 points toward D (late August, 2018-2024)
evidence_quote: the polls were both quite accurate and quite unbiased by historical standards in the past two midterms, 2018 and 2022.

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: One 2026 change to FLIPR was assuming more muted shifts in the national environment when partisanship is high, since late swings in historical generic ballot data have become less frequent: voters lock in earlier and there are fewer true swing voters.
rationale: Partisanship combined with the 24/7 news cycle.
evidence_quote: one of the changes we made to FLIPR this year was to assume more muted shifts in the national environment when partisanship is high

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: Summer is 'silly season' for polls: campaigns release internal polls for attention and fundraising, and by fall pollsters publish fewer outliers and herd more. FLIPR's harsh penalties on internal polls smooth its averages.
evidence_quote: FLIPR applies some pretty harsh penalties to internal polls

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: Race polls suffer selection bias: surprising races such as South Carolina in 2020 get heavily polled, while lopsided ones are ignored. The average Senate race is slightly red because small states have equal representation. The generic ballot is therefore a more common denominator, and FLIPR treats it as the reliable backbone of the national estimate.
evidence_quote: This is why the generic ballot is such a useful instrument, and why FLIPR and other models treat it as a reliable backbone

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: If one party front-loads advertising in summer, polls could show a temporary 'sugar high'. In principle a model could adjust polls for the partisan ad share during fieldwork, but FLIPR does not, since reliable ad data is hard to get. Silver thinks paid advertising's impact is overrated and hits diminishing returns quickly.
evidence_quote: In the perfect world, FLIPR might even adjust its polling averages based on the partisan share of advertising running while the poll was in the field.

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: After Alaska's top-four primary, FLIPR uses primary results mainly to forecast vote shares within each party for November. It derives only limited information on aggregate party shares, by comparing parties' relative primary performance across the House, Senate and governor races; aggregate party shares come from general-election polls plus priors. The post-primary logic mirrors FLIPR's code for California and Washington top-two primaries, adjusted for four-way incentives.
evidence_quote: The model uses primary results in Alaska in a slightly complicated way, but it’s mostly to forecast November vote shares within the same party.

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: In ranked-choice voting, eliminated candidates' votes do not all flow to same-party candidates: a fair number are exhausted because voters rank too few names, and some go to other parties. FLIPR models this, and judged a tie between two Democrats slightly worse for Democrats than one clear leader.
evidence_quote: A fair number of these votes are wasted because voters don’t list enough names on the ballot, and some will go to candidates from other parties instead.

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: When Angie Nixon (under $1 million raised, DSA member) beat Alexander Vindman (over $16 million raised) in Florida's Democratic Senate primary, FLIPR Deluxe's Democratic odds fell from 21 to 11 percent, partly via expert rating changes. Silver suspects FLIPR may have over-credited Vindman's fundraising even though it discounts out-of-state money. FLIPR makes no special provision for similar candidate names on ballots.
quantities: FL D win prob with Vindman = 21 percent (Deluxe); FL D win prob with Nixon = 11 percent (Deluxe)
evidence_quote: Democrats’ chances in Florida have fallen from 21 percent with Vindman to 11 percent with Nixon

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: Much of the historical Democratic bias in midterm summer polls reflected lower Democratic turnout captured only when pollsters switched to likely-voter screens. FLIPR and its predecessors always applied an LV adjustment for this. The Republican turnout advantage may now have flipped because Democrats' college-educated coalition votes reliably in midterms.
evidence_quote: FLIPR and its various predecessors have therefore always made a likely-voter adjustment

title: Are Democrats on a summer sugar high?
statement: Historical summer polling leads that faded: Phil Bredesen led Marsha Blackburn in Tennessee in August 2018 before losing by 11, and Jaime Harrison tied Lindsey Graham into September 2020 before losing by 10. In 2022, race-level polls were too optimistic for Democrats in summer but converged toward the generic ballot by November.
quantities: Blackburn margin = 11 points (TN 2018); Graham margin = 10 points (SC 2020)
evidence_quote: The individual-race polls converged toward the generic ballot

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
statement: After 2025-26 mid-decade redistricting, FLIPR Deluxe found the House map shifted from roughly no bias to a Republican lean of a few points: Democrats are favored to win the House if they win the national popular vote by 3 points or more, and are underdogs below that. At D+7 they are essentially guaranteed a majority, and the 84 percent probability reflects scenarios of polling error or a changing environment.
quantities: House tipping point = D+3 points (Aug 22, 2026); House D win prob = 84 percent (Deluxe, Aug 22, 2026); mean Democratic seats = 232 seats (average forecast outcome)
evidence_quote: FLIPR Deluxe thinks Democrats will be favored to win the House if they win the national popular vote by 3 points or more

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
statement: FLIPR rating bands by win probability: Solid means at least 95 percent; Likely is 75 to 95 percent; Lean is 60 to 75 percent; Toss-up is below 60 percent for either side.
quantities: Solid threshold = 95 percent (win probability); Lean range = 60-75 percent (win probability)
evidence_quote: A lean rating means that one candidate has between a 60 percent and 75 percent chance of winning the seat.

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
statement: On August 22, 2026 FLIPR Deluxe rated 198 seats Solid D, 156 Solid R, 13 Likely D, 37 Likely R, 16 Lean D, 8 Lean R and 7 Toss-up. The asymmetry in Likely R seats means a D+11 environment could turn engineered Republican seats competitive, so gerrymanders could become 'dummymanders'.
quantities: Solid D = 198 seats (Aug 22, 2026); Solid R = 156 seats (Aug 22, 2026); Likely R = 37 seats (Aug 22, 2026); Likely D = 13 seats (Aug 22, 2026); Toss-up = 7 seats (Aug 22, 2026)
evidence_quote: We’d note the asymmetry in the number of “Likely R” seats (37) versus “Likely D” ones (just 13).

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
statement: No single House district has a tipping-point probability near double digits because there are 435 districts. The 48 seats covered have a combined 71 percent chance of deciding control. In a presidential race the comparable fraction would be higher, because outcomes are more correlated and the tipping point is less likely to be a surprise.
quantities: combined tipping-point probability = 71 percent (48 House seats, Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: Because presidential outcomes are more correlated than congressional races, it’s less likely that the tipping-point state will be a surprise.

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
statement: For redistricted seats, FLIPR measures how much the new and old districts overlap to calibrate the remaining incumbency advantage, and it still treats incumbency as meaningful in such cases, more so than some other models. Example: about 60 percent of FL-9's residents carried over, so Democrat Darren Soto keeps some incumbency credit in an R+18 redrawn seat, at 38 percent to win.
quantities: FL-9 population overlap = about 60 percent (old vs new district); Soto win prob = 38 percent (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: It evaluates exactly how much of the new and old districts overlap to calibrate its estimate of the remaining incumbency advantage

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
statement: Democratic incumbents in seats redrawn to roughly R+10 to R+12 (TX-34, NC-1, FL-22) retained 63 to 68 percent win probabilities in FLIPR, largely due to incumbency plus the D+7 environment. Marcy Kaptur in a redrawn R+11 OH-9 was at about 63 percent.
quantities: redrawn seat lean = R+10 to R+12 points (TX-34, NC-1, FL-22); D hold probability = 63-68 percent (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: They would all have been roughly R +10 to R +12 in 2024 under their states’ new maps

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
statement: FLIPR uses its own long-standing regional definitions (Northeast, South, Midwest, West) rather than Census regions. Some states are split between regions; for example some southeastern Florida districts count as 'Northeastern' because the Miami area resembles a Northeastern metro, and parts of Texas count as West.
rationale: Regions feed correlated error and similarity.
evidence_quote: we’ve traditionally considered a few districts in southeastern Florida to be “Northeastern” rather than “Southern”

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
statement: FLIPR cannot account for an event like incumbent Marcy Kaptur's hospitalization affecting her campaign until it is reflected in expert ratings, which feed the Deluxe version.
evidence_quote: Our model can’t account for any effect that has on her ability to campaign, at least until it’s reflected in expert ratings.

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
statement: Candidate overperformance is tracked with Split Ticket WAR scores in the analysis: serial overperformer Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-1) has WAR of R+7 to R+15, while Mariannette Miller-Meeks (IA-1) ranges from R+0.6 in 2014 to D+11.3 in 2024, winning by 0.2 where Trump won by 8.4.
quantities: Fitzpatrick WAR range = R+7 to R+15 points (Split Ticket); Miller-Meeks 2024 WAR = D+11.3 points (Split Ticket)
evidence_quote: Her Split Ticket WAR scores range from a neutral R +0.6 in 2014 to an abysmal D +11.3 in 2024.

title: A tour of the 48 key House races
statement: Extensive gerrymandering has left the fewest realistically competitive House races ever, with most seats rated Solid for one party.
evidence_quote: the number of realistically competitive House races is smaller than ever.

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
statement: FLIPR's rating buckets are defined mathematically: a race is a 'toss-up' when neither party has more than a 60 percent chance of winning.
quantities: toss-up threshold = 60 percent (max win prob)
rationale: Some readers are more comfortable with buckets than percentages.
evidence_quote: We describe a race as a “toss-up” when neither party has greater than a 60 percent chance of winning.

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
statement: The standard generic ballot page put Texas's benchmark at R+4.2, but FLIPR uses a likely-voter-adjusted generic ballot that favored Democrats in 2026, bringing the Texas simple-fundamentals benchmark closer to R+3.
quantities: Texas benchmark, standard generic ballot = R+4.2 points (Aug 2026); Texas benchmark, FLIPR LV-adjusted = closer to R+3 points (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: Our generic ballot page pegs Texas at R +4.2, but FLIPR uses a version of the generic ballot that makes a likely-voter adjustment.

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
statement: Silver describes FLIPR's simple fundamentals, generic ballot plus a state's partisan lean, as essentially what British analysts call a 'uniform swing'.
evidence_quote: Simple fundamentals consist (simply!) of the generic ballot and a state’s partisan lean score, producing basically what our British readers might call a “uniform swing”.

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
statement: A scandal flag is worth several points of vote margin in FLIPR's fancy fundamentals, but Silver Bulletin considers the effect of a scandal to be roughly half of what it was a decade or two ago given high polarization. Multiple scandals are folded into one binary flag rather than treated cumulatively.
quantities: scandal effect vs 10-20 years ago = roughly half ratio (FLIPR 2026)
evidence_quote: Basically, we consider the effect of a scandal to be roughly half what it was a decade or two ago

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
statement: FLIPR uses individual-contribution fundraising from FEC data as a candidate-quality input because money buys ads and staff, proxies a campaign's organizational skill, and proxies voter enthusiasm. It excludes contributions to party organizations, self-funding and Super PAC spending, for practical reasons and because self-funding often signals a lack of organic support.
evidence_quote: self-funding isn’t a good proxy for voter enthusiasm; in fact, candidates often self-fund because they aren’t generating enough organic support

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
statement: Silver worries fundraising may now be a less reliable indicator than FLIPR assumes, because giving is highly nationalized and algorithmized through platforms like ActBlue, and Democrats have had a persistent individual-contribution edge in the Trump era. He names revisiting fundraising as a plausible FLIPR improvement for 2028/2030, especially if candidates like Talarico underperform.
quantities: Talarico in-state itemized individual contributions = 17.5 million USD (as of June 30, 2026); Paxton in-state itemized individual contributions = about 7.6 million USD (as of June 30, 2026); overall fundraising ratio = greater than 7:1 ratio (Talarico vs Paxton)
evidence_quote: part of me wonders whether fundraising is a less reliable indicator than it once was

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
statement: FLIPR handles around 1,000 candidates per cycle and would need ideology estimates for past cycles to train on, so it does not quantify ideology for non-incumbents. For incumbents it uses objective party-loyalty scores from congressional votes; defectors such as Collins get a fancy-fundamentals bonus.
quantities: candidates per cycle = around 1000 candidates (House+Senate+governor)
rationale: Ideology must be objective and available historically to train on.
evidence_quote: FLIPR handles around 1000 candidates per cycle between House, Senate and gubernatorial elections, and we’d also need to have estimates for past election cycles to train the model.

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
statement: In the Silver Bulletin polling database since 1998 (polls in the final three weeks), Texas Democrats have been about as likely to outperform their polling averages as to underperform them. Polls have had an average Democratic bias in recent cycles, but no worse in Texas than nationally, unlike Maine.
evidence_quote: they’ve been roughly as likely to outperform their polling averages as to underperform them.

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
statement: Silver argues gut instinct should get little weight in election forecasting because elections are rare events. Gut feelings usually amount to expecting the same thing as last time, and that reasoning is circular, as with Georgia's skeptics before 2020.
evidence_quote: But in elections, I don’t think one’s gut instinct should usually be given much weight.

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
statement: Before 2022, FLIPR's predecessors used only fancy fundamentals without the simple-fundamentals hedge, so candidate scandals like Paxton's would have carried more weight.
evidence_quote: Prior to 2022, we didn’t use the “simple fundamentals” hedge, so Paxton’s scandals would have gotten more weight in the model.

title: Do I really buy that Texas could turn blue?
statement: FEC fundraising data for federal races is highly organized and serves as one of the better remaining objective benchmarks; gubernatorial fundraising data is much messier.
evidence_quote: Gubernatorial fundraising data is another story.

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: Because partisanship tells far less in governor races (Vermont has a Republican governor, Kentucky a Democratic one), FLIPR treats gubernatorial races as more uncertain and defers more to polls and expert ratings than to fundamentals.
rationale: Voters rationally split tickets for governor since control of a chamber is not at stake.
evidence_quote: it therefore tends to treat gubernatorial races as more uncertain without the crutch of “Kentucky always votes for Republicans”

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: Because it cannot anchor on partisanship as much, FLIPR puts relatively more weight on candidate factors such as individual contributions, scandals and elected experience in governor races. Gubernatorial fundraising data is less reliable, with incomplete databases requiring state-by-state patchwork.
evidence_quote: Because it can’t anchor on partisanship as much, FLIPR really cares about this kind of stuff for gubernatorial candidates

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: For overwhelmingly self-funded candidates such as Rick Jackson in Georgia or JB Pritzker, FLIPR imputes a fundraising total based on party, office type and the state's partisan lean, treating missing individual contributions as missing data rather than zero. Defining 'self-funder' is tricky, because some candidates self-fund for lack of other support.
quantities: Rick Jackson primary self-funding = 100 million USD (Georgia 2026)
rationale: Using zero would be unfair to true self-funders.
evidence_quote: FLIPR therefore imputes a fundraising total based on party, the office type and the state’s partisan lean score

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: FLIPR's fundraising variable uses the total amount raised from individuals, not the number of donors.
evidence_quote: Though FLIPR only uses the total amount raised, not the number of donors.

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: FLIPR's threshold for flagging a scandal is a credible accusation. A dismissal removes the flag only if it shows the accusation was false or not credible, not if it was pro forma. Scandals matter more in gubernatorial races with little other information, especially unpolled ones.
evidence_quote: Our threshold for a scandal is a credible accusation

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: Iowa governor example: simple fundamentals R+3 with a D+6.6 national popular vote forecast; fancy fundamentals D+17 (Sand's large in-state individual contributions, his elected experience, no scandals); blended D+12; expert ratings Lean D, Toss-up and Tilt D; Democratic flip probability 84 percent, while Republicans held 60 percent in the same state's Senate race.
quantities: national popular vote forecast = D+6.6 points (Aug 28, 2026); Iowa gov fancy fundamentals = D+17 points (Aug 2026); Iowa gov blended fundamentals = D+12 points (Aug 2026); Iowa gov D flip prob = 84 percent (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: All of that works out to a fancy fundamentals estimate of D +17.

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: FLIPR does not trust expert raters' implied national environment. It looks at how each outlet rates races relative to its other ratings, then shifts the ratings to match FLIPR's national climate, so in a strong Democratic year a 'Toss-up' rating is treated as more like 'Lean D'. In Georgia's governor race this produced about a 70 percent Bottoms forecast.
quantities: Bottoms win prob = about 70 percent (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: it treats a toss-up rating as more like “lean D”.

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: FLIPR does not use its Senate forecast in a state to predict the governor forecast in the same state, though Silver Bulletin suspects coattails, such as Bottoms sharing the ballot with Ossoff, may have predictive power as ticket-splitting declines, and may examine this in 2028.
evidence_quote: FLIPR doesn’t use its Senate forecasts to predict its governor forecasts

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: With no general-election polls, as in the Kansas governor race, FLIPR relies on fundamentals and de-biased expert ratings.
quantities: Kansas Senate simple fundamentals = R+9.4 points (Aug 2026); Kansas gov R flip prob = 57 percent (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: there are no polls of the Kansas gubernatorial general election.

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: In Alaska, FLIPR uses blended fundamentals to forecast each party's aggregate first-round vote, then allocates votes within each party through a separate process that uses polls, fundamentals and primary results. It simulates the first round with uncertainty and then the ranked-choice rounds from each simulated first round, so different candidate pairs reach the final two across simulations. Within-party RCV transfers are about 85 percent, not 100, and some ballots exhaust.
quantities: within-party RCV transfer share = about 85 percent (empirical); Alaska gov blended fundamentals = R+3.7 points (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: Empirically, within-party transfer shares are more like 85 percent than 100 percent.

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: FLIPR's forecasts are conditional on the major-party candidates remaining the same; it does not account for potential candidate withdrawals or replacements, which are handled by manual adjustment if they occur.
evidence_quote: technically, its forecasts for every race are conditional forecasts on the assumption that the major-party candidates will remain the same.

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: Besides Alaska, FLIPR uses primary results as an extra information layer in states with blanket nonpartisan primaries for some offices: California, Louisiana and Washington.
evidence_quote: Except California, Louisiana and Washington, which also use blanket nonpartisan primaries for some offices.

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: Experience is graded by office: a House member such as Tom Tiffany is rated higher than a county executive such as David Crowley. Appointed roles such as Ohio health director Amy Acton earn no experience bonus. Resurfaced offensive social media posts, such as Crowley's 2010 'Dirt McGirk' account, were flagged as a scandal.
evidence_quote: Tiffany has held the more highly-rated office as a member of the House.

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: Because FLIPR adjusts partisan-sponsored polls against their sponsor, a Democratic Governors Association poll showing the Democrat up 1 in Florida was treated as evidence the Republican was a few points ahead.
rationale: Partisan polls get a prior bias toward their sponsor.
evidence_quote: With the way FLIPR adjusts polls for partisanship, it actually thinks that bolsters the case for Donalds being a few points ahead.

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: Incumbency still means something in unusual, remote states like Nevada, where voters tend to like their incumbents and machine politics matter, consistent with FLIPR's larger incumbency effect in idiosyncratic places.
quantities: Nevada fancy fundamentals = R+13.7 points (Aug 2026)
evidence_quote: incumbency may not be what it once was, but it still means something in an unusual, remote state like Nevada

title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
statement: FLIPR aggregates governor outcomes into the number of governorships, with Democrats at 62 percent to control a majority and a 16 percent chance of a 25-25 tie, and population governed, with a projected 215 million Americans under Democratic governors versus 127 million.
quantities: D majority of governorships prob = 62 percent (Aug 2026); 25-25 tie prob = 16 percent (Aug 2026); population under D governors = 215 million (projected)
rationale: Population governed better reflects the importance of large states.
evidence_quote: In fact, they’re projected to govern 215 million compared to Republicans’ 127 million.

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
statement: Since 2010, the Silver Bulletin generic ballot average has moved by an average of 1.4 points (absolute margin change) between Labor Day and Election Day; only in 2014 did it move by more than 2 points.
quantities: average Labor Day to Election Day generic ballot swing = 1.4 points (cycles since 2010)
evidence_quote: On average in elections since 2010, the margin between Democrats and Republicans in our generic ballot average has swung by a whopping total of… 1.4 points between Labor Day and Election Day.

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
statement: Since 2010 the average absolute error of the Labor Day generic ballot in predicting the national House popular vote is 3.5 points, falling to 2.1 points for the final generic ballot average. Because the 2.1-point Election Day error exceeds the 1.4-point drift, most remaining national uncertainty after Labor Day comes from polling error rather than opinion movement.
quantities: Labor Day generic ballot error = 3.5 points (average absolute, since 2010); final generic ballot error = 2.1 points (average absolute, since 2010)
evidence_quote: In terms of the national picture, most of the remaining uncertainty in the forecast stems from polling error rather than further movement in public opinion.

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
statement: Historical generic ballot table (Democratic margin at Labor Day, on Election Day, and in the House popular vote): 2010 -5/-6/-7; 2014 Election Day -3, vote -6; 2018 +8/+8/+9; 2020 +8/+7/+3; 2022 Election Day -1, vote -3; 2024 Election Day 0, vote -3.
quantities: 2018 generic ballot vs result = +8 / +9 points D (Election Day avg vs vote); 2020 generic ballot vs result = +7 / +3 points D (Election Day avg vs vote)

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
statement: FLIPR's September 2026 seat-translation table gives Democratic House win probability and expected seats by popular-vote margin: D+0-1: 7.4 percent, 211 seats; D+2-3: 50.7 percent, 218; D+3-4: 77 percent, 221; D+4-5: 93.4 percent, 225; D+5-6: 98.9 percent, 229; D+6-7: 99.9 percent, 232; D+9-10: 245; D+14-15: 268. That is roughly 4 to 5 seats per point of popular vote. Democrats need about D+3 to be favored and D+4 to 5 for a double-digit majority.
quantities: D win prob at D+2 to +3 = 50.7 percent (Sept 3, 2026); D seats at D+6 to +7 = 232 seats (Sept 3, 2026); seats per point = about 4-5 seats (derived from table)

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
statement: Silver Bulletin uses different smoothing parameters for different polling series. Generic ballot averages are smoothed heavily because Congress makes less national news, races are local, polling is spread over many races, and generic ballot polls are wording-sensitive and unherded (August 2026 polls ranged from D+11 Zogby to D+2 RMG). Presidential election averages and approval averages put a bigger premium on new data.
quantities: range of August 2026 generic ballot polls = D+2 to D+11 points (RMG to Zogby)
rationale: A polling model should not take a one-size-fits-all approach.
evidence_quote: A polling model shouldn’t take a one-size-fits-all approach to calculate its averages.

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
statement: The goal for polling averages is minimal autocorrelation in their changes: today's average should be the best prediction of the near-future average. If a decline would predictably bounce back, the average is overreacting; if it would predictably keep falling, it is underreacting.
rationale: Learned from building averages that were both over- and under-responsive.
evidence_quote: In technical terms, the goal is for changes in our polling averages to have as little autocorrelation as possible.

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
statement: The RealClearPolitics generic ballot average, being under-smoothed, swung from D+8.1 in late May to D+4.7 by mid-July 2026, a 3.4-point drop that was mostly noise. The Silver Bulletin average, smoother and with a more comprehensive poll set, moved only 1.2 points (D+7.1 to D+5.9).
quantities: RCP swing = 3.4 points (late May to mid-July 2026); Silver Bulletin swing = 1.2 points (same period)
evidence_quote: Because an under-smoothed average will overfit to small fluctuations in the data, a few days of bad polls can move the topline picture fairly dramatically.

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
statement: In presidential years, swing-state polls can be used reliably to infer the national trend, since the same candidates appear everywhere. For congressional races, shifts in one race often reflect local news or an ad barrage and do not extrapolate well; a new Senate poll in one state mostly affects only that state.
evidence_quote: A new poll in Michigan or Maine or South Carolina or Alaska pretty much affects that state and that state only.

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
statement: Trends within a single pollster's series tell more than differences across pollsters, but they take more evidence and time to calibrate.
evidence_quote: Trends within a given pollster’s data (i.e., if the New York Times/Siena College poll shows Republicans gaining ground on the generic ballot) tend to tell you more than trends across different pollsters

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
statement: Uncontested House districts cause slight, predictable discrepancies between the generic ballot and the House popular vote; FLIPR corrects for these.
evidence_quote: FLIPR corrects for these, but they’re minor enough that they can usually be treated as a rounding error.

title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
statement: A single outlier poll (Harvard-Harris R+2) plus other overnight polls moved the generic ballot from D+6.7 to D+6.4 and FLIPR's House odds from 84 to 81 percent, illustrating the model's damped response to individual polls.
quantities: generic ballot change = D+6.7 to D+6.4 points (Sept 2, 2026); House D win prob change = 84 to 81 percent (Sept 2026)

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
statement: FLIPR's dictionary for converting expert rating categories into projected margins: Solid D at least D+18.1; Likely D D+12.1; Lean D D+6.7; Tilt D D+4.4; Toss-up 0; Tilt R R+4.4; Lean R R+6.7; Likely R R+12.1; Solid R at least R+18.1. Ratings from the three outlets are averaged; for Texas Senate, two Toss-ups and one Lean R averaged to an implicit R+2.2.
quantities: Solid = at least 18.1 points margin (expert dictionary); Likely = 12.1 points margin (expert dictionary); Lean = 6.7 points margin (expert dictionary); Tilt = 4.4 points margin (expert dictionary); Toss-up = 0 points margin (expert dictionary)
rationale: Derived from how categories translate on average into vote shares.
evidence_quote: Here’s the “dictionary” that we use:

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
statement: 'Solid' ratings are a censored category, since a Solid race may be 15 or 60 points. FLIPR uses Classic's forecast to impute an expert margin and applies a Bayesian check: if it is implausible that the race would be rated anything but Solid (e.g. a Massachusetts Senate race), the rating has essentially no effect; if the race is plausibly competitive but rated Solid (e.g. a Minnesota race with lean about D+5), it can have a fairly big impact.
quantities: Minnesota neutral-environment lean = about D+5 points (example)
rationale: Without this, Deluxe projections would become too compressed.
evidence_quote: For Solid races, FLIPR basically relies on Classic (polls + fundamentals) to impute an expert margin.

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
statement: In the 14 Senate races with at least a 3 percent tipping-point chance in September 2026, FLIPR Classic averaged D+1.9 while the raw expert ratings averaged R+3.3, and in 13 of 14 the experts were more Republican. The experts thus implied a national environment 5 to 6 points redder than FLIPR's, around D+2 or D+3 versus D+8.
quantities: FLIPR Classic average margin = D+1.9 points (14 key Senate races); raw expert average margin = R+3.3 points (14 key Senate races)
evidence_quote: the expert ratings assume a political environment that’s 5 to 6 points more Republican than the one FLIPR expects.

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
statement: Citing G. Elliott Morris: in midterms since 2010, at about 45 days out, the president's party won only 33 percent of House races Cook rated 'toss-up'. Expert ratings persistently underweight the midterm penalty, and FLIPR's predecessors have long corrected for this.
quantities: president's party win rate in Cook toss-ups = 33 percent (House, midterms since 2010, ~45 days out)
evidence_quote: the president’s party has won only 33 percent of House races that Cook Political rated as “toss-up.”

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
statement: FLIPR de-biases expert ratings by shifting them to match FLIPR Classic's national environment; for example, an all-'toss-up' Michigan became D+5.7 after de-biasing. The adjustment is dynamic and shrinks as experts move their ratings toward the objective environment late in the cycle.
quantities: Michigan de-biased expert margin = D+5.7 points (Sept 2026)
rationale: Experts' value lies in intangibles and private information, not their view of the national environment.
evidence_quote: So FLIPR debiases the expert ratings so that they match FLIPR Classic’s estimate of the national political environment.

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
statement: FLIPR's trendline adjustment shifts older race polls by two-thirds of the subsequent change in the generic ballot for congressional races; a May poll at D+4 with Democrats up 3 since becomes D+6. For gubernatorial races the factor is about 47 percent, made slightly less sensitive in September 2026, with an impact of about a tenth of a point.
quantities: trendline factor, congressional = 2/3 share of generic ballot change (FLIPR 2026); trendline factor, gubernatorial = approximately 47 percent (FLIPR 2026)
rationale: Governor races are less partisan, so the generic ballot is less informative about them.
evidence_quote: In FLIPR, the trendline adjustment shifts “old” polls by 2/3 of the direction of the change in the generic ballot.

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
statement: On Sept. 20, 2026 FLIPR's historical prior (from presidential approval, previous congressional result and polarization, calibrated on all congressional races since World War II) said Democrats should win the House vote by 8.7 points. The LV-adjusted generic ballot was D+8.6. The prior has only a modest effect, being a deliberately conservative nudge, and little when it already agrees with the snapshot.
quantities: historical prior = D+8.7 points (Sept 20, 2026); LV-adjusted generic ballot = D+8.6 points (Sept 20, 2026); Trump net approval = -20.5 points (Sept 2026)
rationale: High polarization dampens swings and is accounted for in the prior.
evidence_quote: This calculation, which is calibrated based on all races for Congress since World War II, has only a modest effect on the model

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
statement: Changes in a forecast should not be predictable: the best prediction of tomorrow's forecast is today's forecast, otherwise predictive information is being left on the table. Forecasts should be evaluated on what they said throughout the cycle, not only on Election Day.
evidence_quote: Put another way, the best prediction of what your forecast says tomorrow should be the forecast today.

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
statement: A bug caused FLIPR to treat unchanged Inside Elections ratings as missing whenever the outlet updated only some ratings, falling back to a crude partisanship-and-incumbency prior. This shifted average Deluxe margins by about 0.3 points (up to about 1 point), favoring incumbents' parties and so slightly lowballing Democrats in Republican-held seats. Fixing it moved Deluxe Senate odds to 65 percent, about 3 to 4 points above what new polls alone would have given.
quantities: average margin impact = ~0.3 points (Deluxe); max margin impact = ~1 points (Deluxe); Senate D prob after fix = 65 percent (Sept 20, 2026)
evidence_quote: FLIPR was treating the other ratings as blank and falling back to a prior based on partisanship and incumbency

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
statement: In Alaska, FLIPR computes fundamentals for each party's combined vote, allocates it among same-party candidates, and then simulates ranked-choice voting, whereas experts rate the post-RCV outcome. A special adjustment now puts expert ratings and Classic on the same scale at each stage; the fix slightly helped Republicans.
evidence_quote: FLIPR now makes an adjustment in Alaska so that the expert ratings and FLIPR Classic are more on the same scale at each stage of the process.

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
statement: FLIPR's category labels are a post-processing step applied after the model runs. 'Lean Democrat' is any race where the Democrat has a 60 to 74 percent chance; Toss-up means neither side above 60 percent.
quantities: Lean range = 60-74 percent (FLIPR labels)
evidence_quote: these ratings are just a post-processing step, a label applied after the model finishes running the numbers.

title: Expert ratings are ignoring signs of a blue wave
statement: Polls showing very red states like Kansas or Nebraska as toss-ups warrant caution, because recent polling error has been concentrated in such states. Classic and Deluxe hedge toward fundamentals there, and de-biased expert ratings still hurt Democrats in Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina.
evidence_quote: History says to be wary of states as red as Kansas polling as toss-ups; they’re where most of the polling error has been concentrated in recent years.

title: Do Republicans really have a money advantage?
statement: Individual contributions to candidates are the only campaign-finance data in FLIPR's fancy fundamentals. They are treated as a measure of grassroots support, so contributions from the candidate's own state or district get more weight; party committee, PAC and Super PAC money and ad reservations are not used.
evidence_quote: Democrats also have an advantage when it comes to individual contributions, which is the only campaign finance data that feeds into FLIPR’s “fancy fundamentals” estimates.

title: Do Republicans really have a money advantage?
statement: FLIPR gives late-entrant candidates 'amnesty' on fundraising: Troy Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner in Maine and had not yet filed a report, gets credit for half of what Platner raised.
quantities: late-entrant fundraising credit = half share of predecessor's total (Troy Jackson, Maine)
evidence_quote: The model gives him amnesty as a late entrant, so he gets credit for half of what Graham Platner raised.

title: Do Republicans really have a money advantage?
statement: In-state shares of itemized individual contributions to 2026 Senate candidates were similar by party: 36 percent for Democrats and 38 percent for Republicans.
quantities: in-state share, D Senate candidates = 36 percent (2026 itemized individual contributions); in-state share, R Senate candidates = 38 percent (2026)
evidence_quote: 36 percent of itemized individual contributions to Democratic Senate candidates are in-state, compared to 38 percent for Republicans.

title: Do Republicans really have a money advantage?
statement: Silver Bulletin's view is that money is closer to overrated than underrated, at least in high-profile campaigns like Senate and presidential races, where earned media matters more than paid media and diminishing returns set in on saturated airwaves.
evidence_quote: Our view at Silver Bulletin is that money is closer to overrated than underrated

title: Do Republicans really have a money advantage?
statement: Super PACs often pay several times what campaigns do for comparable broadcast TV ads, so ad spending does not equal ad impressions and party or PAC cash is less efficient than candidate dollars.
evidence_quote: Super PACs often pay several times what campaigns do for comparable broadcast TV ads.

title: Do Republicans really have a money advantage?
statement: 2026 individual-contribution gaps cited as drivers of FLIPR fancy fundamentals: Talarico $66M vs Paxton $9M in Texas; Brown $25M ahead of Husted in Ohio; Peltola $12M ahead of Sullivan in Alaska; El-Sayed $7M ahead of Rogers in Michigan. Totals: Democratic House nominees $648M vs Republicans $437M; Democratic Senate nominees $329M vs $133M.
quantities: Talarico individual contributions = 66 million USD (Sept 2026); D House nominees raised = 648 million USD (2026 cycle); R House nominees raised = 437 million USD (2026 cycle); D Senate nominees raised = 329 million USD (2026 cycle); R Senate nominees raised = 133 million USD (2026 cycle)

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
statement: Since World War II the party out of the White House has gained in the House popular vote in every midterm except 2002 and gained seats in all but 2002 and 1998. The average swing from the previous congressional election is 7.4 points, with an interquartile range of +4.8 to +10.8. The record is 17.4 points in 2010; 2018 was 9.7 and 2006 was 10.6.
quantities: average out-party midterm swing = 7.4 points (since WWII); interquartile range = +4.8 to +10.8 points (since WWII); 2010 swing = 17.4 points (record); 2018 swing = 9.7 points (Trump I midterm); 2006 swing = 10.6 points (G.W. Bush midterm)
rationale: Thermostatic public opinion checks the president's power.
evidence_quote: The average shift is a 7.4-point swing.

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
statement: The magnitude of the midterm swing has been highly consistent over time even as presidential margins have narrowed, and it hits both popular and unpopular presidents, since popular presidents bring bigger coattails and have more territory to defend.
evidence_quote: The magnitude of the midterm swing has been highly consistent over time, even as margins in presidential elections have diminished.

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
statement: The generic ballot is FLIPR's single most important input but not its final answer; it feeds simple fundamentals and is blended with fancy fundamentals (including incumbency, which helps Republicans as incumbents in most seats), race-level polls (dominant in well-polled races), and in Deluxe, expert ratings calibrated to have little effect on the national vote.
evidence_quote: the generic ballot is the single most important input to FLIPR, but not its “final answer”; it’s blended with lots of other data.

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
statement: FLIPR's House popular vote forecast is the turnout-weighted sum of its 435 district forecasts. It is more Republican than a simple average because Republican districts have grown faster since the 2020 Census (FLIPR embeds a population growth model), Democratic districts have more ineligible residents (non-citizens and disenfranchised felons), turnout rises with competitiveness while safe urban seats are low-turnout, and red-state Senate races lift House turnout in those states.
quantities: FLIPR House popular vote forecast = D+7.9 points (Sept 29, 2026); LV generic ballot = D+9.6 points (Sept 29, 2026)
evidence_quote: our D +7.9 forecast is formulated by summing up FLIPR’s forecast for each district, weighted by projected turnout.

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
statement: FLIPR replicates quirks of the official House popular vote tally: uncontested districts (including whether states count ballots in them), same-party top-two contests in California and Washington, and ranked-choice districts, where it uses the post-RCV tally in simulations where RCV is triggered. Its historical House popular vote estimates adjust for uncontested districts.
evidence_quote: FLIPR tries to faithfully replicate the official tally of the House popular vote

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
statement: FLIPR's generic ballot estimate is a 'now-cast'. Classic and Deluxe blend in a prior from midterm history since World War II conditioned on presidential approval and other factors, with influence fading to zero by Election Day; in late September 2026 the prior and the current estimate were very close.
evidence_quote: the prior’s influence on the model fades to zero by Election Day.

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
statement: Forecasts that start near 50/50 tend to have bigger probability swings than lopsided ones for the same change in fundamentals, which is why FLIPR's Senate odds (to 72.6 percent) moved more than its House odds.
quantities: Senate D win prob = 72.6 percent (Sept 29, 2026)
evidence_quote: forecasts that start out near 50/50 tend to have bigger probability swings.

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
statement: Silver says Silver Bulletin/FiveThirtyEight forecasts have essentially never been on the opposite side of the conventional wisdom; differences have been in degree of confidence: more cautious than consensus about Clinton in 2016, and confident that Biden's 2020 lead could withstand a 2016-sized polling error, which it did even though 2020 polls were more biased.
evidence_quote: general election polls were actually more biased in 2020 than in 2016, but Biden’s lead was big enough to absorb the blow.

title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
statement: Between Sept. 7 and Sept. 29, 2026 the generic ballot moved from D+6.5 to D+8.9, about 2.5 points, larger than the post-Labor Day swing in most recent midterms. FLIPR's launch odds on Aug. 11 were about 55 percent for the Senate and 85 percent for the House, within a few points of prediction markets, which FLIPR's publication itself influenced.
quantities: generic ballot shift = D+6.5 to D+8.9 points (Sept 7-29, 2026)
evidence_quote: On Sept. 7, they led by 6.5 points; now that lead has expanded to 8.9 points.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: FLIPR's core constraint is that the forecast is 'party-neutral'. Polling averages may be predictably biased, for example a red state's polls understating the Republican or a blue state's understating the Democrat, and fundamentals correct for that. But the direction of error in the blended forecast is assumed unpredictable; no party-specific assumption such as 'polls always underestimate Republicans' is built in, which Silver would call unskewing.
rationale: Past directional biases are consistent with chance given small effective samples.
evidence_quote: we assume that the direction of the bias of our polling averages might be predictable, but the direction of the bias in our blended forecasts (polls + fundamentals + expert ratings) isn’t predictable.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: FLIPR simulates four layers of polling uncertainty: (1) a uniform national error across all races; (2) demographically or geographically correlated errors, e.g. Democrats beat polls among Hispanics but Republicans in the Midwest; (3) a statewide error shared by a state's Senate, governor and House races; (4) a single-race error. In presidential years most uncertainty sits in layer 1, while in midterms it is more evenly spread across the four.
rationale: Midterm errors in 2018 and 2022 were largely unbiased overall but regionally significant.
evidence_quote: For the midterms, they’re more evenly distributed between the four layers.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: In Silver Bulletin's pollster database, a simple average of all polls in the final three weeks of the 2016, 2020 and 2024 general elections overestimated Democrats by 3.8 points. Midterm polls in 2018 and 2022 were almost completely unbiased in aggregate, and off-year and special election polls in the Trump years were biased toward Republicans by 1.3 points on average.
quantities: Trump presidential years poll bias = 3.8 points toward D (2016, 2020, 2024 final 3 weeks); off-year/special election bias = 1.3 points toward R (Trump era)
evidence_quote: they overestimated Democrats by a margin of 3.8 percentage points.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: In the nine cycles since 2008, polls were systematically biased against Democrats once (2012, by about 3 points with Obama beating RCP averages in all 11 toss-up states), against Republicans four times (2014, 2016, 2020, 2024), and roughly unbiased four times. Five biased cycles splitting 4-1 happens 37.5 percent of the time with a fair coin.
quantities: 2012 pro-R poll bias = about 3 points (national and state); probability of 4+ of 5 same direction = 37.5 percent (fair coin)
evidence_quote: if you flip a fair coin 5 times, then 37.5 percent of the time, either heads or tails will come up at least 4 out of 5 times.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: FLIPR does not assume any individual poll is unbiased: its house-effects adjustment pulls firms with systematic D-vs-R differences, such as Marist's Democratic-leaning 2026 numbers, toward the consensus.
evidence_quote: FLIPR adjusts their polls to be closer to the consensus, as we do with any firm that shows these systematic differences.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: Race-level polls are blended with fundamentals that reflect state partisanship: in South Carolina, a polling average of Graham +2.6 became a forecast of Graham +5.3. By symmetry, Democrats are expected to outperform their polls in blue states such as Minnesota.
quantities: SC polling average = R+2.6 points (Oct 2026); SC forecast = R+5.3 points (Oct 2026)
evidence_quote: our forecast shows Graham winning by 5.3 after blending in fundamentals that account for how red South Carolina usually is.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: Treating state polling errors as independent coin flips is the key modeling mistake: because FiveThirtyEight modeled correlation, it gave Trump 29 percent in 2016 while coin-flip models gave him 1 percent or less. Correlation matters most among demographically similar states; in 2016, a miss with non-college whites concentrated in Midwestern swing states decided the race while national polls were fairly accurate.
quantities: FiveThirtyEight 2016 Trump probability = 29 percent (final forecast); coin-flip models' Trump probability = 1 percent or less percent (2016)
evidence_quote: Precisely because it didn’t do this, FiveThirtyEight’s final forecast gave Trump a 29 percent chance in 2016

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: In the final 2024 Silver Bulletin presidential forecast (about 50/50), the single most likely scenario was Trump sweeping all seven swing states, which happened, and the second most likely was Harris sweeping all seven, reflecting correlated errors.
evidence_quote: But the single most likely scenario was Trump sweeping all seven key swing states

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: Error correlation lies on a spectrum: presidential years are near uniform national swing; congressional races in presidential years are in between, with coattails and party-line voting; midterms are in the middle; off-year, runoff and special elections are near independent coin flips and produce many surprises, such as Scott Brown in 2010 and Doug Jones in 2017. Many 2026 FLIPR changes sharpened the presidential-year versus midterm distinction.
evidence_quote: Presidential years are very much on the “uniform swing” side of that spectrum whereas midterms are somewhere in the middle.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: Since 2016 the Silver Bulletin database includes 246 qualifying polls covering 36 special/off-year races across 27 election dates; Democrats usually did better than these polls predicted. Larger historical midterm polling errors exist in the deeper archive, e.g. 1994 and 1998.
quantities: special/off-year polls since 2016 = 246 polls (36 races, 27 dates)
evidence_quote: since 2016, a total of 246 qualifying polls covering 36 distinct races across 27 unique election dates.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: Silver's theory, not built into FLIPR, which makes no turnout assumptions about bias direction: polls oversample enthusiastic and high-social-trust respondents who are also more likely to vote. In high-turnout presidential elections the oversampling dominates and low-propensity Trump voters are missed; in low-turnout elections those voters also stay home, and pollster corrections may overcorrect.
evidence_quote: FLIPR doesn’t actually make any assumptions about turnout.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: A truly random sample is impossible today: people screen calls and online panels cannot be randomly pinged. Pollsters weight demographically (e.g. education, race) to correct nonresponse, but partisan and enthusiasm-driven nonresponse is a mixed bag because self-selection also acts as a de facto likely-voter screen. Silver calls the 2024 Selzer Iowa poll the last gasp of traditional telephone polls that made little effort to correct for partisan nonresponse.
evidence_quote: The dirty little secret of polling these days is that it’s impossible to get a truly random sample of voters.

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: In early FiveThirtyEight years the polling averages were an intermediate step in the model and not always surfaced publicly; Silver Bulletin now displays polling averages separately and then blends them with other information.
evidence_quote: In the earlier FiveThirtyEight years, our models basically did the same thing, but the polling averages were more of an intermediate accounting step

title: What if the polls are wrong again?
statement: FiveThirtyEight's 2012 model called every state correctly, but its internal diagnostics gave only a slim chance of a perfect score (Florida was about 50/50). Correct calls can mask margin errors; 2012 polls overestimated Romney by about 3 points.
evidence_quote: Our internal diagnostics gave us only a slim chance of getting a perfect score.

title: Welcome to midterm silly season 🤡
statement: On Oct. 15, 2026 FLIPR forecast a D+7.8 House popular vote with an 80 percent prediction interval of roughly D+4 to D+12, leaving a 10 percent chance of an outcome beyond each end.
quantities: House popular vote forecast = D+7.8 points (Oct 15, 2026); 80% prediction interval = D+4 to D+12 points (Oct 15, 2026)
evidence_quote: This spans from roughly D +4 to D +12.

title: Welcome to midterm silly season 🤡
statement: By design, the error bars on FLIPR's national popular vote forecast narrow little in the final weeks, because little is learned about the national environment late in modern midterms. Its ingredients, such as presidential popularity, economic perceptions, enthusiasm and incumbency advantage, are detectable early, while individual races stay more dynamic as polls accumulate.
rationale: The cake goes into the oven early.
evidence_quote: The other thing I’d note is that the “error bars” on the chart aren’t narrowing much. That’s by design.

title: Welcome to midterm silly season 🤡
statement: Late in a midterm, most remaining uncertainty is measurement error, polls being wrong, rather than opinion changing; to the extent they are wrong, they have probably been wrong all along. Silver recommends mentally shifting all competitive races 3 to 4 points toward either party as a stress test.
quantities: stress-test shift = 3 to 4 points (all competitive races)
evidence_quote: Most of the remaining uncertainty in the election is this kind of uncertainty — about the polls being wrong, not about anything changing.

title: Welcome to midterm silly season 🤡
statement: The closing days of campaigns feature more pollster 'discipline', or herding, so the late poll dataset is slightly censored: pollsters are reluctant to publish outliers that defy the consensus.
evidence_quote: We’re probably getting a slightly censored dataset at this point, with pollsters reluctant to publish seeming outlier results that defy the consensus.

title: Welcome to midterm silly season 🤡
statement: Most elections, and nearly all midterms, lack late focal-point events. Exceptions with dynamic finishes were 2008 (financial crisis, debates) and 2016 (the Comey letter on Oct. 28, a canonical October Surprise). In 2024 the drama was concentrated in a 10-week summer window.
rationale: Midterms are hundreds of separate elections with no single focal point.
evidence_quote: Since they consist of what are technically hundreds of separate elections across the country, it’s hard to have focal point moments like you can get in a presidential year.

title: Welcome to midterm silly season 🤡
statement: How much polling error a party can absorb depends on where the error is located: in 2026 Democrats had less tolerance for an adverse error in the Midwest for the Senate.
evidence_quote: Most importantly, Democrats have less tolerance for a polling error working against them in the Midwest.

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
statement: In each of FLIPR's 40,000 daily simulations, the uniform national forecast error is drawn from a Student's t distribution, and additional random draws simulate correlated errors (e.g. systematic error among Hispanics) and uncorrelated local errors (e.g. one congressional district).
quantities: simulations per day = 40,000 simulations (FLIPR Deluxe)
rationale: Fat tails for national error.
evidence_quote: In each sim, FLIPR draws a random number from a Student’s t distribution to simulate uniform, national polling error.

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
statement: Silver Bulletin defines a 'normal-sized polling error' as 3 to 4 points in the same direction across states, about the margin by which polls underestimated Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024. Larger systematic errors are in the tails.
quantities: normal-sized systematic polling error = 3-4 points (Silver Bulletin rule of thumb)
evidence_quote: I’m choosing 3-4 points since that’s basically what we refer to as a “normal-sized polling error” around these parts.

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
statement: Splitting FLIPR Deluxe simulations into thirds by the national error draw: when the error is modest (within about 1.3 points), Democrats win the House 100 percent (238 seats) and the Senate 87.8 percent (52.4 seats). With an error against Democrats (R+1.4 or worse, averaging 3.5): House 81.4 percent (224), Senate 37.7 percent (49.7). With an error against Republicans (averaging 3.5): House 100 percent (254), Senate 99.3 percent (54.6).
quantities: Senate D prob, modest error = 87.8 percent (Oct 17, 2026); Senate D prob, error vs D = 37.7 percent (Oct 17, 2026); Senate D prob, error vs R = 99.3 percent (Oct 17, 2026); House D seats, modest/vsD/vsR = 238/224/254 seats (Oct 17, 2026); tercile boundary = about 1.3 points (national error)
evidence_quote: On average in this scenario, the forecast overestimates Democrats by 3.5 points

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
statement: FLIPR's probabilities reflect the estimated error of its blended forecasts (polls plus fundamentals, plus expert ratings in Deluxe), not just the error of the polling averages; Silver notes that 'polling errors' in this context are technically forecast errors.
