evidence_quote: The probabilities you see in FLIPR are based on the errors it estimates in these blended forecasts and not just the error associated with the polling averages on their own.

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
statement: FLIPR simulates regional and demographic polling errors without privileging any one, considering Midwestern underperformance by Democrats, as in 2016, alongside Southern underperformance, Hispanic overperformance, Midwestern overperformance and others. Even with national error held near zero, Senate win probabilities stay uncertain, for example Texas only rising from 71.5 to 76.0 percent for Talarico.
quantities: Talarico win prob default vs modest-error = 71.5 / 76.0 percent (Oct 17, 2026)
rationale: Congressional races are correlated but less than presidential ones.
evidence_quote: FLIPR does consider exactly this scenario, although it doesn’t privilege it.

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
statement: In Alaska, FLIPR explicitly plays out ranked-choice reallocations, so minor Republicans' votes mostly transfer to incumbent Dan Sullivan, making FLIPR more bearish on Peltola than models that look at first-round margins.
evidence_quote: I think this is because it’s explicitly playing out the RCV process when other models might not be.

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
statement: When polling averages are thin, as in South Dakota, the advanced FLIPR versions heavily hedge toward fundamentals rather than taking polls at face value.
evidence_quote: The more advanced versions of FLIPR heavily hedge toward the “fundamentals” in these cases

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
statement: Uniform-shift stress tests on Senate polling averages: as-is, Democrats 54-46; polls overrating Democrats by 2 points, 52-48 Democratic; by 3 points, a 50-50 tie; by 4 points, Republicans 52-48. Many narrow leads, as in the 2012 and 2016 presidential maps, make the outcome sensitive to small systematic errors.
quantities: Senate seats, 3-pt error vs D = 50 D seats (Oct 17, 2026)
evidence_quote: With a 3-point polling error, though, Maine and Texas turn into narrow GOP wins, and Democrats would top out at 50 seats.

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
statement: Republicans would need roughly a 5-point uniform error to make the House a toss-up in October 2026. Competitive House races are spread evenly across the map, so regional misses tend to offset when overall polls are right.
quantities: uniform error needed for House toss-up = about 5 points (Oct 2026)
evidence_quote: Republicans would need something like a 5-point uniform polling error to turn the House back into a toss-up

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
statement: Predicting polling error means predicting the behavior of pollsters, who are aware of past errors and adjust their methods.
evidence_quote: So in predicting polling error, in some sense you’re predicting the behavior of human beings and how they adjust to changing conditions in the polling landscape.

title: The good, bad and ugly outcomes in the Senate
statement: FLIPR counts certain independents toward Democratic control, such as Seth Bodnar in Montana.
evidence_quote: More likely in the form of independent Seth Bodnar — whom FLIPR counts toward Democratic control

title: My pet peeve about the polling error debate
statement: Benchmarking FLIPR's correlation structure: a Monte Carlo treating each Senate race as independent using Deluxe race probabilities gives Democrats 91 percent to win the Senate. Assuming perfect correlation gives the tipping-point state's probability, 72 percent in Texas. FLIPR Deluxe's 76 percent is much closer to perfect correlation than to independence.
quantities: independent-races Senate D prob = 91 percent (Oct 20, 2026); perfectly correlated Senate D prob = 72 percent (= Texas tipping point); FLIPR Deluxe Senate D prob = 76 percent (Oct 20, 2026)
rationale: Accounts for both national and regional correlated errors.
evidence_quote: So FLIPR Deluxe’s current 76 percent odds for Democrats are closer to the perfectly correlated scenario (72 percent) than the perfectly independent one (91 percent).

title: My pet peeve about the polling error debate
statement: In the Silver Bulletin pollster database (polls in the final three weeks of congressional, gubernatorial and presidential elections since 1998), there is almost zero correlation in the direction of polling error between cycles. Pollsters are about as likely to undercompensate as overcompensate for past errors, so there is no zig-zag pattern either.
rationale: Pollsters have strong incentives to calibrate toward unbiased results but polls are too imprecise to do so reliably.
evidence_quote: Instead, there’s almost literally zero correlation in polling error between cycles.

title: My pet peeve about the polling error debate
statement: Silver's simulation of random cycle-level polling error used a standard deviation of 2.8 points, matching the variance in the actual historical data. Random draws easily produce streaks such as seven straight cycles underestimating Republicans, which shows how narratives overfit to noise.
quantities: cycle-level polling error SD = 2.8 points (historical, used in simulation)
evidence_quote: A standard deviation of 2.8 points.

title: My pet peeve about the polling error debate
statement: FiveThirtyEight/Silver Bulletin forecasts treat the direction of systematic polling error as unpredictable because pollsters self-correct: the model need not 'fix' bias as long as pollsters are expected to recalibrate. Polls today are 'mini-models' as much as pure measurements. FLIPR does not play the guessing game on direction.
evidence_quote: A lot of the reason FLIPR and most of the other models regard polling bias as being unpredictable is because pollsters themselves have a lot of incentive to account and adjust for it.

title: My pet peeve about the polling error debate
statement: In the 2025 interim elections polls badly underestimated Democrats: Abigail Spanberger beat her Virginia polling average by 6 points and Mikie Sherrill beat hers in New Jersey by 9, one of the worst misses in a well-polled race, comparable to Collins in 2020.
quantities: Spanberger beat polls by = 6 points (VA gov 2025); Sherrill beat polls by = 9 points (NJ gov 2025)
evidence_quote: And in New Jersey, Mikie Sherrill beat her polls by 9 points

title: My pet peeve about the polling error debate
statement: The pollster database groups elections into two-year cycles; in this analysis non-November elections (off-year, specials, runoffs) were split into an 'interim' bucket, with a December runoff after a presidential election counting toward the next interim period. Table values are simple averages of all polls, so well-polled races weigh more.
evidence_quote: The data in this table is just a simple average of all polls in our pollster ratings database, so more well-polled races have more influence on it.

title: My pet peeve about the polling error debate
statement: Pollsters combat partisan nonresponse by matching to Census demographics, anchoring to past reported vote, tweaking likely-voter models, and sometimes herding or withholding outliers. Non-college and low-social-trust voters, who lean Republican, respond less. Enthusiasm cuts both ways, since enthusiastic respondents both answer polls and vote: it may explain El-Sayed's primary overestimate, while in 2014 the enthusiasm gap exceeded pollsters' expectations.
evidence_quote: They can match to Census Bureau demographics, or they can anchor to the past reported vote.

title: My pet peeve about the polling error debate
statement: Models that treated races as independent coin flips, giving Trump about 1 percent in 2016 versus FiveThirtyEight's roughly 30 percent, have died out. Most 2026 competitor models look reasonable to Silver, and the remaining differences are in how errors are modeled, how polls and fundamentals are blended, and how aggressively averages update.
evidence_quote: The models that wrongly treated races as a series of independent coin flips have died out, and deservedly so.

title: Fake polls are a real problem
statement: FLIPR takes its House, Senate and governor horse-race polls from The New York Times poll database, which is fast, comprehensive, vetted, and explicitly modeled on the old FiveThirtyEight schema and inclusion criteria Silver helped design. Silver Bulletin maintains its own databases for presidential approval, the generic ballot and certain other series. In 2024 it relied on the post-Silver FiveThirtyEight feed instead.
rationale: No point recreating work done the same way.
evidence_quote: The literal answer is that we take our polling data from The New York Times, subject occasionally to some manual additions and overrides.

title: Fake polls are a real problem
statement: Manual overrides on the NYT feed: 11 permanently banned pollsters (known or believed to have fabricated data or committed gross misconduct, e.g. Strategic Vision, Research 2000) are ignored; 'nonprofessional' DIY firms such as SoCal Strategies and ActiVote are excluded; Rasmussen Reports polls, not listed by the NYT, are added manually; and polls are occasionally added before NYT lists them, though Silver Bulletin generally waits a day or two in case a poll failed vetting.
quantities: permanently banned pollsters = 11 firms (Silver Bulletin list, Oct 2026)
evidence_quote: We have a list of 11 permanently banned pollsters

title: Fake polls are a real problem
statement: Silver Bulletin turns on a polling average for a race once there are three distinct polls from at least two distinct polling firms.
quantities: minimum polls for an average = 3 polls (from at least 2 firms)
evidence_quote: we turn on the average for a race once there are three distinct polls from at least two distinct polling firms.

title: Fake polls are a real problem
statement: New or unknown pollsters start with fairly low pollster ratings by default, and FLIPR has precautions against being overly influenced by any one poll; removing the fabricated Wedgewood polls left FLIPR's averages and forecasts basically unchanged.
evidence_quote: new/unknown pollsters start with fairly low ratings by default.

title: Fake polls are a real problem
statement: Silver Bulletin prefers to 'just plug it into the average', weighting established pollsters more, rather than subjectively filtering individual polls, which might reflect an aggregator's rooting interests. It avoids dissecting individual polls, with exceptions for top-rated independent firms like NYT/Siena.
rationale: Least-worst alternative; outlier attention is preferable to herding.
evidence_quote: But it’s probably the least-worst alternative versus applying some sort of subjective filter to polls

title: Fake polls are a real problem
statement: Statistical fraud detection: Strategic Vision's fabricated polls (exposed 2009) and Research 2000's (2010) showed far more of some trailing digits (e.g. 5, 7, 8, 9) than others, a canonical sign of forged results, since humans are bad at generating random numbers.
evidence_quote: Strategic Vision “polls” exhibited statistical patterns — namely, being far more likely to contain some trailing digits (such as 5, 7, 8 and 9) than others

title: Fake polls are a real problem
statement: The fabricated Wedgewood polls had a mild, inconsistent Democratic house effect of about 0.6 points versus Silver Bulletin averages computed as of the day before their final field date. They were often the first polls in sparsely polled races and favored progressive candidates.
quantities: Wedgewood house effect = about 0.6 points toward D (vs Silver Bulletin averages)
evidence_quote: their “polls” were about 0.6 points more favorable to the Democratic candidate on average.

title: Fake polls are a real problem
statement: Silver Bulletin computes retrospective polling averages for dates before its averages launch (FLIPR launched Aug. 11, 2026), and they closely resemble other aggregators' averages.
evidence_quote: For dates before then, I’ve used our retrospectively-calculated polling averages instead

title: Fake polls are a real problem
statement: New fake-poll risks include manipulating high-volume prediction markets through outlier or fake polls in sparsely surveyed races, discrediting the polling industry, and AI-assisted fabrication that may also defeat vetting.
evidence_quote: One of them is publishing fake polls to manipulate prediction markets.

title: Do these Senate-governor splits make sense?
statement: In midterms from 1998 to 2022, in states with both a Senate and governor race and at least one qualifying poll in the final three weeks, either both Democrats or both Republicans beat their polls in 68 percent of cases. FLIPR models this with a statewide error draw in each simulation affecting House, Senate and governor races in the state.
quantities: same-direction poll error rate, Senate vs governor = 68 percent (midterms 1998-2022)
evidence_quote: In 68 percent of these cases, either the two Democrats or the two Republicans overperformed their polls in both contests.

title: Do these Senate-governor splits make sense?
statement: Projected Senate-governor ticket splits do not narrow on Election Day: across midterms from 1998 to 2022 the average split projected by final polls was 17.3 points and the actual split 17.5, with the split larger than projected in 53 percent of cases. Regression shows adding Senate polling to governor polling, or vice versa, adds no meaningful predictive power for the final outcome.
quantities: average projected split = 17.3 points (midterms 1998-2022); average actual split = 17.5 points (midterms 1998-2022); share with larger split than projected = 53 percent (midterms 1998-2022)
evidence_quote: What’s not true, though, is that ticket splits get narrower on Election Day.

title: Do these Senate-governor splits make sense?
statement: The median gap in margin between same-state statewide contests (Senate, governor, at-large House) was about 25 points in 1990, about 13 in 2014 and 8 in 2022 (DDHQ data), and FLIPR projects about 6 in 2026. The median is used because individual splits can be huge, e.g. Vermont 2022.
quantities: median split 1990 = about 25 points (DDHQ); median split 2014 = about 13 points (DDHQ); median split 2022 = 8 points (DDHQ); median split 2026 projected = 6 points (FLIPR)
rationale: Nationalized politics.
evidence_quote: Based on FLIPR’s current projections, we expect statewide ticket-splitting to decrease even further, with a median gap of just six points in 2026.

title: Do these Senate-governor splits make sense?
statement: FLIPR uses Alaska polls that explicitly report post-RCV results as well as first-round polls. It projects first-round shares and simulates ranked-choice rounds, accounting for voters who do not rank every candidate and those who cross party lines, so a candidate projected at 47 percent in round one can still be a 96 percent favorite.
quantities: Kreiss-Tomkins first-round share = 47 percent (Oct 2026); Kreiss-Tomkins win prob = 96 percent (Oct 2026)
evidence_quote: some Alaska polls explicitly forecast the results after RCV, and FLIPR uses these too.

title: Do these Senate-governor splits make sense?
statement: FLIPR forecasts are rounded to one decimal place, so a displayed '100 percent' means greater than 99.95 percent.
evidence_quote: Our forecasts are rounded off to one decimal place, so her chances are greater than 99.95 percent, not necessarily exactly 100.

title: Do these Senate-governor splits make sense?
statement: FLIPR's fundamentals have no variable for a non-incumbent's ideology (e.g. El-Sayed's progressivism); for incumbents, party-loyalty scores from congressional votes capture bipartisanship, which predicts overperformance. Voter views on ideology appear to be priced into the polls instead.
evidence_quote: But we don’t make any similar calculation for non-incumbents.

title: Do these Senate-governor splits make sense?
statement: Example of large projected splits in FLIPR, October 2026: New Hampshire with Democrat Pappas winning Senate by about 10 and Republican Ayotte winning governor by about 10, a roughly 20-point split; Vermont with Balint D+32 for House and Republican Scott R+3.6 for governor at nearly 70 percent; Texas Senate D+2.9 versus governor about R+3; Iowa Senate D+1.4 versus governor D+8.4.
quantities: NH projected split = nearly 20 points (Oct 2026); VT governor projected margin = R+3.6 points (Oct 2026)
evidence_quote: the model expects nearly 20 points of ticket splitting in New Hampshire

title: Do these Senate-governor splits make sense?
statement: In late October 2026, FLIPR's topline had barely moved for weeks given stable polling and a dearth of new polls relative to past cycles, so most remaining uncertainty was potential polling error rather than late shifts.
evidence_quote: at this point, most of the remaining uncertainty in our forecast comes down to potential polling error, not late shifts in the polls themselves.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: The point of building a model is to set clear rules ahead of time so you do not rely on gut or ad hoc mid-stream assumptions; FLIPR gives an independent daily opinion from rules locked months earlier. Silver keeps a list of possible changes for next cycle rather than making subjective in-season adjustments.
rationale: Avoid hedging and herding during 'silly season'.
evidence_quote: the whole point of building a model, in some sense, is to set clear rules ahead of time so you don’t have to trust your gut or make ad hoc assumptions in midstream.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: On Oct. 25, 2026 FLIPR and Polymarket Senate race probabilities correlated at 0.99. Silver estimates that plugging Polymarket's race odds into FLIPR's correlation structure would yield 65 to 70 percent for Democrats, close to Polymarket's topline, versus FLIPR's 75, so the disagreement is about individual races, not total uncertainty. FLIPR appeared to lead markets by a couple of days after Labor Day, and markets may have reacted to FLIPR's launch.
quantities: FLIPR-Polymarket race correlation = .99 correlation (Oct 25, 2026); FLIPR Senate D prob = 75 percent (Oct 25, 2026); Polymarket Senate D prob = about 2/3 probability (Oct 25, 2026)
evidence_quote: Overall, there’s far more agreement than disagreement; the correlation coefficient is .99.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: FLIPR does not use early-voting data, except insofar as pollsters' assumptions about early voting are reflected in polls. Silver is skeptical of early-vote analysis, though Joel Wertheimer argues it can help if focused on which party turns out unlikely voters.
evidence_quote: markets may be building in some information — or assumptions — based on early voting data, something that FLIPR doesn’t really look at.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: Prediction markets tend to become more confident as elections approach. Silver argues this misapplies the time-decay principle: late in a modern midterm most uncertainty is whether polls were right all along, which does not shrink until results arrive, and FLIPR assumes little late poll movement, an assumption tweaked in the 2026 rebuild.
evidence_quote: Most of the remaining uncertainty in the race isn’t about how polls will change over the final week-and-a-half, but rather about whether there will be another major polling error again

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: With a D+9.5 likely-voter generic ballot (about a 12-point swing from 2024), FLIPR's simple fundamentals for the red-state tranche were: Alaska R+0.2, Florida R+1.1, Iowa R+1.2 (about R+1), Ohio R+1.6, Texas R+1.9, with a big gap to Kansas (blended R+4.4). Minnesota was D+13 in the generic-ballot baseline.
quantities: LV generic ballot = D+9.5 points (Oct 25, 2026); Alaska simple fundamentals = R+0.2 points (Oct 25); Texas simple fundamentals = R+1.9 points (Oct 25); Kansas blended fundamentals = R+4.4 points (Oct 25); Minnesota baseline = D+13 points (Oct 25)
evidence_quote: Alaska is only R +0.2, Florida R +1.1, Iowa R +1.2, Ohio R +1.6, and Texas R +1.9.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: Because fancy fundamentals credit past winning margins only to incumbents, FLIPR may underrate strong non-incumbent candidates with 'proof of concept': Sherrod Brown (won Ohio by almost 7 in 2018, lost by only 3.6 in 2024 while outrunning Harris) and Mary Peltola. Races with appointed incumbents, like Husted in Ohio, are treated as open seats.
evidence_quote: Our “fancy fundamentals” calculation incorporates past winning margins for incumbents, although not for non-incumbents like Brown.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: FLIPR lacks a mechanism for a non-incumbent's ideology; in Michigan, El-Sayed's fundraising made fancy fundamentals better than his polls, and Silver thinks accounting for his ideology would bring FLIPR close to Polymarket.
evidence_quote: FLIPR doesn’t really have any mechanism to account for El-Sayed’s progressivism, even though I think it would be reasonable to do so.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: Whenever polls and fundamentals disagree, FLIPR raises the race's uncertainty; for example Minnesota had an 11 percent chance of a Republican win and was the tipping point 7 percent of the time despite a D+13 baseline.
quantities: Minnesota R win prob = 11 percent (Oct 25, 2026); Minnesota tipping-point prob = 7 percent (Oct 25, 2026)
evidence_quote: Whenever there’s a disagreement between polls and “fundamentals,” uncertainty tends to be higher, and FLIPR accounts for this.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: Internal campaign polls carry a typical 3 to 4-point bias toward their sponsor, so in FLIPR logic a Republican internal showing the Republican up only 2 is evidence of a toss-up, and a candidate's own internal showing him up 1 is worse news for him than opposing internals showing him down 2 or 3.
quantities: typical internal poll bias = 3-4 points (toward sponsor)
evidence_quote: In FLIPR logic, that’s actually a worse poll for him than Republican internals showing him trailing by 2 or 3.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: In Florida, partisan lean scores lag reality because domestic migrants are heavily Republican and voter registration keeps trending red. Silver names accounting for domestic migration trends in partisan lean as one of the more obvious future model improvements.
evidence_quote: One of the more obvious improvements in our model in future years would be to account for these domestic migration trends in our partisan lean scores.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: Highly inelastic states with few swing voters, such as Louisiana, Mississippi and South Carolina with large Black populations and conservative evangelical whites, make big Democratic overperformance unlikely; Silver judged 3 to 5 percent more grounded than markets' 8 to 13 percent for Louisiana and Mississippi. New Hampshire, by contrast, is one of the most elastic states.
evidence_quote: Louisiana and Mississippi are extremely inelastic states, with very few true swing voters.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: FLIPR assumes independents Dan Osborn (Nebraska) and Seth Bodnar (Montana) would caucus with Democrats. Third-party candidates get asymmetric, feast-or-famine distributions. In Montana, a three-way race with a Democrat taking 22.5 percent, the forecast is assumption-driven and volatile, hinging on tactical voting.
quantities: Bankhead projected share = 22.5 percent (Montana Senate, Oct 2026); Alme projected margin over Bodnar = 8 points (Oct 2026)
evidence_quote: FLIPR builds in some slightly complex assumptions about third-party candidates in cases like this, seeing them as having asymmetric distributions that are a little bit feast-or-famine.

title: Let’s talk shop about every Senate race
statement: Alaska and Maine are among the states least correlated with national outcomes, so a party can win them on a bad night or lose them on a good one.
evidence_quote: Alaska, up in the Arctic Circle, is one of the least correlated states with the Lower 48.

title: The 83 remotely competitive House races, according to FLIPR
statement: FLIPR defaults to fundamentals more in House races than in Senate races because House races have fewer reliable polls; many are partisan or small-sample, and FLIPR weights these less. In NY-17, a Harris district, Lawler trailing by only 1.1 in polls still had just a 17 percent chance.
quantities: Lawler win prob = 17 percent (NY-17, Oct 27, 2026)
evidence_quote: Generally speaking, FLIPR defaults to the “fundamentals” more in the House because there are fewer reliable polls than in the Senate.

title: The 83 remotely competitive House races, according to FLIPR
statement: On Oct. 27, 2026 FLIPR Deluxe gave Democrats a 95 percent chance of winning the House, with an average projection of 239 Democratic seats to 196, a net Democratic gain of 24, and a national popular vote of about D+8. Since late August the model had added one Solid D and 14 Likely D seats, and removed three Solid R and nine Likely R seats.
quantities: House D win prob = 95 percent (Oct 27, 2026); projected D seats = 239 seats (Oct 27, 2026); projected net D gain = 24 seats (Oct 27, 2026)
evidence_quote: we’re well past FLIPR’s average projection of Democrats netting 24 House seats and ending up with a total of 239 to Republicans’ 196.

title: The 83 remotely competitive House races, according to FLIPR
statement: FLIPR's categories are algorithmic: Solid is above 95 percent for one party, Likely 75 to 95 percent, and a toss-up is any race where neither party reaches 60 percent. Only four House toss-ups remained, which shows FLIPR does not hedge into toss-ups.
quantities: Solid threshold = 95 percent; Likely range = 75-95 percent; toss-up threshold = 60 percent
evidence_quote: Our categories are determined algorithmically — a “toss-up” is any race where neither party has a 60 percent chance of winning.

title: The 83 remotely competitive House races, according to FLIPR
statement: FLIPR's House seat distribution in late October 2026 was asymmetric, with a long right tail of possible Democratic gains; the asymmetry is clearer in Classic and Lite, which bake in fewer expectations, than in Deluxe.
rationale: Many Likely R seats could flip in a wave.
evidence_quote: If you look carefully at FLIPR’s seat distribution chart, you might notice it’s slightly asymmetric.

title: The 83 remotely competitive House races, according to FLIPR
statement: The battleground expanding late in a race, with seats moving from Likely R toward competitive, is a hallmark of a wave election.
evidence_quote: The battleground expanding late in the race is a hallmark of a wave election.

title: The 83 remotely competitive House races, according to FLIPR
statement: In toss-up districts like WI-1, KY-6 and MT-1, FLIPR discounts Democratic polling leads with fundamentals; for example, WI-1's D+2.4 fundamentals offset incumbent Bryan Steil's 3-point polling lead to make a toss-up.
quantities: WI-1 fundamentals = D+2.4 points (Oct 2026)
evidence_quote: FLIPR discounts those with the fundamentals and still gives Republicans a slight edge in all three.

title: 13 maps for the morning after the midterms
statement: FLIPR forecasts 506 races per cycle in 2026. In about 20 percent of simulations, Senate control comes down to exactly one state. Republicans hold the House in about 1 in 20 simulations, and Democrats win the Senate but not the House in about 1 in 1,000.
quantities: races forecast = 506 races (2026); sims where Senate decided by one state = about 20 percent (Oct 31, 2026); sims with R House hold = around 1 in 20 probability (Oct 31, 2026); sims with D Senate but R House = about 1 in 1000 probability (Oct 31, 2026)
evidence_quote: in about 20 percent of FLIPR simulations, control of the Senate will come down to exactly one state.

title: 13 maps for the morning after the midterms
statement: Senate and gubernatorial races within a state are deliberately correlated in FLIPR's simulations, so a strong Senate candidate's overperformance tends to pull the same party's governor candidate along in that simulation.
evidence_quote: Note also that Senate and gubernatorial races are deliberately correlated in FLIPR

title: 13 maps for the morning after the midterms
statement: Conditional on a low-probability headline outcome, such as Republicans holding the House, FLIPR's simulations are typically disasters for the same party across the board and rank around the 95th upset percentile, reflecting correlated national error.
evidence_quote: conditional upon Republicans holding the House, everything else is likely to be a disaster for Democrats, too.

title: 13 maps for the morning after the midterms
statement: Silver's 'upset percentile' for a simulation scores each race by how unlikely the winner was: a 49 percent winner earns 1 point, a 1 percent winner 49 points. Branch averages are weighted 50 percent Senate, 25 percent House and 25 percent governors, then ranked as a percentile among 40,000 simulations, with no adjustment for the map's overall direction.
quantities: Senate weight in upset score = 50 percent; House weight = 25 percent; governor weight = 25 percent
rationale: With 506 races, some upsets are almost certain.
evidence_quote: A race where a candidate who had a 49 percent chance of prevailing wins gets 1 Upset Point; a race where a candidate who had a 1 percent chance pulls a rabbit out of their hat is worth 49 Upset Points.

title: 13 maps for the morning after the midterms
statement: FLIPR has no provision for irregularities in tallying or certifying the vote. For 'morning after' analysis, Silver applied state-specific margin thresholds for when a result would be clear by Wednesday morning: about 0.5 points in fast-counting states like North Carolina, up to 3 points in slow-counting states like Alaska and California.
quantities: decisiveness threshold, fast-count state = 0.5 points (e.g. North Carolina); decisiveness threshold, slow-count state = up to 3 points (Alaska, California)
evidence_quote: There’s no provision in FLIPR that accounts for irregularities in tallying the vote.

title: 13 maps for the morning after the midterms
statement: At FiveThirtyEight, showing readers random cross-sections of simulations backfired: readers scrolled to weird maps and used them to doubt the forecast. In 2024 the single most frequent simulated map occurred exactly.
evidence_quote: Our customers tended to scroll through the simulations until they’d encounter one of the weirder maps

title: Where polls and fundamentals clash
statement: FLIPR's rule for blending polls with fundamentals: the more polling a race has, and the more recent and reliable the surveys, the more it defaults to the polls. In sparsely polled red states it hedges heavily toward fundamentals or lands between the two.
evidence_quote: Its rule is pretty simple: the more polling there is, and the more recent and reliable the surveys, the more it defaults to them.

title: Where polls and fundamentals clash
statement: FLIPR uses the generic ballot within 'simple fundamentals' even though it is poll-based, because it is the best measurement of the national environment, fits a partisan climate with predictable state patterns, and avoids the idiosyncrasies of state polling.
evidence_quote: But the generic ballot is our best measurement of the national political environment

title: Where polls and fundamentals clash
statement: On Nov. 2, 2026 FLIPR simple fundamentals: Georgia D+6, North Carolina D+7, Michigan D+9, Maine D+17; Alaska, Ohio, Iowa and Texas R+0.3 to R+2. Fancy fundamentals: Iowa D+1, Ohio D+2, Texas D+8, Maine R+7 (Collins), Alaska worse for Peltola after her scandal flag was activated. Blended Maine D+4; blended Texas, Iowa, Ohio, Alaska and Florida all R+3 to D+3.
quantities: generic ballot = D+8.9 points (Nov 2, 2026); LV-adjusted generic ballot = D+9.2 points (Nov 2, 2026); Maine simple fundamentals = D+17 points (Nov 2); Maine fancy fundamentals = R+7 points (Nov 2); Maine blended = D+4 points (Nov 2); Texas fancy fundamentals = D+8 points (Nov 2)
evidence_quote: Alaska, Ohio, Iowa, and Texas range from R +0.3 to R +2 on the simple fundamentals.

title: Where polls and fundamentals clash
statement: On Nov. 2, 2026 FLIPR's Senate win probability for Democrats was 79 percent in Lite (polls only), 78.7 percent in Classic (adding fundamentals), and highest in Deluxe (adding expert ratings). Lite still gave Republicans a 10 percent chance to hold the House because it accounts for systematic and regional polling misses.
quantities: Lite Senate D prob = 79 percent (Nov 2, 2026); Classic Senate D prob = 78.7 percent (Nov 2, 2026); Lite R House hold prob = 10 percent (Nov 2, 2026)
evidence_quote: Democrats’ Senate win probability in our polls-only Lite model — 79 percent — only drops to 78.7 percent after the fundamentals are incorporated in our Classic model.

title: Where polls and fundamentals clash
statement: Fancy fundamentals' candidate-specific factors are incumbency, individual fundraising, elected experience and scandals. Ideology per se is not used, though party-loyalty scores from congressional voting are. Scandal flags can be switched on during a campaign, as Peltola's was late in 2026.
evidence_quote: We don’t account for candidate ideology per-se, but we do calculate party loyalty scores based on congressional voting records.

title: Where polls and fundamentals clash
statement: The polls-versus-fundamentals comparison includes only races with at least three polls from two unique pollsters, matching the threshold for publishing a polling average.
evidence_quote: Note that we’re only including races that have at least three polls from two unique pollsters in this analysis.

title: Where polls and fundamentals clash
statement: In most battleground Senate races in November 2026, the Democrat's polling lead was within a normal-sized polling error of flipping, so FLIPR's base case of a 53-47 Democratic Senate could easily become 51-49 or a Republican hold.
evidence_quote: It wouldn’t take much for FLIPR’s base case — a 53/47 Democratic Senate majority — to turn into 51/49 or even a Republican hold.

title: FINAL FLIPR 2026 midterm election forecast
statement: FLIPR models House, Senate and gubernatorial elections jointly in each simulation, enabling joint outcome probabilities. Final 2026 values: Democratic sweep 82.2 percent, Democratic House with Republican Senate 14.2 percent, Republican sweep 3.4 percent, Republican House with Democratic Senate 0.2 percent.
quantities: D sweep = 82.2 percent (final); D House / R Senate = 14.2 percent (final); R sweep = 3.4 percent (final); R House / D Senate = 0.2 percent (final)
evidence_quote: FLIPR models House, Senate and gubernatorial elections jointly, meaning that we can calculate the probability of things like Republicans holding the Senate but losing the House.

title: FINAL FLIPR 2026 midterm election forecast
statement: Topline numbers are typically based on 40,000 simulations and include a small amount of sampling error.
quantities: simulations = 40,000 simulations (FLIPR topline)
evidence_quote: They are typically based on 40,000 simulations and include a small amount of sampling error.

title: FINAL FLIPR 2026 midterm election forecast
statement: Summary of FLIPR's polling averages: they account for registered versus likely voters and house effects, weight more reliable polls more heavily, and apply a 'timeline adjustment' revising outdated polls toward generic-ballot trends. FLIPR uses an LV-adjusted generic ballot.
evidence_quote: They also include a “timeline adjustment”, where outdated polls are revised to reflect trends in the generic ballot.

title: FINAL FLIPR 2026 midterm election forecast
statement: Final 2026 Senate polling averages in battlegrounds: Texas D+3.3, Ohio D+3, Michigan D+4.9, Maine D+3.9, Iowa D+1.1, Kansas Democrat up about 4. At launch in August the Senate was near a toss-up; by the final update Democrats' Senate odds were just a few points below their House odds at launch.
quantities: Texas polling average = D+3.3 points (final); Michigan polling average = D+4.9 points (final)
evidence_quote: Democratic candidates lead in our polling averages of every major battleground state, including Texas (D +3.3), Ohio (D +3), Michigan (D +4.9), Maine (D +3.9), and Iowa (D +1.1).

quantities: D governorship majority prob = 90.2 percent (final); tie prob = 5.8 percent (final); population with D governor = 231.2 million (projected)

statement: Final Kansas governor polling average influence scores: AtlasIntel (2,038 LV, Oct 28-Nov 1) 3.25; NYT/Siena (736 LV) 2.37; YouGov (2,085 LV) 1.96; Emerson (800 LV) 1.92; Washington Post (801 LV) 1.81; Survey 160 (1,267 LV) 1.76; SSRS (838 LV, Oct 20-26) 1.02; Global Strategy Group, a Democratic partisan pollster (600 LV), 0.79; co/efficient (Sept 8-10) 0.11; YouGov (Sept 24-Oct 4) 0.10. Weights decay steeply with age once newer polls exist.
quantities: AtlasIntel influence = 3.25 influence score (KS gov final); September poll influence = 0.10-0.11 influence score (KS gov final)
rationale: Recency weighting.

title: FLIPR 2026 Governors forecast

At 50-50 Republicans control via the vice president, and Democratic seats include aligned independents.

Final values: Texas tipping point 12 percent (VPI 1.0, elasticity 1.04), Maine 12 (VPI 12.0, 1.07), Ohio 11 (1.8, 1.02), Kansas 10 (6.7, 1.06), Michigan 10 (1.6, 1.00), Iowa 9 (4.6, 1.05), Minnesota 7 (2.1, 0.94), Alaska 7 (VPI 17.1, elasticity 1.27), New Hampshire 4 (4.6, 1.13).

The Senate tipping point was about D+4.5.
quantities: Senate 50/50 point = D+4 to +5 points (final); D win prob at D+6-7 = 83.4 percent (final)

statement: The final Senate polls-versus-fundamentals table shows blended fundamentals that are almost exactly a 47/53 to 49/51 weighted average of simple and fancy fundamentals in every state where they differ. Examples: Alaska simple R+1.2, fancy R+5.2, blended R+3.3; Georgia D+6.0, D+17.8, D+12.1; Kansas R+7.8, R+1.3, R+4.4; Maine D+16.4, R+6.9, D+4.3; Massachusetts D+42.1, D+34.1, D+37.9. That implies a simple-fundamentals weight of about 0.46 to 0.49 for Senate races in 2026.

rationale: Consistent with methodology saying simple fundamentals get almost half the weight.

statement: Final Senate polls versus blended fundamentals show how far polls diverged: Kansas polls D+4.1 versus blended R+4.4; Florida polls R+6.1 versus blended R+0.0; Iowa D+1.1 versus R+0.0; Maine D+3.9 versus D+4.3; Michigan D+4.9 versus D+9.9; Louisiana R+4.0 versus R+10.7; Alaska D+3.1 versus R+3.3.
quantities: Kansas polls vs blended = D+4.1 vs R+4.4 points (final); Michigan polls vs blended = D+4.9 vs D+9.9 points (final)

title: FLIPR 2026 Senate forecast
statement: Race-level poll influence scores on the final Texas Senate average: NYT/Siena (1,215 LV) 2.51, AtlasIntel (1,678 adults) 2.01, Emerson (500 LV) 1.84, Trafalgar (a Republican-classified partisan pollster, 1,089 LV) 1.79, Research Co. (450 LV) 1.70, Quantus 1.22, YouGov (2,138 LV) 1.07, Beacon/Shaw (Oct 15-19) 1.04. Older and lower-rated polls get progressively less influence.
quantities: NYT/Siena influence = 2.51 influence score (TX Senate final); YouGov influence = 1.07 influence score (TX Senate final)

title: FLIPR 2026 Senate forecast
statement: For ranked-choice contests, the most-competitive-races chart shows the average simulated margin after the final round, while the full-slate table shows first-round vote shares. Margin charts show 10th to 90th percentile intervals, covering 80 percent of outcomes.
quantities: interval coverage = 80 percent (10th-90th percentile)

title: FLIPR 2026 Senate forecast
statement: FLIPR draws most election polls from the NYT poll database but collects generic ballot and congressional approval polls itself. It includes polls from a few pollsters the NYT excludes and excludes surveys from banned or non-scientific firms.
evidence_quote: We also include polls from a few pollsters that The New York Times excludes from their database, and exclude surveys from firms we ban or that don’t meet our standards for being scientific surveys.

title: How to judge an election model
statement: Probabilistic forecasts should be judged by calibration over a large sample of true out-of-sample predictions; for example, of 100 events forecast at 30 percent, 27 to 34 occurring is good. Backtesting does not count, since any competent model fits past data and may be overfit. Silver considers bragging about backtested results a negative sign compared with explaining why a model makes structural sense.
rationale: Overfitting to random features of past data.
evidence_quote: Backtesting doesn’t count.

title: How to judge an election model
statement: Over the 18-year FiveThirtyEight/Silver Bulletin track record of published out-of-sample forecasts, sports forecasts were extremely well-calibrated, while politics forecasts were well-calibrated but somewhat underconfident, with too few upsets relative to model expectations. Significance is hard to assess because polling errors are correlated across states.
quantities: track record length = 18 years (2008-2026)
evidence_quote: Our politics forecasts were pretty well-calibrated too, although actually a bit underconfident: there were actually too few upsets relative to what our models expected.

title: How to judge an election model
statement: Calibration alone is insufficient: a model forecasting everything at 50/50 is perfectly calibrated but useless, so discrimination (e.g. Brier score) also matters. Under a Bayesian view, a very low-probability event occurring (e.g. 0.03 percent) is much more damaging to a model than a 30 percent event.
evidence_quote: A 0.03 percent chance happening is much more suspect for your model than a 30 percent hitting.

title: How to judge an election model
statement: A model can also be judged by whether betting on it would have made money against markets and consensus. In 2016, with FiveThirtyEight giving Trump about 1 in 3 and markets offering 5-1 or 6-1, the model implied a large Trump bet. In 2026 FLIPR led Polymarket's Senate odds over time, reaching the same place faster.
evidence_quote: If you trusted our model in 2016, you should actually have made a large bet on Trump

title: How to judge an election model
statement: A well-constructed model responds proportionally, in magnitude and direction, to new evidence. For example, a set of very strong NYT/Siena polls raised Democratic Senate odds about 2 points, reasonable because odds were already favorable and NYT/Siena was expected to lean somewhat Democratic.
quantities: Senate odds change from NYT/Siena batch = about 2 percentage points (Nov 1-2, 2026)
evidence_quote: The third thing I always look at is whether a model responds proportionally to new evidence.

title: How to judge an election model
statement: To tell luck from skill, test the model's structural hypotheses against results, for example that incumbency matters less, that midterm state errors are correlated less than in presidential years, and that governor races are less partisan. Judge margins, not just calls: a 1-point loss where the model was confident is a bad forecast even if the call was right.
evidence_quote: For all of this, by the way, margins ought to matter and not just the final calls.

title: How to judge an election model
statement: Silver's pre-registered list of possible FLIPR changes: (1) treat polling errors as persistent for specific candidates such as Collins, against which he has a strong prior; (2) a fancier undecided-voter adjustment by state lean; (3) credit WAR or past margins for non-incumbents; (4) include non-individual fundraising sources; (5) account for candidate ideology; (6) improve partisan lean for midterm versus presidential electorates, registration and migration; (7) remove the expert-ratings layer; (8) force the House popular vote estimate closer to the generic ballot, currently 1 to 1.5 points apart by design; (9) use early voting, which would be a beast; (10) de-emphasize polling generally. Changes 1, 2, 4 and 10 would likely help Republicans in 2026 and 3, 5, 8 and 9 Democrats.
quantities: House popular vote vs generic ballot gap = 1-1.5 points (intentional, 2026)
rationale: Keeping a list ahead of time avoids being overly results-driven and fighting the last war.
evidence_quote: I always think it’s helpful to keep a mental list of these ahead of time so you’re not too overly driven by results and wind up fighting the last war.

title: How to judge an election model
statement: FLIPR moved slightly toward fundamentals in its 2026 rebuild but remains truer to polls than some competitors, especially for the national environment. Silver warns that models with strong fundamentals that override polls are easy to overfit and have a middling-to-poor track record.
evidence_quote: models that make stronger assumptions about fundamentals and let them override polls are easy to overfit, and frankly have a middling-to-poor track record.

title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
statement: FLIPR's prior formula, based on all midterms since 1948, maps a presidential net approval of -20 to a national environment of about D+9, which matched the 2026 generic ballot and is similar to Democrats' 8.6-point House popular vote margin in 2018.
quantities: net approval input = -20 points (Trump, Nov 2026); implied national environment = D+9 points (prior formula)
evidence_quote: If Trump’s net approval ratings are -20, then our formula based on all midterms since 1948 would peg the national environment at D +9

title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
statement: In the final FLIPR Deluxe forecast, treating race outcomes as independent would have given Republicans just a 5 percent chance of holding the Senate; with nationally and regionally correlated errors it was 18 percent.
quantities: R Senate odds if independent = 5 percent (final forecast); R Senate odds, FLIPR = 18 percent (final forecast)
evidence_quote: If you were to treat FLIPR Deluxe simulations as a simple Monte Carlo simulation, where the outcome in each race was independent, then Republicans’ winning odds would be just 5 percent.

title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
statement: Sorting Senate states by FLIPR's projected margin, the final tipping-point state was Ohio, with Brown +3.4; a uniform Democratic underperformance of 3.3 points would still yield a Senate majority. FLIPR's final Senate win probability was about 80 percent in each of Lite, Classic and Deluxe.
quantities: tipping-point margin = 3.4 points (Ohio, final); final Senate D prob = about 80 percent (all versions)
evidence_quote: the tipping-point state is Ohio, where Sherrod Brown is forecasted to win by 3.4 points.

title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
statement: In practice FLIPR adds about a point or two to Democrats' raw polling average in blue states and subtracts the same in red states, consistent with recent polling errors. In effect it assumes red-state polls somewhat overrate Democrats, except where strong candidate-quality factors such as in Texas and Maine counteract partisanship.
quantities: typical partisan pull on polls = 1-2 points (toward state lean)
evidence_quote: In general, the model adds a point or two to Democrats’ raw polling average in blue states, and subtracts the same amount in red states.

title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
statement: FLIPR's final House popular vote projection was D+7.9, more conservative than its LV-adjusted generic ballot of D+9.3 for technical reasons such as turnout weighting. Background conditions alone (an average 7.5-point midterm swing from 2024) would imply about D+5; FLIPR forecast a 10.5-point swing.
quantities: final House popular vote forecast = D+7.9 points (Nov 3, 2026); final LV generic ballot = D+9.3 points (Nov 3, 2026); background-only environment = roughly D+5 points (7.5-pt avg swing); FLIPR projected swing = 10.5 points (from 2024)
evidence_quote: Its projection of the House popular vote, which is slightly different and more conservative than its generic ballot estimate, is D +7.9.

title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
statement: Some pollsters worried that voters were misreporting past Trump votes because he had become unpopular; if so, polls weighting to recalled past vote could overrate Republicans by a point or two by miscounting Trump voters as Harris or other voters.
quantities: possible past-vote weighting bias = a point or two points toward R (2026)
evidence_quote: If so, polls that weight toward past vote recall could be overrating Republicans by a point or two

title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
statement: FLIPR does not consider most 'other signals' such as primary turnout, special election results, early voting, and party spending or behavior; individual-contributor fundraising is the exception. Silver weighs them informally. For early vote, he favors looking at whether parties turn out unlikely voters and at state experts with strong track records.
rationale: Individually unreliable, though possibly informative collectively.
evidence_quote: FLIPR doesn’t really consider most of these, other than fundraising from individual contributors

title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
statement: Midterms usually trend steadily against one party rather than see-sawing (Republicans 2006 and 2026, Democrats 2010 and 2014), and sometimes, as in 1994 and 2014, the losing party does even worse than polls; counterexamples like 2022 are rare and may reflect small samples.
evidence_quote: Instead of the back-and-forth that you can get in a presidential year, usually things just get continually worse for one party

title: It's Judgment Day for Trump (and for pollsters)
statement: In 2026 the generic ballot tracked Trump's approval nearly one-for-one. Only 20 percent strongly approved and almost half strongly disapproved. A late uptick in approval came mostly from weak disapprovers moving to weak approval, as happens when partisans 'come home' near elections.
quantities: strong approval = 20 percent (Nov 2026)
evidence_quote: Only 20 percent of voters strongly approve of his performance in office.

title: Who’s ahead on the generic congressional ballot?
statement: The final 2026 Silver Bulletin generic ballot average, frozen Nov. 3, 2026, was Democrats 51.8 percent and Republicans 43.0 percent, a D+8.8 margin.
quantities: final D share = 51.8 percent (Nov 3, 2026); final R share = 43.0 percent (Nov 3, 2026); final margin = D+8.8 points (Nov 3, 2026)
evidence_quote: Democrats ended with 51.8 percent support on the generic congressional ballot to Republicans’ 43.0 percent.

title: Who’s ahead on the generic congressional ballot?
statement: The default generic ballot average combines polls of adults, registered voters and likely voters. When a pollster releases multiple versions, it prefers likely voters, then registered voters, then adults, because the target is people who plan to vote.
evidence_quote: If a pollster releases multiple versions of the same survey, we use the likely voter version before the registered voter version.

title: Who’s ahead on the generic congressional ballot?
statement: Each generic ballot poll gets an 'influence' score from its pollster rating, sample size, recency and how often the pollster publishes; recent or large polls from mediocre pollsters can outweigh better-rated ones. Weight is divided among a pollster's multiple recent surveys, and daily tracking polls are adjusted so interviews are not double-counted.
rationale: No single pollster should dominate.
evidence_quote: Each poll gets an “influence” score based on its pollster rating, its sample size, its recency, and how often a pollster is publishing numbers.

title: Who’s ahead on the generic congressional ballot?
statement: Final 2026 generic ballot influence scores for the top polls included AtlasIntel (3,566 adults, influence 1.47, D 56-41), TIPP (1,158 LV, 1.37), NYT/Siena (3,494 LV, 1.32), Echelon Insights (3,644 LV, 1.18), Cygnal (1,500 LV, 1.15), Emerson (1,000 LV, 1.09), Zogby, Marist and NBC/Hart (1,000 RV, 0.95).
quantities: AtlasIntel influence = 1.47 influence score (final week 2026); NYT/Siena influence = 1.32 influence score (final weeks 2026); NBC/Hart RV influence = 0.95 influence score (final week 2026)

title: Who’s ahead on the generic congressional ballot?
statement: State-level generic ballot benchmarks combine the generic ballot average with each state's partisan lean and elasticity, shown under four scenarios: the current generic ballot, a neutral environment (0), Democrats gaining 5 points, and Republicans gaining 5 points.
quantities: scenario shift = 5 points (benchmark scenarios)
evidence_quote: We show four versions of these benchmarks: one based on the current generic ballot, one assuming a neutral political environment (generic ballot = 0)

title: Who’s ahead on the generic congressional ballot?
statement: Silver Bulletin provides retrospective generic ballot averages for every cycle from 1994 to 2024, calculated by applying the current methodology and pollster ratings to past polls, as a downloadable XLSX ('Generic Topline All Cycles'), along with a download of every 2026 generic ballot poll in its database.
quantities: historical coverage start = 1994 year (retrospective generic ballot averages)
evidence_quote: Note that these are calculated retrospectively for previous cycles based on our current methodology and pollster ratings.

title: Who’s ahead on the generic congressional ballot?
statement: The generic ballot chart's shaded bands show where 90 percent of polls are projected to fall.
quantities: band coverage = 90 percent of polls (chart)

title: How popular is Donald Trump?
statement: For the presidential approval average, when a pollster releases multiple versions, Silver Bulletin prefers the all-adult version, then registered voters, then likely voters, because all Americans have a say in how popular the president is. This is the opposite of the generic ballot preference.
rationale: Approval measures the whole public, not just voters.
evidence_quote: If a pollster releases multiple versions of the same survey, we use the all-adult version of the poll before the registered voter version.

title: How popular is Donald Trump?
statement: Silver Bulletin also publishes approval averages restricted to RV/LV polls, a better gauge for midterm performance, and to all-adult polls, plus strong versus somewhat approval. For pollsters that do not ask intensity, the strong/somewhat split is prorated so it lines up with the topline.
evidence_quote: a handful of pollsters don’t ask about strong versus soft approval, so we prorate the averages

title: How popular is Donald Trump?
statement: As of Nov. 4, 2026 Trump's approval was 38.3 percent and disapproval about 59 percent, after an all-time low of 36.3 percent; 21 percent strongly approved and nearly 49 percent strongly disapproved.

evidence_quote: Donald Trump’s approval rating recently hit an all time low of 36.3 percent.

evidence_quote: We’re tracking how the public feels about Trump’s handling of four topics: the economy, immigration, trade and tariffs, and the cost of living.

title: How popular is Donald Trump?
statement: Silver Bulletin provides retrospectively calculated daily approval averages for every president since 1945 (Truman onward) as a downloadable 'Historical Approval Averages' XLSX, plus a download of every Trump approval poll in its database.

evidence_quote: Note that these are calculated retrospectively; Substack wasn’t around during the Eisenhower administration.
